It decks the earth and cheers our path, As through the world we go; Unlike the buds that droop and die, It leaves us not in woe. It grows in sympsthetio hearts That only truth employ, Above deceit and selfishness A. fount of hope and joy, When the autumn nights are gloomy. When winter winda are cold. The flower of friendship fsdeth n3t, Its faithful Isavesaafold.

cuff on the wrist is worth two on the ear. Character is the diamond that sceatehes every other .stone.—Barfol. Why is a ship the politest thing in the world? Because she always advances with a bow. Never despise humble services; when large ships run aground, little boats may pull them O. A Watering-place Conundrann—With whom do the mer- in tids dirt n With the swelle of the ocean. "Dying in poverty," says our cynic is nothing. It is living in poverty that comes hard on a fellow." " Sam,:l have lost my watch overboard. It lies here in twenty feet of water. Is there any way to get it? "Ye.,," says Sam; "there are divers ways." "It is remarkable that you are always forgetting my name" said a quasi acquaintance named. Flint. Why," said Quilp," it is a very hard name ti remember." WHOSE BOY Am I?—l'd just like to know whose boy I am. Every morning when the postman comes, he says, " Hal-lo ! whose little boy are you ?" Then I have to say: "Papa's, an' mamma's, an' grand-pa's. an' grana-ma's, an' uncle Charlie's, an' aunty Lou's, an aunty May's, an' " But when I ain't through, he's gone, an' he always laughs when he is going. I like to be some folks' boy, but not everybody's. When Ido things papa likes, such as pick up chips, and don't cry when Pm hart, then I'm papa's boy. An' when I'm hurt, an' do cry, then I'm mamma's boy. An' when any of my gran'-mas come, they say, when I'm right there before !ese, "An' where's gram-ma's boy to-day?" An' cook says: "Be my good little boy," an' las' night a man came on our steps an' he said, "My son, is this Mr. Nelson's house?" an, when I said no, he said, "Thank you, my boy;" an' a p'liceman said jus' now, "Run in my boy, or you'll freeze." I don't like to be a man's boy that I never haven't seen before at all, I don't.—Babyland. THE' DISCOVERY or COAL IN BELGIUM.—" Non Angli- sed Angeli," said the gallant Pope Gregory when the beau- tiful captives from Britain were brought before him. That British women, undeforrned by stays or fichus or high- ' -'heeled boots, should be thus described, was natural enough, ter that an Englishman concerned in coal mining should be mistak, n for an angel is curious. According to a paper -read by M. Edouard -de Laveleve to the recent meeting of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers at Liege this ap- pears to have been the Case. A legend, authenticated by ascient documents, tells of a blacksmith of the village of Plaineveaux, near Li6ge, named Houllos,who was complain- - -ing of the -dearness of his wood feel, when an angel ap- peared and advised him to go to the heights of Publemont, hard by, where he would find a black earth that might be used as fuel. He did so, found it, and used it so success- fully that it thenceforth bore his name, "houille," and bears it still in France and Belgium. But Father Bonilla, who transmits the legend, suggests that in the old Latin manu- script there is a copyist's error of Angelus for Angles, a version that greatly improves the credibility of the story. —Gentleman's Magazine. , _RAILWAY SERVANTS.—There are at present in the United Kingdom quite 3251300 railway men, including officers, - clerks, hotel servants, steamboat men, canal men, factory operatives &c., as well as railway servants proper. The latter number about 160,00 C men. These are engaged in traffic, and include signalmen. pointsmen, switchmen, and gatemen; enginemen,firemen, and cleaners; yard firemen and shunters; carmen, gangers, platelayers, and packers; head and under passenger guards; goods guards and brakf men; passenger station men, including inspectors, foremen, &slippers, checkers, callers-off, loaders,, and porters. Rail- way men belong, as a rule, to the class of labourers or that of small tradespeople. When they enter the service of the companies they begin at the lowest rung of the ladder. They are not appointed as stationmasters, nor inspectors, nor guards, nor enginemen, nor signalmen, when first they join. These appointment's are, in most instances, the result of selection among applicants who have served an apprenticeship. Years of special training are necessary in order to acquire a thorough knowledge of the detailed working of our rapid transport systems. The engine driver mast begin as a cleaner; after acquiring an acquaintance with the various parts of a locomotive he must serve a long apprenticeship as a fireman, in order to gain the knowledge of the working of an engine in motion, and of the intricate system of signalling by which the traffic is regulated, and to obtain the experience that is necessary to fit a man for the responsibility and the emergiences that continually arise in handling a machine so complex and powerful. The signalman, also, is obliged to acquire a thorough knowledge of the work he has to perform—work requiring great skill and constant watchfulness and presence of mind. In like manner the. stetion %ester, the inspector, the guard, the shunter, and the'porter have to be trained to their work, tied have to master the system of labour upon which they are employed before they can be counted upon as efficient servants. OUR FOREIIOTHERS —ln the early days of Britain not many convolutions of the famous "grey matter were de- minded of common folk. A good development of the wild _ b tests' instincts—courage, devotion, watchfulness, readiness of. eye and hand—were much more useful than abstract intellect. Abstractions in truth were so foreign to that ample, vigorous, healthy race that it had scarcely words to express a dozen. If the English matron had less brains than her husband, she had enough, backed by strong nerves and tierce resolve. From what we see among our leas -sophisticated kinsp- °pie it is easy to sketch her portrait. A tall figare, broad of W dot sod bosom beyond what elegance approves. Her cropped head is bound tight in linen—dirty —whieh twists round the neck and falls over her shoulders. The eyes are pale and frowning, for she was brought up in the shade of woods, and the sunshine annoys her in these open British fields. tribe marks probably on brow and chin. Shapely hands—for ehe has slaves to work—ready with the staff, which she even takes to bed. A woman quite opposed in every way to methetic notions, but one whom friends trust and foes regard. Her husband stands towards her both as friend and foe. He is married for good and all. It occurs to him only as a casual and uninteresting fact that the" Welsch" }muse queen grows pretty. He enjoys the privileges of his state unhindered—sits in his chief's hall the livelong night, singing his song in turn, and often fight- ing ; puzzling with drunken gravity over a riddle; wonder- ing at the Roman mint/ and applauding them boisterously; r Ming off his settle and snoring among the bones and rushes when nature can stand no more ale, and waking fresh for another bout or a foray. ISleantime his wife sits at home awl spins. TEA DattecereG.—The Dean of Bangor has lately called public atte Ilion to the manifold evils which he conceives are being wrought amongst us by the prevalence of tea- drinking. His gloomy forebodings predict little less than ma general physical and moral decadence as a people and.. nation if we preserve in our addiction to the pleasures of the tea-pot. While it is true that tea, like every other be -erage, is liable to abuse, and likely to produce certain w 41-defined bodily derangements which long have been -r cognised by our profession, the maladies which are fairly t•aceable to the drinking of tea are relatively so trivial, Vett the melancholy views of the worthy dean will not fiad support either in general popular observation, or in medical experience. If tea be pure, and free from poisonous facings," the daily drinking of an infusion of it, in any- thing like moderate quantity, is free from all risk, either immediate or remote. It is well known to medical prac- titioners that there is a common form of dyspepsia, which is especially prevalent amongst the poor, which is mainly due to the excevive conenmption of tea. The subjects of this disorder are commonly found to have been trying to "live" chiefly OD tea, which Ma been supplemented only by ellen supplies of the coarsest solid tood. Such poor persons drink t a with every meal, and between their meals, from any infusion which "keens" continously, and which Is consequently largely charged with the instringent matters which tea-leaves freely yield on prolonged maceration. Under these circumetances, the excessive drinking of tea produces a variety of chronic gastric catarrh. In persons predisposed to the disorder, the consumption of strong tea will undoubtedly produce and keep up palpitation of the heart, this possible and removable cause of cardiac de- rangement should always he sought in the treatment of cardiac neuroses. These are the chief and ntmoet human Me from which tea-drinking is fairly responsible. On the other hand, infusion of tea ne a harmless restorative and stimelant, which has taken a high and lasting place amongst harnan comforts. Properly used, it refreshes after fatigue, eelivene the dull, and cheers the depressed, while it•aids digestion, promotes the removal of effete material, and has some protective virtue against the extremes of heat and cold. No secondary depression follows these good effects. As an article of diet for soldiers on active service, especially in hot climates, the value of tea has been often proved, and is attested by the higliest authorities.—British Medical Journal. s' RUPTURES "—WHITE'S MOC-VAIN LVE1:11 TRUSS is the most effec`ive invention for the t,ettment of Hernia. div.head: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORN-
div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORN-
OLT U RE, &c.

HORSE DOCKING.—At the Newcastle Police Court, on Tuesday an ostler and his master were charged at the instance of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Ani- mals with cruelly ill-treating a horse by catting off a por- tion of its tail. It was stated that the catting off a portion of a horse's tail to improve its appearance was a custom that prevailed all over England, an4was known as docking. Three veterinary surgeons stated that the docking of a horse's tail entailed upon the animal great suffering. The Bench said that in consideration of that being the first pro- secution in the north of England they would inflict only a small fine, but if another case came before them the penalty would be a heavy one. GOVERNMENT AGRICULTURkL RETURNS IN FRANCE.— While we are engaged in our insular and amateur way in working out for ourselves with more or leas success the probable produce of this year's wheat ern), our French neighbours have just been presented with the official esti- mates of their Government. An approximate return of this year's French wheat crop, based upon the reports sent in by the Prefects was officially published in Paris on Sunday. The yield for 1883 is now estimated at 100,646,216 hectolktres—this Is 5 per cent. under average—the area sown is given as 6,718,729 hectares. The yield per hectare is 14.98 hectolitres, and the average weight per hectolitre 76 32 kilogrammes. DRYING THE Cows.—ln response to the question," When should cows go dry?" the Dairy sayr —There is such a thing as burning a candle at both ends. One may easily do this in the dairy. This kind of thing may go on when one milks the cows up to the time of calving or near it, and even encourages it by feeding for that end. Bat then it may not; and it is the dairyman's business to know all about it, and not take any general rule for his guide. There is no rule without a multitude of exceptions, and there are cows that will not go dry, but will milk from calf to calf. But, as a rule, to be contracted and expanded judiciously and safely, it might be said that a cow should be dried off six weeks before she is due to calve; that up to that time she should be liberally fed in the usual manner; thathence- forth her food should be curtailed, or even changed to dry hay; and if her condition is reduced somewhat, so much the better—it will make it safer for herand the calf. The milk- ing may be done once a day, or not wholly completed, leav- ing a little in the udder. We have even taken a little milk several times a day from a eow in this condition' with the effect of rapidly drying the udder. But it is a dangerous thing, and one to be avoided, to leave any considerable quantity of milk in a cow's udder at this time.—Prairie Farmer, U.S.A.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

BARREN FRUIT TaxEs.—There are more of these amongst Pears and Appless than there_is any need. It is waste of land to allow trees to grow year after year and not bear fruit without anything being done to assist them. Some- times the variety is at fault—that is, a kind unsuited to the locality has been planted. In such cases one would think that there is no better remedy than to cut down the tree and replace it by one more suitable. We are, however, not going to recommend such drastic measures. We would sug- gest, in the first place, that it should be proved that the variety is not known as one likely to do in the locality. A tolerably good idea may be formed bv comparing the foliage and habit of growth with those in the neighbourhood. Some grow upright, others pendulous; some spread out their branches, in others they hug the trunk; some have long, narrow, pointed leaves, others broad and obtuse. The thickness of the young shoots is a characteristic by which others may be recognised, for there are scarcely two trees alike out of some scores of sorts. Many of the barren trees in old gardens are seedlings, and it is notorious of these that they rarely prove so good as their parents; and should they happen to be amongst the fruitless ones they will be admi- rably adapted for the purpose we are about to recommend, which is to cut them down and graft, about which we may have more to say later on. If thy are in suitable soil and growing freely, nothing need be done to them at present. If there is any doubt on this point, saw all the thick branches off within a yard of the trunk; and, as some of them are cif great weight, it is necessary to saw on the under side quite an inch upwards, otherwise they are' apt to split down for a considerable distance. The next operation is to cut a trench round the tree one yard distant and down as far as the roots go, then commence to undermine the tree, and with the aid of a fork, more soil may be moved from the roots till the headless trunk can be svroyed' to and fro, giving proof that the top root is broken—always a de- sirable act. Opportunity should now be taken to raise the tree higher, by,placing soil under each side as the plant is swayed over. There are not many that are not benefited by being thus raised. We have met with instances where the stems of the trees have. been as much as a foot in the soil, through continual addition in the way of manure, Sze., bat chiefly the result of some operation necessitating the re- moval of soil, which was wheeled on the gardena proceed- ing most ruinous to the trees. We advise filling the trench with the best soil procurable, but no manure; covering the roots with the same; and the wok for the present Is com- plete. "Trees that have not borne satisfactciry crops, but are meritorious kiuds, will require different treatment. As in the previous case, a trench should be dug, but'only half wly round the tree, using the fork at the same time to re- move the soil so as to free the roots, which should have their points directed upwards as much as possible; one holding the roots whilst another places soil under them. All the jagged ends of the roots should be cut smooth with sharp knife. As we are now writing of trees about 12ft. high or more and the same through, we do not consider it advisable to cut all round such a tree the first year, but to leave the other half for another year. By then the roots that have been cut will have formed numerous at their ends which will support the tree. TRE FRONT GARDEN.—Dahlias are damaged so much by frost as to be of no further service, and it becomes a ques- tion what had best be done with them. Some make a rush and take them up as soon as nipped by frost. We are in no such hurry, not being apprehensive that they will take any harm for some time yet. It is more natural that they should go to rest by degrees. Their decaying tops, it may he alleged, are unsightly in the front of dwelling-houses, I and demand their speedy removal, but, by a little trimming up anl shortening, this objection may be diminished. -Use every meats to keep them in the ground as long as possible. Remove the dead tops of all other plants destroyed by frost or otherwise, for they soon become offensive if they exist in quantity. Roses may now be planted. We have just transplanted some that were put in as 'cuttings about this time last year. They had all flowered daring the season, and the object in moving them was to give them more space. Standard roses that have given a prolific crop of suckers during the season should have the soil removed till their source is discovered, and with a sharp knife remove them close to the roots ; or the plants may be taken up, cleared of suckers, and replaced,. .

THE WINDOW.--141E LIYACINTIT.—A few weeks back we advised the cottager to pot these, with the view of having them in flower in the middle of March. We may remind those cottagers who have a greenhouse, that they may still pot some, and yet overtake their neighbours who have only the window to depend on. The bulbs should be in the coolest place possible till they have mat? 3 one inch or so of growth. Plunged out of doors, with sc—nething to keep off the wet, is the place for them. Fuchsias : Leafless plants of these may be placed in the cellar, or any out of the way place, light even not being desirable for them for a few months. They will not require much water, but must not be allowed to get so dry as to shrink the soil, so that it leaves the sides of the pots. Bring others into a state of reat by degrees Pelargoniums will need most careful water- ing from this time. Yellow leaves and lanky growth are the symptoms of over-watering.
How to get a good l wife.—Take a good girl and go to the parson. . .

Look on other lit-es besides your own; see What their troubles are, and how they are borne.—George Eliot. The first in conversation is truth, the next good sense, the third good humour, and the fourth wit.—Sir W. Temple. Student (reciting) : " And—er—then he—er—went— and—er—" The dais laugh. Professor: "Don't laugh, gentlemen. To err is human." There seldom was a day that did not bring its oppor- _ _ _

tunity for doing good that never could have been done before and never can be azain. It must be improved then or never.—Golden Rule. PRoonEss.—Here, I.say, is the true moral: that man has to make progress along divers lines in obedience to a diver- sity of aspirations and p6wers, the sum of which is truly his nature; and that he fails and falls short until be learns to advance upon them all, and to advance upon them har- monionsly.—Matthew Arnold.

A little girl recently went to visit her grandfather in the country. She is fond of milk, but firmly refused to drink any while there, without giving any reason. When she re- tutu d she was asked, "You had nice milk there to drink, hadn't you ?" "I guess I didn't drink any of that milk," she itnlignantly replied. "Do you know where grandpa got it? I saw him sque:!ze it out of an old cow ! " In fie private journal of a lady recently deceased there were found these words :—" I expect to pass through this world but once. Any good thing, therefore, that I can do, or any kindness I can show, to any fellow creature, let me do it now. Let me not defer or neglect it, for I shall not pass this ray again." These words are worthy to be placed where we can see them every day. Each day, each week, each year, comes but once. A 'TENDER REMEMBRANCE.—AS a certain musician, who had a very bad voice, was singing one day, he took notice of a woman who fell a crying; imagining that the sweet- ness of his melody awakened some passion in her breast, he began to sing louder, and she to weep more bitterly. He bad no sooner ended his song, than going to the lady he as%ed her why she cried. "Oh!" she said, "I am the un- fortunate woman whose ass the wolves destroyed yesterday, and no sooner did I hear yon sing, but I thought on my poor ass, for surely never were voices so much alike." div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 3, 1833.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 3, 1833.
TOWN COUNCIL MEETING.

The last meeting of the Town Council for the present 1 municipal year was held in the Council Chamber at the I Town Hall on Tuesday. There were present—His Worship I the Mayor (John Crosfield, Eeq ), Aldermen Pickmere (ex. Mayor), Kean, Burgess, Davies, Webster, and Chandley ; and Councillors 'Ashton, Dixon, Caldwell, Wright, Marsh, Burgeas, Taylor, Wallington, Woolfall, Monks, W. Pier- point, Bolton, J. Pierpoint, Brown, Whittle, Litton, Fran- comb, and Hutchinson; W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), and T. Lonadin (borough surveyor).
Alderman BURGESS : How much?

Councillor WALLINGTON replied that they could not tell, but if they extended the width there would be less land to sell, and more expense of making streets. Councillor CALDWELL WO in favour of a few feet being added to the width originally proposed if necessary. The MAYOR said the widening of Bridge-street had been before the Council from time to time, and it had been the unanimous opinion—at least, he had understood it so—that it was one of the mast important improvements that could be effected in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He thought him- self that it would be a great mistake to delay doing it. (Hear, hear.) As regarded the manner of purchasing tut buildings, it was found necessary that that should be done quietly and secretly, but he had no doubt that the contract being completed all particulars would be given. It was im- possible to say exactly what the cost of the alteration would be, but 'be believed Mr. Councillor Wright had given them some notion of the value of the land they proposed disposing of, and if it realised what he estimated the cost to that Corporation would not be very great. It was quite right and proper for Councillor Monks to be adverse to in- creasing the rates extravagantly, as all of them should be opposed to that, but improvements like this must be canted out, and he agreed with Councillor Wallington that if they intended to proceel with it they should do so at once. (Hear, hear.) On Councillor Monks' atnendmeat being put to the vote, lonly the proposer and seconder appeared in favour of it, and it was accordingly lost.

Councillor PLATT, in reply to previous speakers, said the committee would be willing to insert in the minutes "that the street be widened not lees than 50 feet." For his own part, he voted in committee for more width, viz., 55 feet, which he thought was as narrow as they ought to have it. Fifty feet hid been fixei, so that they might be unanimous in the matter. He hope." they would succeed in getting a foot or two more, as sft. would not add much to the exoettse, but 101 t. additional would do so. Tney must take into con- sideration the back land they would sell for business pur- poses, and they would be crippling this if they had a width of 60ft. (Rear, hear.) He was smewhat surprise.' to hear the remark of Councillor Monks that Warrington at the present tune was stationary, because he heard of works tming increased in miny departments. Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., he believed, were enlarging their work, al.to Rylands Bros., the White Cross Company, the Midland Railway Carriage Works, ikc., and since he came into that room he had been told of an important extension about to be made to a brewery in that town, and which would increase the rateable assessment. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the committee's secrecy in effecting some preliminary purchases, they had thus saved several thousand pounds. That counc had been taken in the interests of the ratepayers of the borough and in tbe interests ef the corporation, and he hoped that when the time came they would be able to present such a statement that they might be forgiven for any little ir- regularity that had taken piace. He did not think the slightest parallel could be drawn between Sankey-street and Bridge-street. The latter would always be an important thorotighfare, being in reality the only means of communica- tion between the two cGunties. The committee would look into tke several purchases as they came More them, and would do all that was necessary, and that with the greatest economy. (Hear, hear.) Ciuncillor BURGESS thought the exact widtk they in- tended to make the street should be decided.
The TowN CLERK sail that plans had bean arranged showing 50 feet.

The SIAYOR thought they should let the minutes remain as they were. Alderman PICKMERE said that as an old inhabitant of Bridge-street he thought 50 feet was quite wide enough, and fully cap ible of accommodating the traffic. If they took more land from that side it would cost them a great deal more money.
The Tows CLERK, in reply to a question, said a definite plan must be laid before the Lonsl Government Board before it could be sanctioned.
After some further discussion, the minutes of the commit- tee in their original form were approved of.
THE PAVING OF THE STREETS. Alderman KEAN moved the confirmation of the proceed- ngs of the Paving and Sewerage Co.nmittee, and the motion was seeonded.

Councillor MONKS referred to the unsatisfactory condition of Arpley-street and Museum-street, and asked whether the Committee intended to take any steps for the formation of these streets, which were very dangerous. On Saturday night last a lady had had a very heavy fall in consequence of tne irregularity of the street.

Alderman WEllsrEu. s tid he could speak fe,lingly as to Museum-street. The pole of water and the want of light made it very dangerous indeed. Alderman BURGESS said he had beton an eye witness to a cart-load of cinders being put down for the reptir of the streets referred to. lie suggested that as soon as the houses were built, the streets should be formed without delay, for tenants paid for the construction bf the streets as well as the building of the houses from the time they ent3rel upon a rent; and every day the owner left a street unformed he did it at the cost of his tenants.
CounoilEar BURGESS thought the committee should pave net the streets simply on which new houses were built, but the whole of the sEreets under the control of the cum- inittee..

Alderman PICKMERE said there was one pot street which tbe committee seemed to preserve in order to show how Warrington was paved in ages gone by; that was the street teem Mill-street throuc!-J1 the market to King-street. He oeished something could be dune by the committee to im- prove that thoroughfare. Councillor J. FIEF/POINT thought that streets should only be formed when seven-eighths of the land was built upon or taken for building purposes.

Alderman KEAN'saia they must remember that many of the houses referred to as ben]; built upon new streets were erected by workingmen who borrowed their money from build- ing clubs, anl who would feel it a hardship to be called upon to pay for constructing the streets immediately after build- ing. The committee had that to consider. If the property b-longed to men of wealth, then there would be no difil-. catty. With respect to Arpley-street, he might say the owner, Lord Winmarleigh, had promised to ,p tve it if the com:nittee waited a certain time. lhey had waited seven times the length of time mentioned, yet no move was made by his lordship or his agent' The proceedings of the committee were alopted. THE MTIMMING CLUB AND THE BATHS.

On the proceedings of the Town Hall; Park, and Baths Committee coming up for confirmation—on the mot'oa of the Meozon, seconded by Councillor CALDWELL—some cm• versation took place on the proposal to allow the Warring- t m Swimming Club the exclusive use of the Biths from seven to eight every Tuesday evening. It was pointed out that the privilege could be withdrawn at any time, and that the resolution did not mean that the privilege was to last for ever.—Councillor Warrnx, as president of the club. said the privilege was really necessary if they were t 3 carry on the functions of a swimming club; and he charged Mr. Aldsrman Webster with having tried to prevent the privi- lege being enjoyed.—Alderman Wians-rsn observed all he had done was to intimate that if any ratepayer wished the use of the smimming bath during the hour it could be with- held. He, however, protested that be had not done any- thingto prevent the club having the use of the bath.—The proceedings were confirmed.

he.was afraid that his Worship, in his generosity, would try to wipe it out. This was a matter, kowever, which ought to be decided and discussed on its merits, because the charge was a frightful one. He cJald only find in the re- port three suggestions and observations taken on two days; and the Mayor hal a men in his own employ who could have given a great deal more information for less than a sovereign.._ •

Couricillor BOLTON moved as an amendment that the account be not paid without particulars. Councillor CALDWELL said all this pointed to the fact that they were a pretty lot of people to do the town's business. If he managed his own like that he would soon be up a spout. (Laughter.) The Mavow said he looked upon the report himself in a very diff !rent light. He thonght it was an admirably drawn out report, and that it might prove to be of very great value if anything is ever done at the river to make it navigable every day in the year for vessels drawing eight feet. He might say that when he spoke of the survey costing .£2OS or £250, he did not contemplate that would cover all the work Mr. Barry had done. He thought that would be simply for making the survey and reporting; but Mr. Barry had sent in a bill which included attendahce on the Committee in the House of Commons, where he was bound to be, and a lot of other items of that sort, amounting to .£lB4 8s 2d. He knew at the time some town councillor asked how much Mr. Barry was to be paid, and whew the question was put to the Town Clerk he said they could not get these big civil engineers to say beforehand what their charge would be. They would not do it, therefore they were compelled either to employ Mr. Barry or let the thing go without having any represen- tation in the Committee Room of the House of Commons. They were bound to do that in self-protection. It was very - hard having to paw this money, but it had to be done; and he did not thing theta was any way out of it. It would be a very ungentlemanly thing, he should think. for the Coun- cil to object to pay a civil engin'er when he was engaged and employed by them.

Councillor MONKS thought Mr. Barry should be asked to furnish a det tiled statement. There was nothing dis- courteous in that. He had no doubt they should have to pay the bill; the question was whether they should pay it in a lump sum.

Councillor WALLINGTON said Mr. Barry lied certainly nude a big hill, and they might grumble, but they would certainly have to pay it, and they might as well do it at once without any trouble. A'derm en WEBSTER said that if they could have the river deepened from Runcorn to Warrington they could snap their fingers at the Canal Company. The charge was very ex- traordinary, but the report would be useful some day or other. Alluding to that part of the proceedings which re- lated to the suggested handing over of the School of Art to the Corporation, Alderman Webster said that he thought nobody would accuse him of being inimical to the interests of that school, for he had been one of its most active sup- porters; but he did object to the manner in which this pro- posal had been sprung upon them. A meeting of the Council of the School of Art had been con- vened for another purpose, and there and then the Mayor had been asked without any further considera- tion to approaeh the Town Council for the purpose of hav- ing the School of Art takeu over. That was a matter which ke said ceuld not be so easily disposed of, and he thought that before any such meeting of the School of Art had been held distinct n)tice should have been given.to every ine.n- ber of the Council of thit Institution, so that the question could have been discussed in all its bearings. The MAYOR said that if there was any fault it lay with the secretary of the School of Art. Alderman WEBSTER added that if the School of Art were transferred to the Corporation there would be a death, struggle between the Free Museum and Library and the School of Art, for the present income could not maintain both institutions, and both would suffer. Councillor BURGESS thought that the two institutions could not be carried on with a penny rate. If the rate were 111 or 2d then he should have no objection to the School or Art being taken over by the Corporation. Councillor BOLTON proposed his amendment in favour of a detailed statement, and hinted that Mr. Barry's report bad been compiled from another report made 20 years ago. He also objected to the Mayor spending a single copper, urging that the charge was one which the ratepayers ought to meet. Councillor MONKS seconded the amendment. Alderman DeevrEs suggested that they should approach Mr. Barry in a c inciliatory spirit, with the oleiect of getting him to reduce his charge. After Some conversation it was agreed that this course should be adopted. The Ma.Yort, referring to what had been said about the School of Art, remarked that Alderman Webster was not present at the committee meeting of the school when the matter was discussed. There was a large committee, he be- lieved about eight gentlemen present, and they were every one unanimous in recommending that the building should be in the possession of the Town Council. He believe 1 that the principal reason was that it was desirable that the School of Art should always he kept open, and if it was the property of the Corporation that would be secured; oth wise, it might so happen that some dee, it might fail, and be closed. As regarded the cost of maintaining it, he was not in a position to say what that would be but the secretary, Mr. Owen, said that V.O or £so' a year would cover the ex- pense of keeping it open. But of course there had been nothing definite done. They would see from the form vf the resolution that the Town Clerk was to report to the General Purposes Committee as to what respensibility would devolve noon the Corporation • by acceding to the request of the School of Art. Of course there was this con- sideration : that the Museum only had a penny rate, and it was a question whether the members of' the Museum Com- mittee would be content to part with any of that money for the School of Art. The Museum' was benefited to some extent by the space which had been occupied by'the School of Art. It was a matter that must not be dealt with 'hastily, and the arguments muet be considered on both sides for and against. It WAS a delicate thing to ask the Library and Museum Committee to part with any ot their money; and it was for them to say whether they think, it better to spend money in maintaining the School of Art or in, maintaining the Museum. It was for the Council to consider whether they would take over the School of Art and maintain it. It WAS a fortunate thing that the resolution was worded as it was, because no one present was committed to anything. There had only been OM meeting of the School of Art Committee, and one of the General Purposes COrrimittee, and therefore he hoped that Alderman Webster's wrath at the hasty manner in which the work had bem done would cool dowu, and that he would look upon those who had done it in a little mere friendly spirit than he seemed to do. (Laughter.) The proceedings of the committee were then condemeed.

div.head: HAUB° MS OF REFUGE.
div.p: HAUB° MS OF REFUGE.

The Tows CLEW( read a communication from the secre- tary of the National Refuge Harbour Society of Great Britain (Mr. F. Johnson) asking the Corporation to adopt a petition to Parliament, as had been done in other places, praying for steps to be taken to secure better harbour accom- mcdation along the coasts, so that the serious losses to life and property might thereby be mitigated.
HYDRANTS IN THE BOROUGH: NEGOTIA.TIOYS WITH THE
WATER WORKS COMPANY.

The MAYOR moved and the Ex-MaYoa seconded the con- firmation of the proceedings of the Watch Committee. Connc nor PLATT, referring to the report of the Fire Bri- gade Sub-Committee with respect to the laying down of hydrants in the borough, said that the Sub-Committee had now done all they possibly could in the direction of laying down these hydrants until they had larger mains. Alterman WEBSTER askel whether the negotiations with the Waterworks Company had progrees-d at all since the last meeting. The MAYOR: There has been nothing done since the last meeting. The only resource that the Corporation now has is to go to the Local GOvertiment Board, represent to them the condition we are in, and see what powers we can obtain to alter the present state of things. Alderman WEB3TER: Vill that be the General Purposes Co:mnittee's duty? The MAYOR: The General Purposes Committee's duty. _ _
Die irceelinge were cenfirmed.
THE WIDENING OF BRIDGE STREET.

Councillor Pixrr moved the confirm itioa of the pro- ceedings of the Street Improvement and Lighting Commit- tee. He said he regretted very much the absence of the chairman of the committee (Mr. Broadbent), and no doubt they would all still more regret the cause of that gentleman's absence. With reference to the minutes of the committee, the most important subject mentioned in them was the widening of Bridge-street, and they would see the committee had re- commended a width of 50 feet. The committee had gone carefully into the cost, and It was estimated at £31,000; in that estimata they had allowed every latitude and they were not at all likely to exceed the amount. rhey expected they would have from 5,000 to 6,000 yards of land for re-sale. The committee, he might add, had already obtained Reveral plot,' of land in view of the cJntemplated improvement. Councillor WRIGHT seconded the motion.

Alderman BURGESS said that when the question was last before the Council it was thought desirable not to fix the width' of the street, and he was'unprepared for the course adopted now. He believed they shou.d find it recorded that the opinion of the Council was the width of Bridge-street should not be less than 50 feet, now it was proposed to make that width absolute. He suggested that the width should be left open,—left, for instance, as it was in the minutes, that it should not be less than 50 feet, and the exact width could be determined afterwards. The worthy alderman further suggested that another lamp should be placed on Warrington bridge, which he thought would be a great ad- vantage: , The TOWN CLERK Said that the width was fixed in order that plans might be prepared and submitted to tke Loc 11 Government Board.

Councillor MONKS said he rose to propose a resolution, and before he did that he would-just like to say what he had to say on this matter because he was not one of those who believed that this imProveinent as necessary. He thought it would tend to the -advantage of the town if the Council could make up their minds to postpone the im- provement fora time. He must express his regret for the bareness of the figures which had been supplied under the promise wbichwas made that an estimate of the nett cost Amid be given as to the widening of Bridge-street. What had been said that night fully justified the astion he had felt inclined to take, because instead of the nett cost being from £3,000 to £5,000 he thought it would bs very, very much larger. Of course, the whole thing would depend upon the value of the lend which they would have to sell. From the knowledge of the value of the propeller, and from what he saw of the value of the property in Bridge-street, he doubted very much if they would get the price that land would be got for in Sankey-street. He knew that there was land to be sold, or to be leased rather, in Sankey-street, where the parties would be very glad to get a shilling a yard, and he thought they would be glal to get a 20 years' purchase on that. The 1 Ind in Sank ty-street was worth about a£l a yard, and more eligible land than that in Bridge-street, so that that would reduce the gross cost to abeut £20,000. That was a very much larger sum than they were given to understand would be the nett cost when this improvement W 49 talked about. Therefore he must press again for a more detailed estimete of the cost of this improvement than was given in the Street Improvement Committee's minutes. There was another thing he felt called upon to protest against, and he did it with this feeling—he did not know who was respon- sible, and he did no blame anyone, but he could not help but feel that 'the purchase of the property was being carried through without the authority of that Council, and in an nnbusinesslike way, 'and the sooner the Council knew how they stood it would be in the interests of both the buyers and the sellers. He would protest agains: the manner in which the purchases had been made. He believed he was right in saying that the rateable value of Warrington was stationary, and he thought that under the circumstances it was not wise to go on increasing the debt; it was large enough. They would find th it the total amount of debt for which Warrington was responsible was £280,000 odd, and there was £IDI,OOO for the purchase of thegas works, and that they might say was property which was earning its own dividend. He could not shut his eyes to the fact, whether they liked it or not, that there would be a large expenditure hereafter for water, whilst their sewers and streets were not completed to the satisfaction of the ratepayers; also that they had a still further expenditure for the manufacture of minure, and to the extension of the depot at Longford. Altogether, he thought that they had a-very large expmdi- ture for what he called the necessities of the Corporation, ard until these were fairly met, and the growth of War- rington justified them in the further expenditure, such as the widening of Bridge-street, it would be far better if they held their hand until they were satisfied that that time had come. He was acting that night as he would act if he had to pay the piper, and he thought before they committed themselves to this large expenditure they ought to recln- eider their position and know exactly how they stood. He knew that the feeling of the Council was in favour of the improvement. He simply expressed his views, and entered his protest against the manner in which the matter was being pushed through. He begged to move that the minutes be confirmed, with the exception of the one referring to the improvement of Bridge-street. C mncillor Dr. MACKIE rose to reply to Councillor Monks' remarks, but the Mayor ruled him out of order, saying that the amendment had not been seconded.

Alderman DAVIES facetiously observed that he would second the amendment to enable Dr. Mackie to proceed. (A laugh). - Court&llor D. MACKIE was sorry that Aldsrman Davies gave such a lame excuse for seconding the amendment. (Laughter.) He did net advocate that scheme because it was cheap, and that they could _make anything by it in the shape of getting 4?2-- per cent, for only what cost them 4 per cent. That part of the.town was the hotbed of disease, and all the property about there required cleaning, and that ceuld only be done by demolishing one side of the street. He did not take it to be a question of the relative cost of the sites. Their aim was to get rid of that property, which was a serious detrim eat to the town, taken in a sanitary point of view, let alone that of appearance, which also ought not to be omit'ed. They should have all that part of Bridge-street pulled away, and he hoped that in course of time they would see Market-gate cleared. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that that would be effected in the same Triet way that the present improvemeet was proposed. Alderman DAVIES, the seconder of the amendment, said that although Councillor Monks had called npen the Council to pass the amendment, it was not owing to the proposer being opposed to improving Bridge-street by widening it. (Hear, hear.) On the contrary, be thought Councillor Monks had as great a desire as any member of the Council to effect improvements in the town. but he had spoken of the great responsibilities resting upon them in he shape of borrowed money, and he was anxious that they, like any men of business, should sea how and when they would be in a positioe to discharge their liabilities. At present the total debt owing by their town was £280,000, trut, as had been pointed out, £190,000 of that sum was in respectof the pur- chase of the Gas Waks. Fortunately the receipts from the Gas Works were now rather more than was necessary for discharging the interest and sinking fund required to pay that money, and they had a little profit out of that ivhich would go towards the improvement of Bridge-street. Councillor Monks desired them to hesitate for the reasons stated. It was quite true what Councillor Monks said, that the town for the last three or four years had not been pro- gressing as it did before. He supposed, however, that War- rington was.not worse off than its neighbours, all of whom more or less had teen labouring under the general depres- sion in trade. The shopkeepers complained severely, and he was afraid that the price of the land which they proposed to sell when widening Bridge-street would fall far short of what they expected to realise. Dur- ing the last seven or eight years that end of the town had not progressed as a trading portion of the bteroueh. If the Connell thought they were in a position to spend the town's money in carrying out this improvement he would offer en objection, and he hoped that at the proper time the corn- tpittee would lay before the Council a detailed statement of how they had spent the money, and would justify what they had done in the presence of a commissioner, and those who had objected to the original proposal. They might take Councillor Monks's caution as a wise word spoken at the right time. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WALLINGTON wished to point out that if they delayed in buying the property at once it would cost a great deal more hereafter. They sliould enter into their negotia- tions at once. If they made the street more than 50f1. wide they should rememb-r that by so doing they would be in- creasing their expenses, and it would "cost more than at,ooo

div.head: MIRIEETS : SUGGESTED EXTENSION
div.p: THE MIRIEETS : SUGGESTED EXTENSION

Aldermin CHLNDLEY, in moving the adoption of the pro- c xdings of the Markets Committee, said there was nothing important on the minutes, but one of the questions of the future was the extensien of the market by pulling down the block of property, of which Mr. Geddes shop formed a part.
Councillor LirroN seconded the motion, and it vra3 agreed
NO COMMENT.
The proceedings of the School Attendance, Library, Museum and Art', Cemetery. Sanitary, and Gas Committees were confirmed without comment. WoOMR BARRY'S CFIARGRS: THE SCHOOL OF ART.
The MAYOR moved, and the EX-MAYOR seconded, the confirmAtion of the proceedings of the Genaral Purposes Committee.

Councillor Dr. MACRTE, referring to the charge of £5OO 14a 61 by Mr. J. W. Barry for his survey of the river from Warrington to Runcorn, asked why what was at one time .stimated at £2OO, had now risen to £3OO more. The doctor subs( quently quoted from a newspaper report of the proceedings of the meeting at which Mr. Barry was ap- pointed, and from which it appeared the ex-Mayor had thee stated he was informed by the Mayor that the report would cost about £2OO, that the Mayor had promised he would I)3Y whatever the report cost above that amount, and that the Town Clerk had intimated the £3OO would come out of the borough funds. He would be the last man to hold the Mayor to any statement made in the exclement probably of the moment, and he had not the slightest wish to put anything upon his worship, but he would remind the Coun- cil that 30 or 40 years ago a much more extended and much more difficult report was obtained for £2OO. If the large amount of £5OO arose from a rise in professional chargee then it could not be helped; if the Mayor and ex- Mayor had been misled, then he supposed they would have to overlook the matter.

The Ex-Mason said he did tr-..t see why Dr. Mackie should have "lagged" his name into this question— (laughter)—because he had only repeated to the Council what the Mayor had told him. Hi had himself been against the report, because he thought it would not be worth two- penc9. (Laughter.) He might say that the charge of £5OO arose, he believed, from the engineer waiting so long on the Parliamentary Committee in London; but still the amount seemed enormous. What he had understood the Mayor to say was that the cost of the survey of the river and the land adjoining would not be moril than £2OO, but then, in midition to that, there was 61111,e evidence before the Parliamentary Committee, which the Mayor had not thought of. Councillor BURGESS: Are we to understand from what has just been said that Mr. Barry's charges for attending before the Parliamentary Committee are £300?
The TOWN CL: The actual cost of the report is £316, and the cost of attending on the Committee, settling clauses, &c., is £lB4 odd, the two sums amounting together to £5OO 14s. 61

Councillor Mows said he hoped the account woad be withdrawn, and that they would be furnished with a detailed statement of how the amount was made up, in order that they might sea how the matter stood. He ale() hoped the M tyor would not be tempted to make any offer. (Hear. hear.) Either the charge was a fair one which the Corp iration ought to pay, or it was a charge which the Mayor ought not to pay. (Hear, hear.) He trusted the Mayor would take that view of It; but

div.head: VOTE OF THANKS TO THE MAYOR.
div.p: VOTE OF THANKS TO THE MAYOR.

At the conclusion of the ordinary business, Alderman PICEMBRE rose and said: Mr.M tyor, with your permission I should like to saw a few words. There has been a good old custom connected with the Corporation of this town for many years, and I remember that when I first entered the Council ih 1854 that what I am about to do to-night was done at that time, viz, moving a resolution that the best thanks of this Council be given to his worship the Mayor for the manner he has conducted the bu9inets of

the C'orporat;on. (Applause.) In the Mayor's presence I do not wish to flatter him unnecessarily in anything I may say about himself, for it is difficult to speak in a man's face of his kindness of heart, his affability, im- partiality, and fairness with which he has conducted the proceedings of this Council. But I may say that Ido not think any Miyo‘• has ever excelled him who has, had the honour of filling; the chair before him. (Applause.) I only hope he mty enjoy many, many pleasant years, and that he will remember during years to come that when he was Mayor of Warrington he was esteemed and respected by all members of this Council. (Hear' hear.) This is-a formal resolution I am going to propose, but at the same time we as representatives of the inhabitants of this town cannot re- sist the temptation we feel of alluding to the, work he has _done outside the Council. (Hear, hear.). He has laid the foundation, or rather prepared the foundation, el an insti- tution which will secure happiness and recreation to many generations yet to come. (Applause.) He has done other things in the town of great benefit to it, and as Mayor of the borough has had many opportunities in private of bestowing his charity on those who needed it, whicla charity never comes to the ears of the public. (Hear, hear.) On all these grounds I am sure you will unanimously pass the resolution I am about to bring before. you. Alderman Holnys is not here to-night; I may say' he- has almost had the perquisite of moving this resoluion—he has done it so many times. (Laughter.) I can only say lam personally gratified in having the opportunity of doing it in his place. I beg to move,—"That the best thanks of this Council be pressnted to the Worshipful the Mayor, John Crosfield, E-q , for the able and satisfactory manner in which he has sustained the dignity of the important office of Mayor of this borough during his year of offi'ce ;. and for the unvary- ing courtesy, kindness, and impartiality displayed by him when presiding ever the deliberations of the Council and in hit intercourse with its members."

Alderman BURGESS seconded the proposition of the ex- Mayor, which be remarked required no words of his to recommend it. to their notice. They bad had the civic chair occupied by a townsman of their own, a gentleman born in the borough, and of a family which bad conferred great benefits on the town. (Hear, bear.) The dignity of the office had been sustained in a way that be thought it was impossible for anybody to excel. He had seen a good many Mayors of Warrington in his time, but he was quite sure of this, that the Mayoralty of the town had never been more imp trtiallv discharged than at the hands of the present Mayor. (Applause.) He should have been glad it Mr. Cros- field had seen his way to occupy the chair another year— (hear, hear)—but it appea.ed in the Mayor's judgment, and be was the person to jadge of the matter, that it was not in his province to again undertake the duties. Con- sequently they had to thank him, and the Council offered him their very best thanks for the way the duties of the office had been discharged, and his courtesy and impartiality on all occasions. (Hear, hear.) Warrington would never want a worthier Mayor than Mr. Crosfield. (Applause.) Alderman DAVIES remarked that although he desired to say everything suitable to the occasion, he found it a deli- cate matter to speak well of a man when that man was present. They could observe the hesitation of the previous speakers because they could not express exactly all that they felt towards the Mayor. (Hear. bear.) A celebrated personage in a very celebrated book said "The heart of man is de- ceitful above all things and desperately wicked.' (Laugh- ter.) It was in the nature of mafi to speak sarcastic and bitter things of each other, but they found it more difficult to choose their words whorl they wished to speak w ll of a man atho was present. At that moment he felt a very strong desire to speak well of the Mayor of Warrington—

(applause)—but all that he could say was that Mr. Crosfield had done his best, and that best was excellent. (Applause ) It had given satisfaction and pleasure to everyone in the town. They wished him good health and prosperity, and that in the future he would meet with that great success that had attended him during the time he had been Mayor of Wallington. (Applause.) Alderman WEBSTER, in supporting the resolution, re- marked that when Mr. Crosfield was appointed Mayor he felt a certain degree of doubt as to how he would be able to conduct the business of the Council and the duties of the new office he had undertaken, knowing, as he (Alderman Webster) and they all did, the general impulsiveness of the Mayor's character. (Laughter.) He was pleased to say, however, that the chair had never been occupied by a gentleman of more impartiality, and that he had acted as a mayor ought to act. (Hear, hear.) The nama of Crosfield in Warrington was very generally and warmly esteemed. So far as himself was concerned, his Worship's father was, 35 years ago, one of his w.armest Meads, and when he (Alderman Webster) was a young man did certain things for him which he should never forget, and through which the flame of the Crosfield family would always be cherished by him. The Mayor would retire with a consciousness that he had done his duty, and with the esteem and regard of every member of the Council. (Ap- plause.) _

• Alderman CIikNDLEY in a few remarks, spoke of the con- sistent manner in which his Worship had discharged the duties of the 'Mayoralty, and expressed the hope that Mr. Cresfield in future years would look back on that period he had been chief magistrate of Warrington with feelings of satisfaction and pride. (Hear, hear.) Councillor MONKS said he was very glad indeed to add his testimony to the manner in which the Mayor had con- ducted the duties of the Moyoralty. I was exceedingly gratifying to members of his own party, because he recog- nised the Mayor as a L;beral, to hear such flattering expressions of opinions from those on thq other aide (Hear, hear) Councillor Dr. MACKIE, in adding his testimony to the efficiency of the Mayor's services, took occasion to refer to Mr. Crostield's appointment twelve months since. He wished to assure him that if his friends had taken a different course and not introducA him to the Council in such a questionable manner that he would have had the full and en- tire vote of, he might say, the whole of the Council, and had Mr. Harrison known it sooner he would have retired. He thanked the Mayor for the fair, honourable, and straight- forward way he had treated those who felt it necessary to vote against him on that occasion. Certainly in his own case there had never been the slightest shadow of a shade of recognition that he was the Mayor's opponent. (Hear, hear.) One thing struck him in connection with what fell from the lips of the last speaker. Mr. Crosfleld had adopted a course different to most of his predecessors who had de- clared that they would know no politics during the year. The retirirg Mayor had maintained his position outside that Chamber as a liberal Mayor of that town—(hear, hear)— and he hoped in the future Mayors would consistently main- tain their position whether Liberals or Conservatives. In conclusion, Dr. Mackie expressed the hope that the fact of him and others having voted against the Mayor 12 months ago would never be recalled by the latter to the last day of his life. (Hear, hear.) On the resolution being put to the Counoil, there was a general chorus of "Ayes." The Mayon, on rising to respond, was received with ap- plause. He said: Mr. Ex-Mayor and gentleman, you can well understand that it is very difficult to express myself snitably in replying to the kind speeches which have been made about me. I can only say that lam sincerely thank- ful to you for your kindness to me. I had no idea when, I took the office of Mayor that I should have such a pleasant occupation. It has been a matter of great pleasure, gentlemen, to preside over you. (Applause.) I have received from everyone the greatest courtesy and the greatest kinlness, and I am thankful to hear my friends say that they consider I have behaved impartially. ,(Hear, hear.) I have striven my very best to be strictly im- partial, as I consider it is the bounden duty of every Mayor not to show favour to this party or the other. (Hear, hear.) I must also specially thank Dr. Mackie for the very kind way he has spoken of me. I never felt in the least degree hurt through any gentleman not voting for me when I was elected, because I know the circumstances some gentlemen were in compelled them to vote in the manner they did. It did not affect my mind in the least degree. I hope I have never shown any feeling towards those members different than I have shown to the rest of the Council. (Hear, hear.) From my heart, I have no feeling against any man in this Council. I c msider you all my friends. (Applause.) I cannot sit down without expressing my thanks to the Town Clerk, the Deputy Town Cleric, and tbe Borough Surveyor. lam sure the assistance and kindness I have received from them i something wonierful, and I can tell any gentleman, whoever he is, that miy follow me, thatahe may be sure his services will be very much lightened by the ab!e assistance of the officials of the Corpora ion. (Ap- plause.) I must not omit to mention Mr. Chorley. Everyone knows Mr. Chorley's kindness, and that he is al ways ready and willing to do all he posiibly can for any Mayor of this b wem,eli. (Hear, hair.) I thank you most heartily for the very kind and flittering way you have spoken of me, and lam only sorry I am not more worthy of it. (Aoplauee). The Council then separated.
We blindly follow Providence and ask no questions when we are led towards wealth,. but when we are led towards poverty our theology gives way and we suddenly begin to doubt.

Dionysius, reproving his son, for bad conduct, said," You never knew me do so." "No," replied the youth; "but you hadn't a king for a father." "And you won't have a son a king," said the monarch. It is a physical as well as a moral fact that it is in the power of every person to improve his own beauty as well as bearing by a constant control of passion and temper, and a deep and constant cultivation of the intellectual faculties, pure affections, and the moral nature.

HIGH Anus.—We ard always the better, all of us, for having aimed high, for having striven to see and know things as they really are, for having set Ourselves to walk in the light of that knowledge, to help forward great designs, and to do good.—_-_Vatthew Arnold. _ _

Johnson-, on first coming to Pembroke College, Oxford, was poor, and hardly able to keep up a decent appearance. An acquaintance meeting him one dav, observed, Why, Johnson, yonr shoes are capped! " Capped," answered Johnson promptly ; "well, and why shouldn't they be ? aren't they fellows?"

Professor-Ball, of Dublin, placed on record a fine specimen of an Irish bull in his speech at the meeting of the British Association. He was talking about the correctness of time- keepers, and he told his audience that none of their watches kept exact time, "for," said he, "some of them lose one way and some lose the other."

Nobody (said William Lloyd Garrison) ought to despair whose cause is just. Nobody is justified in despairing if he has a righteous cause to. uphold. It may not be given him to see him triumph, but that it is only a. question of time; it is an immaterial thing; but the right itself, why, there is no power on earth can ever stay it. None can ever defeat it in the end; God himself is- pledged to its final victory._

ALL COMMUNICATIONS MUST BB AUTHENTICATED.—A correspondent to a Yankee newspaper was in the habit of sending the editor paragraphs of the enormous eggs a pecu- liarly large race of fowls used to produce. At length Mr. Editor stopped the literary contributions thus: "To X.Y.Z. —Please acompany future notices of 'big eggs' with several ones of ordinary size, not for publication but as a guarantee of good faith." A " BOWTON " GIRL AND ERR DRESS —lt is stated that a Bolton girl went to Manchester to have a new dress made, and on being asked for a description. of tho one she re- quired, she said she wanted it " med up th' neck, an' deawn to th' bond; a diamond back an' a belt on; a walking length an' a striding width, wi a great big tuck and a &mince on '." and she further observed that "me and my hlli 'ul fetch id on Setterda fleet." It is needless to add that this novel explanation created much amusement.

A QUEER STORY.—The origin of the word "quiz" is due to Quin. Be bet one hundred pounds. with a nobleman, one evening, that, by the next morning at breakfast-time, there would be a word in most people's mouths that was never heard before. That night, when the theatre had closed, he got all the "supers" and others whom he hired, furnished each with a good lump of chalk, and, instructed one and all to go through the principal streets of London and chalk on the flags the word "Quiz." The next morning people were startled by seeing such an unusual sight. Some believed it was significant of danger—that a secret enemy was near, and that this was his watchword so the word went the rounds in a most amazing way. It might be said to be not "ii most people's mouths,"'but "in everybody's month." Quin, of course, won the wager.—London, Society. Fent PROFIT EXPECTED.—A few weeks since a railroad oollision on one of the roads leading out of New York killed, a-nong others, a passenger living in an interior town. His remains were sent home in good shape, and a few days after She funeral the attorney of the road called upon the widow to effect a settlement. She placed her figures at twenty thousand dollars. "Oh ! that ME is unreasonable," replied the attorney. "Your husband was nearly fifty years old." "Yes, sir ?" "And lame 2" "Yes." "And his general health was poor ?" "Quite poor." "And he probably woald not have lived over five years?' "Probably not. sir." "Then it seems to me that two or three thousand dollars would be fair compensation;' "Two or.three thou- sand!" she echoed. "Why, sir, I courted that man for ten years, run after him for ten more, and then had to chase him down with a shot-gun to get him before the preacher. Do you suppose I'm only going to settle for the bare cost of shoe leather and ammunition 2" RECENT EVENT AT AN HOTEL.—" Who's there?" There was no answer, and the queer noise stopped. "Anybody there?" No answer. "It must have been a spirit," he said to himself. "It must be a medium. I will try." Aloud—" If there is a spirit in the room, it will signify the same by saying ay—no, that's not what I mean. If there is a spirit in the room it will please rap three times. Three very distinct raps were given in the direction of the bureau.. "Is it the spirit of my sister " No answer. "Is it the spirit of my mother 2" Three raps. "Ate you happy ?" Nine raps. "Do you want anything?" A succession of very loud raps. "Will you give me any communication if I get up 2" No answer. "Shall I hear from you to-morrow 2" Raps very loud in the direction of the door. "Shall I ever see you ? " He waited long for an answer to his last ques- tion, but none came. The spirit had gone; and after think- ing about the extraordinary visit, he turned over and fell asleep. On getting up in the morning he found that the spirit of his mother had carried off his watch and purse, his trousers, and his great•coat downstairs in the ball.

MISCELLANRILTS. The races at Shrewsbury next Tuesday and Wednesday fortnight will, it is stated, be the last to be held there. A person named Devlya, who had been lecturing tgainst Romanism, was attacked by a mob at Barrow, and seriously maltreated. A telegrantlas been received in London announcing That the Australian cricketers intend coming to England next

• enmmer. Sentence of death has been passed, at Norwich assizes, upon Thomas Lyons Day for the murder of his child, aged nix years, at Ipmetch, in August last. The South-Western Railway Company have offered a substantial reward tor information respecting the late attempt to wreck a mail train near Dorchester. A youth named Thomas Osbortie was killed on Tuesday . Morning on the London and North-Vicstern Railway, be- tween Dudley Pert and Span Lane. Thomas Wales, a Leeds bating man, who has lately sus- tained heavy tEsses, attempted to commit-suicide on Satur- day afternoon by cutting his throat with a razor. A sturgeon weighing nearly 601bs. was, on 'Saturday. •capturod in 'Portsmouth Harbour, who leaped out of his punt and caught the royal fish by the tail in shallow

'water. During last week there was a decrease in Lancashire of, 15 farms and 32 cattle in the total 'number affected by foot- and-mouth-disease; leaving 165 farms and-220 cattle still! affected. The Stourbridge Improvement 'Commissioners have re- solved at a Bp, cial meeting to petition Her Majesty for a charter of corporation for Stourbridge and neighbouring townships. The Newcastle-on-Tyne 'magistrates havecommitted Wm. Alexander Ogilvie for trial, charged with having, as manager of the Northern 'Counties Bank, engaged in a' con- -spiracy to defraud. The ironworkers of Middlesborough, Stockton, and Hart- lepool have resolved to send in a claim that Bs. per ton be the minimum rate of wages, and that the basis of •payrnent he raised by 10 per cent. Thirty-three stacks of grain, out of a total of forty-one, -were burnt on Monday morning anCatlinwell Farm; Airlie. The cause is unknown. The damage is-estimated--at £B6O. -whicl. is covered by insurance. -A mass meeting of colliers was held at Dudley on Mon- day, when it was resolved net to accept the award made by 'Mr. Haden Corser, to the effect that 'the men are .not •entitled to an advance of wages. The coroner for West Middlesex held an inquest on Tues- day on Mary Ann Martin, who died from the effects of an 'unlawful operation. A verdict of "Wilful murder" against -some person or persons unknown was recorded. Mr. Henry Maillard, editor of the Guernsey Comet, whilst inspecting the sceneof a-fire at a chicory manufac- •tory in 'Guernsey, on -Saturday, was knocked down by a falling wall, and had one of his legs broken and received other serious injuries. Alderman Baker, an ex-Mayor of 'Portsmouth, has drawn 'up a memorial to Lord `Northbrook asking for recansidera- tion of the sentence en the-seaman Endersley, who was re- cently sentenced by tourt-martial to-five years' penal servi- tude for-striking a ship's corporal on board ship. At Rowley, Mary Hibbs has been remanded for unlaw- fnlly wounding George Hadley, miner. On Saturday night, during a quarrel between Hadley and the prisoner's husband, the prisoner-seized a poker and dealt Hadley a heavy blow on the head, inflicting a shocking wound and severing an artery. A shocking accident occurred on Monday morning to Jos. Ashton, a relief-signalman in the employ of the Manchester, Sheffield, and •Lincolnshire -Railway Company. The de • ceased, who was officiating at Barnsley, was going along the line to his box, when•he was knocked down and killed on the-spot by a passenger-train goingto Sheffield. An explosion, resulting in the death of one man and serious-injury to three others, took place on Tuesday morn- ing in a coal pit at Little .Lever, worked by Messrs. T. Fletcher and Sons. The explosion Appears to have been due to-the want of -care on the part of four colliers, who commenced work with naked lights in a place where only a few hours previously there had been a fall of roof, followed by an accumulation of gas. At Glasgow, on Tuesday, a musician named Henry Orme- rod was fined two guineas, with the alternative pf 30 days' imprisonment. for wilfully destroying the music score of -"The Merry Duchess," belonging to the Kate Bentley Corn- pany, who were performing in Glasgow last week. The prisoner had been dismissed, and his action was in way of revenge. The score destroyed was the only copy of the composition in Scotland. FRATBRNAL FIGHTING.—At the Sheffield :Police Coura on Monday, Mr.' G. Eadon, manufacturer, appeared in answer to a " peace " summons taken out by his brother, Mr. Vincent Eaden, auctioneer. The defendant considered himself aggrieved over some money matters arising out of his fathers will, and had twice assaulted his brother. For this he had been bound over. He now refused to be bound over again, and was sent to prison for four months. GALLANT RESCUE OF A FAHILY.-1 fire occurred bn Monday morning in the bedroom of a -small dwelling-house at Birmingham, occupied by a labourer at the gasworks. A mechanic named James Murray burst open the front door, rushed through the flames and dense smoke, and carried out a man, his wife, and three children, in succession, unassisted. They received attention from neighbours, and all eventually recovered. The fire was caused by a candle igniting drapery while the people were asleep. An inquest was held on Monday morning respecting the death of Edward Spicer, solicitor'selerk,who held a position of responsibility in a leading Birmingham firm;and whose body was found in the canal on Sunday. It was shown that the deceased was highly respected; but of late be had been greatly depressed in consequence ef having to break off his marriage engagement through ill-health. The banns had been publisht-ti in the Hrmingham Parish Church. A verdict of temporary insanity was returned. A Donn= TRAGEDY.—A coroner's inquest was held on Tuesday at Gosport, Hants, on the body of a woman named Farmer, who died from the effects of her husband's illus- age. It was proved that the husband, a carter, threw a frying pan full of hot fat.cver his wife, and then threw her downstairs, breaking her thigh. The unfortunate woman died on Monday night. Previous to ,her death the husband was kicked by a horse and died. Tae jury returned a ver- dict of" Wilful mu-der" against the dead man. The Rev. John Banks, a Roman Catholic priest, was, on I Tuesday, charged before the Liverpool stipendiary magis- trate with embezzling £B3l belonging to Bishop O'Reilley. The prisoner bad been arrested hiParis. He admiited his culpability to the fullest extent and expressed his contrition, but his advocate put it to the court that he was neither a trustee in the statutory sense, nor "a clerk or servant," and that therefore ne criminal charge could lie against him. The' prosecuting solicitor also saw great diffi- culties in the way of a conviction, and the magistrate dis- charged the prisoner. CHURCH AND STAGE.—The Rev. Dr. Kay, of Edinburgh, who recently caused great sensation by his defence of the theatre, has resigned his pastorate. On the fast day he held what was called a sacred service in the Drill Hall. Professor Blackie presided. Mr. Howard, of the Lyceum Theatre, re- cited songs arai read Shakesperian selections, and perfor- mances were given by the Lyceum orchestra and Bavarian Band. On Sunday, Dr. Kay, after communion service, in- formed the congregation of hie resignation. The Drill Hill service, he said, was a mistake, and he regrettei having caused anybody grief. The congregation was deeply affected -by the intimation. OUTRUNNING A MAGISTILITE —At Pevensey sessions, Sussex, on Saturday, James Snell was charged with bnrglarionsly entering the farm buildings of Mr. Bretton, one of the local justices of the peace. Mr. Bretton and four other gentlemen secreted themselves in a barn, and during • the night a man, supposed to be Snell, entered the premises, and, after killing ten fowls, put them in a bag fer removal, when he was disturbed, and ran off followed by the magis- trate and his party. He, however, managed to outrun' his pursuers, and ma4e good his escape. Since then Snell was , traced to London. where he was arrested. The prisoner was committed for trial. ENGLISH PATENTS.—The following patents amongst • others, published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal were sealed during the week ending October 27th, 1883 : Henry Houldsworth Grierson and Thomas O'Maher, Man• chester, for iraprovemente in machinery or apparatus for cutting, shaping, or forming teeth of wheels, such improve- ments being also applicable to other purpose;; Wm. Wilson Hulse, Manchester, improvements in machinery for cutting metals; Robert Simpkin Piercy, Blackburn, an improved feed for rollers and purifiers, also applicable as a feed for other milling purposes; Joseph Slater Lewis, Birkenhead, improvementgin insulators or apparatus for carrying over head electric telegraph or other wires; George Ashworth • and Elijah Ashworth, Ma.nchester, improvements in and applicable to carding engines; Joseph Thompson, Bolton, improvements in apparatus for indicating the velocities of air currents; John Langton, Leyland, and James Gregson, Preston, improvements in looms far weaving.—List supplied by Mr. George Davies, CE., Fel. lost.P.A., patent solicitor, 4, St. Ann's-square, Liverpool. EXTRAORDINARY BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.—An ex- traordinary breach of promise case came before Mr. Justice Denman, at the Manchester Assizes, on Tuesday. The plaintiff was a barmaid formerly of the Manchester Limited Restaurant, and now residing in Leeds, and the defendant, - George Thomas Lee, landlord of the Union Hotel, Man- chester. Before the defendant took his hotel he was out of ' business, and spent a good deal of time in the company of the plaintiff. Miss Cox said the defendant had seduced her under promise of marriage, and in cress-examination she said they had stayed together aeseYeral places. She used to ledge in the same honse as a waitress named Polly Kirby, and several gentlemen friends used to call upon them. The gentlemen had played cards all night. and she and Kirby had taken their share of the winnings. They had as much spirits to drink as they wanted. These were sup- plied to a married man named Tierd,who gave her a diamond ring and other presente. The defendant also gave her presents. She denied that she was Herd's mistress. The defendant denied that he had ever promised to marry the plaintiff. He stayed all night with her at her lodgings, within a week of being introduced to hen—The Judge said ' the case was one such as had not happened in his expe- rience before; it was dirgraeeful to both parties. The plain- tiff's admission was disgraceful, and the defendant had ad- mitted what was disgusting.—The jury found for the plain- tiff, damages 405.. and said if the matter rested with them they should give costs to the plaintiff. • CA,i,CUTTA EXHlBEriGg.—There is every indication that this Exhibit,ion will be a great success The numter ef visitors is expected to be so large that arrangem.nts are being made for an encampment outside the city.
