FEARFUL COLLISION IN TIIE IRISII SEA.— A fearful col- lision, involving the loss of two vessels and fifteen lives, happened late on Tuesday night in the channel between Anglesea.and the frish coast. The London and North- Western Railway Company's new steamer Holyhead, a fast boat particularly adapted for the cattle traffic, left Dublin about eight o'clock. About mid-channel she met the Ger- man barque Alhambra, outward bound from Liverpool with coal, with a crew of twenty-five. The captain's daughter was also on board. By some error on one side or the other the steamer ran into the barque and cut her nearly in twain, with the result that she sank almost instantly. • B-ats were lowered from the Holyhead, and picked up thirteen ol the German seamen, but the master, his daughter, the mate. and ten sailors were unfortunately drowned. It was found that the Holyhead was also in a sinkir.g condition, and time was barely affordei for leaving the steamer in the boats when she foundered, taking down the quartermaster and a deck hand. Happily the night was fine, but it was only after several hours' pulling, and when the weather was changing for the worse, the the survivors were rescued by a Car- narvon schooner, kindly attended to, and landed at Holy- head on. Wednesday afternoon.

ADVENTORES OF A JOURNALIST.—At Clitheroe, on Satur- day. Alfred Wallace Kelly, who described himself as one of the journalistic staff of the eVere York Herald, was charged on remand with obtaining food and lodgings by false pre- tences frotnlames Whiff, licensed victualler, Swaß Hotel, Whalley. On Tuesday the prison! r went to the hotel and representing himself as a gentleman of means was taken in. On Wednesday he . ordered a carriage and pair and drove to Stonyhurst College. On returning. at night he ordered dinners for himself and six others and nine bottles of cham- pagne were drunk. On the following morning a bill amount- ing to £6 14s. 101. was presented to him and it was then found that he had no money," and he was given into custody. While he was at the hotel the prisoniv treated everybody aleout, and drinks ware supplied.—Police Constable Wadcson stated that be saw the pris oner on his arrival on Tuesday. Prisoner wanted to treat him, but he declined, Prisoner saia be was a reporter from the New York Herald and he had been sent over to England to ," Write up Stonyhurst 'College."—ln ex;elanation of his conduct the prisoner had stated that he had got entirely bewildered with drink, and did not know what he was doing. He had lost all his lug- gage, and had given all his money away while bordering on delirium tremens. He also stated that he was informed that the landlord treated persops at his expense after he Went to bed on Wednesday night. He had only been .in England sii days, and had dined with a Roman Catholic priest in Manchester previous to going to Whalley. He had many friends in England, including a well-known authoress. On coming to his senses he was astonished to find himself in such a predicament, as he was very respectably connected. —After hearing the evidence the Bench dismissed the case. ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN RAILWAY STATION.—For some weeks past painters have been busily decorating Runcorn railway station, and on Thursday morning, about nine o'clock, they were engaged ,painting the canopy which pro- tects the entrance to the afation. A scaffolding .composed of a plank resting upon two ladders was improvised for the work, and upon this two men were standing, when Peck 'e 'bus, driven by a young man,drew up to the parapet. In doing so the vehicle struck one 'of the !Adders, bringing the scaffolding to the ground. One of the men -saved himself by jumping upon the 'bus, but the other wor'eman, named . Grosvenor the other thy at Carnarvon.—Sir Charles Dilke was Troent.d on Thursday with the freedom of the burgh of Paisley. In acknowledging the .mpliment be reviewed the work of the Com- missioners engaged in the French treaty negotia- tions: He declared himself in favour of c)mmercial treaties, but said he had no right to say that the Cabinet ' were favour.ble to them,though he knew th tt they desired a trade arrangement with Spain. When the Franco-Belgin treaty should run out, if we should abstain altogether from the conclusion of commerc:al treaties, we might find our-, selves face to face with a Whole system of treaties made. not by . British negotiation, but directly against British trade—made, in fact, in the special interests of other countries—which be did not think would be desirable. Their nartial protection wets not enabling the French people to hold their own. Their catton trade was dwindling very steadily, and their woollen trade was not the trade it was a few years ago.

It is officially stated that the loss of life by the collision in the Irish Channel bltween the steamer Holyhead and the German ship Alhambra is now believed to be fifteen. The Pall Mall Gazette says it is out of the question that priority should be given to the London Municipal Bill. The Franchise Bill is fixed for next Session, and whether a London Bill accompanies it or not depends upon London itself.

On Wednesday night a number of men and girls assem- bled outside the house of a farmer named Johnstone, near Newry, and puffed smoke through the keyhole. Johnstone fired among them, wounding four seriously. He has been arrested.

The analysis of the results of the municipal elections on Thursday shows that the balance is considerably in favour of the Conservatives. Notwithstanding the Conservative gain, however, the Liberals are still predominant in most of th- town c:uncils, especially in the larger boroughs, thrott6t.out the country.

Amongst these may be men- ' tinned Mr. J. Warrington Wood, Mr. S. L. Fildes, A R.A., IMr. H. Woods, A,R.A , Mr. E. F. Brewtnall, member of the Society of Painters in Water Colours, and others. Exhibitions of the students' works have at various times been held, many of these have been found to. possess great merit, and we doubt not their exhibitton has been productive of much gaol in quickening a taste for art in the community. It is hoped the exhibition about to Us held will produce similar good results. It would appear that from this point the success of the school as an educational medium began to be aesured. The number of students increased, their success in competitive and r ther examinations was most marked, its influence was now for the first time felt far and near, and altogether it seemed to promise great benefits to the town. We tired that in 1834, the schoo', which now poesesse4 a large stock of casts and examples, was provided with new furniture and appliances, and additional accommodation was fotind. The teacher, •Mr. Collinson, extended his operations to several' of the private and public schools in the town, the Diocesan Training and tire Clergy Daughters' School being included in his list. • Ten classes weekly were (pined in the school during the year, confined to the last four days of the week, six of those public and four special classes. During this year, two exhibitions were held—one in February, confined to works produced in the school; and one in August, com- posed of the pr-ze drawings from all the schools in connec- tion with the Department. The former was visited by up- wards of 2,000 persons, the latter by 2,857. The Govern- ment Inspector several times visited the Warrington school, and we are told that in his report to the Science and Art Department tile school was referred to as "fully successful." The report for the year 1854 stated that in the competitive exhibitions of students' works at Gore House, the Warrington stedents had been very successful, bronze medals having been awarded to them in five different stages. Considering the recent establishmeet of the school, that success was remarkable and above the average of even the oldest established schools The Depart- ment allotted to the school one prize studentship sad two pupil teacherships. These exhibitions were celcu'ated not only to encourage the deserving students, but to meet wants already felt in the internal economy of the school. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE ENTOMOLOGICAL SOCIETY. —The usual monthly meeting of this society was held on Monday, in the Free Library, William Brown-street, the president, Mr. S. J. Capper, in the chair. A paper was read by Mr. Henry Capper on "Darwinism and Beauty." After reviewing Dr. Darwin's theory of the development of beauty through the agency of sexual selection, he pointed out that although this theory threw much light on the subject, it also left much unexplained; for instance, why the colours nd mat kings produced should be of a most refined type, or why beauty should exist throughout nature. They had, therefore, to look for something beyond; and since man's intellect was capable of appreciating and, to some extent, imitating this beauty, and since it was highly improbable that it had been created solely for his gratification, they were irresistibly led to the conclusion that it was the pro- duct of an intellect alike in kind, but immeasurably grander than man's own. The paper led to an animating and in- teresting discussion. Mr. F. M. Pierce exhibited a specimen of Labidura Giigantea taken in bis office, Titbebarn-street, and Mr. von Sobbe and Mr. Wilding some recently-captured 010. bful lopidetera.

div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 3, 1883.

WE have been favoured this week with a plethora of political oratory, and we hail it with satisfaction as one of the very best means of awakening the interest of the people in questions which vitally affect their welfare. Cabinet and ex-Cabinet Ministers, together with a host of lesser lights, have been busy at work, and all have been more or less instruc- tive. On Monday evening Lord RICHARD GROSVENOR and Mr. OSBORNE MORGAN at- tended a great Liberal demonstration at Car- nprvon, in the very room in which Sir Sur- FORD NORTHCOTE spoke some days previouslY, and from all accounts it would seem that in point of numbers the gathering of last week cannot be compared with that of Monday, whilst the speeches on the last mentioned day must have effectually dispelled some of the fallacies previously circulated by the Toil magnates. If any one really believed all Sir STAFFORD NOKTHCOTE said on the question of finance in his effort to prove that the pre- sent Government is more extravagant than its predecessor, such an one has only to peruse the speech of Lord RICHARD GROSVENOR tO satisfy himself that Sir STAFFORD'S figures are mythical ; and on the other hand the enthu- siasm which greeted the vigorous Liberalistn enunciated by Mr. OSBORNE MORGAN is a clear indication that the visit of the Leader of the Opposition in the Lower House has been of no effect. We question, indeed, if he has made a single convert. At the moment when Lord R. GROSVENOR and Mr. 0. Molt' GAN were holding forth at Carnatvon, Mr; LEONARD COURTNEY was delivering an act' dress, brimful of wisdom to his constituents at Liskeard ; and Sir HENRY JAMES was coun- teracting the evil effects, if any, of Mr. GIB' SON'S recent visit to Dumfries, by a slashing, party speech in the same borough. A perusal of the learned gentleman's remarks leads us to express the hope that he may never, as it is rumoured, be persuaded to quit the poi cal arena for the Speaker's chair. He has before him a bright political career. The same evening Mr. A. ARNOLD, the member for Salford, spoke at Oldham on his favourite subject of the franchise The hon memt er had no difficulty in showing how little sympathy the Conservative leaders have in common with the working classes on this question, and that the latter too of.en blindly follow mistaken friends. This question is no doubt an important one, and will one. day have to be dealt with, but the time as 1101 yet arrived for so doing. him. Sir S. NORTHCOTE was amongst his - neighbours at Culmstock on Wednesday. He , presided over an agricultural gathering, but he had no words of encouragement to offer, and his remarks were altogether dull, stale, and unprofitable. Alr. ARNOLD has put the teach- ings of the Tory leaders so neatly and so concisely in the following sentences that we need make no apology for quoting them here. The Conservative leaders, he tells us, say in effect to their followers :—" Accept the present distribution of power, of land, of wealth; shut your eyes to the evils of the laws which have given so much of your beau- tiful island for the enjoyment Of a few thou- sand families and their dependants ; close your thoughts upon the possession of 2,000,000 acres of the very choicest soil by improvident corporations which pay nothing to the revenue, while you of your penury pay in your eating and your drinking, and in- directly in your share of the profits of trade which comes to you as wages. Pretend to believe that it is the manifest destiny of this country. an arrangement of Providence, that 50.000,000 acres of the soil should be settled to the uses of 7,000 people ; cheer and ad- mire the sinecure system, a type of which calls upon you to pay 1,650 generals in your army, and to employ about zso of the num- ber; fall down and worship the method by which £150,000,000 of public property in the hands of the Church is so distributed that we have to listen to piteous appeals for the increase of small benefices and for the sup- port of poor curates with large families. Accept all this, and much more like it, as the groundwork of Conservatism, and then come and help us to rule the country. Fill your head with Tory tracts, close your eyes with Tory glue, stuff your ears with Tory wool, put your head in the Tory bag, and call yourself a Conservative workingman." This is not by any means an exaggeration. It is the sum and substance of Tory teaching, And it need not, therefore, surprise the Tory party that it is so barren of results. In these days something more substantial is required. It is refreshing to turn from the perusal of the utterances of the Tory chiefs to the bracing speeches of Sir CHARLES DIME and Mr. GOSCHEN, both of whom are now in Scotland. The latter, as we all know, occupies an isolated position on the franchise question, but on every other point his Liberalism is of the right stamp; and the vigorous manner in which he advocates it is of great service to his party. Sir CHARLES DIME has this week given a lucid, dis- passionate, and comprehensive review of the work of the past session; he has brought Out in bold relief the obstructive tactics, though somewhat veiled, of the Opposition ; conclusively answered the recent adverse criticism of the Government measures and policy; and he has shown that if the working classes of this country are to derive any bene- fit from legislation it is to the Liberal party they must look, and more especially to the Radical section thereof. We sincerely hope the working classes mill always view their interests in this light and act accordingly.

A Pool-BATE FOR Currox.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, en Monday, the magistrates sanctioned the levying of a pocr-rate of 9d in the ifor the township of Clifton. THE RIGBY CHARITY, RUNCORN.—Thursday, being All Saints Day, sixty aged widows each received a flannel petti- coat after divine service at Runcorn Parish Church, in accordance with the terms of the Rigby Charity. 110NOTTEL TO A RUNCORN MAN.—The Humane Society have awarded a bronze medal to M. Thomas Cooke, assur- ance agent, Church-street, who rescued a child from drown- ing in the Bridgewater Canal, Roncorn, about two months

ago. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, WIDNES. —On Thursday evening, Mr. E. Brereton VV illiams, of Liver- pool, delivered a lecture in Widnes National Schools on the temperance question. There was a large audience, and the Rev. J. Wright Williams presided. We understand that Mr. John Holford, conductor of ! Ellesmere-street Chapel choir, has in the Press a service of song compiled by himself. The work is entitled "Pilgrim ! Street," and is founded on the popular story of that name by Hesba Stretton. It contains an original piece. UNITED CHESHIRE AND LANCASHIRE PERMANENT BUILDING SOCIETY.—It will be seen from the advertising , columns that the annual meeting of this society will be held in Holy Trinity girls' school on Thursday evening next. We understand that a favourable balance sheet will be presented. The anniversary sermons in connection with St. John's Presbyterian Sunaay School, Runcorn, were preached on Sunday by the Rev. John Johen, formally a Wesleyan minister in the town. The rev, gentleman also preached a sermon on Monday evening. There were crowded congrega- tion e at each service, and the collections amounted to £2l. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS, RUNCORN.—To-morrow ' the annual sermons in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions will be preached in St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, , by the Rev. C. W. L. Christien, of Burslent. On Monday evening the annual meeting will take place in the same edi- fice, when an address will be delivered by the Rev. Sylvester Whitehead, formerly a missionary in China. At the Chester Assizes, on Tuesday, Charles.Rowson, 42 years of age, labourer, was charged with having criminally assaulted Mary Jane Ellis, eleven years of age, living with her parents in Canal-street, Runcorn, on the 4th August.— Mr. E. Burke Wood prosecuted, and Mr. E. Honoratus Lloyd defended the prisoner.—The jury found the prisoner guilty of the attempt, and he was sentenced to two years' imprisonment with hard labour. THE RECENT PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR AT RUN- CORN—The total receipts of this baz tar, held a few weeks ago, amounted to £l6l 6s, including a donation of £5 from Mr. John Simpson, £2 2s from Mr. W. N. Salt, and Li from Miss Salt. The expenses amounted to £2B 13s 6d, leaving a profit of £133 12s 61, which has been equally divided between the circuit and trust funds. I A SHIP'S CAPTAIN INJURED AT RUNCORN.—ShortI y alter Midnight on Wednesday, Captain Roberts, of the schooner Mergaret, lying in the canal between Weston Point and Run- corn,fell against the cabin skylight, inflicting a fearful gash over his right eyebrow. The wound bled profusely, and ! , Dr. Moaritz was called to his aid and the bleeding was stop- ! ' ped. Had the doctor's arrival been delayed another hour it ! is stated the injured man would have died. A LITCHI' ASHTON POACHER.—John Waterworth was charged at the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, with using a net for -the purpose of taking game on laud belon&- ing to Lord Gerard, at Ashton, on the 16th March, 1881.— Mr. Claydon, who prosecuted, said that prisoner had been in I gaol for a week, and Lord Gerard, feeling he bad had suf- ! ficent punishment, desired to withdraw the prosecution.— The prisoner was discharged. LUTHER COMMEMORATION AT RUNCORN.—The members of Bethesda Chapel, Runcorn, intend to commemorate the birth of Martin Luther, the great Protestant Reformer, on Sunday evening, the 11th inst., and the occasion will be a , most interesting one. The Rev. J. D. Thomas will preach ; a sermon on the subject "Just with God," and at the con— clusion the service of song, entitled 'The Reformetion," will be given by the choir, which will be assisted by the members of other Nonconformist choirs in the town. Mr. , Francis Fairhurst will conduct. I WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr. G. H. Panby prosecuted the following persons for neglecting to send their children regu- larly to school :—John Martin, Catherine Bishop, Walter Bushell, John Law, William Mather, George Richards, Michael Qeinn, Mary Grierson, Thomas Smith, Philip Keogh, John Kelly, Stephen White, Thomas Lee, Hugh Gallagher, Martin Elolland, James Fallon, Elizabeth Cross, John Kniveton, and John McCann (two cases). The usual fined of 5s was imposed in each case. The sons of Thomas Turner was ordered to be sent to the Hightown Truant School. A WIFE DESERTER AT WIDNES.—Joseph Risley was brought before the magistrates at Widnes Petty Sessions, en Wednesday, on a charge of ths.continued neglect of his wife ' and child two months' old.—Mr. Scannell, the relieving officer, stated the wife and child were admitted to VVhiston Workhouse on August 7th. They were in great distress, the ' child being ill and the mother suffering from epileptic fits. They remained their until the Bth of October, when the pri- soner sent for them from Warrington, but he was sub- sequently sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for stealing ; fruit, and his wife and child were again in the workhouse.— ' j The prisoner,. who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to a

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 3, 1882:

from a slight attack of fever, from which he is now entirely convalescent. I have mentioned one of the attractions of West End London Sunday afternoons. Mr. Borne Jones's studio affords another. .He has a quaint old house • near the West Kensington station, and at the end of his garden he has fitted up a gallery where his works may be leisurely inspected in that good light which they certainly require. You approach this gallery by a back lane from Matheson-road, and the visitor needs no introduction or special invitation. Yon preeent your card and write your name in a book, and there is the gallery open of a Sunday afternoon—you may.make your visit as short or as long as you like. I fancy this hospitality of the painter must be better known to Ameri- can English visitors, or perhaps the latter rely on their op- portunities at the Grosvenor.

It was curious to see how immediately the explosion on the underground railway told on the tratfic. The late hour at which it occurred prevented its being known in the West End till the morning, and, whether it was accident, or a wise provision of the company, at many of the stations the newspaper posters were not exhibited. Still it was remark- able to see how deserted the platforms were, though in all probability the cause was less alarm of danger than fear lest the trains would not work punctually. It was fully a day before the public recovered confidence, and the takings of the Omnibus Company were appreciably affected: I had almost forgotten one of the Art Exhibitions opened this week, and of singular interest. Those who knew Ph:z only by his book illustrations, would, I think, be both in- structed and delighted by the collection of pictures, water colours, and sketches, now for the first time exhibited to Londoners. I believe part of the collection had already been shown at Liverpool. They show the artist to have pos- sessed not t,nly humsur, but a feeling for beauty, and a sense of the value of composition, far which he has not generally got credit. There is much that reminds one of John Leech, and a little of Rowlandson, though of course without this extravagance. Many of the drawings were for sale, and on the first day of the exhibition many were sold.
BLED TO DEATII AT RUNCORN.

FATAL QUARREL WITH A STEPMOTHER. I A fatal occurrence of a most awful nature occurred at 1, Prescot Teirace, Perry-stree., Rune ye), en e; it ll' iy night. The tenants of this house are Semael Astiley, a iabourer, and his wife, Sarah, with whom byes a sree•eeii named Rtbert and a lodger n trned Thom es itoden. Fr.s fa oily ap- pears to have lived unhappily together. for :+t,prEother, who has an infirmity in her legs, is addicted Ti orunken• nese, and occasional squabbles take place. Robert Ashley was employed as a labourer at Messrs. Mathieeon's Chemi- cal Works, Widnes, and on Saturday he returned home from , his work between six and seven o'clock. He was sober, but the stepmother, although Boden declined to say she was drank, had had a drop of liquor. The stepmother demanded his hoard money for the past week, amounting to 133, but he refused to pay her for no other reason, according to the woman's statement, than that he was hot tempered and " was up to these little tricks." A quarrel was the conse- quence, and Ashley struck his stepmother several times on the head and face. She was sitting in the corner of the kitchen on a round chair with her head near the window, and when he aimed another blow at her she quickly removed her head, and his fist crashed through a pane of glass with such force that he fell forward with his arm through the aperture. The quarrel seems to have now finished, and Ashley sat down to the table to partake of the tea which had been prepared for him without noticing that he had , sustained any injury whatever. After the lapse of some , time, he suddenly saw that he was bleeding profusely from the arm, and in alarm shouted "Mother, mother, fetch the doctor; send for help." The woman ran out of the house , "like somebody wild" and fetched in several neighbours, while a person was despatched for Drs. MacDougall and Robinson. Neither of these gentlemen were at home, and the neighbours adopted measures they thought necessary. They bathed his hands and forehead with water, and ad- ministered brandy to him, hut blood continued to flow in a stream, and he lay listless in his chair. Boden, the lodger, who was in bed, was awakened, and he lent his aid. No wound could be found to explain whence the blood pro- ceeded, and Bowden went to Dr. Robinson's surgery. Whilst he was away, the Rev. George Hack, Wesleyan minister, who had been informed of the occurrence, went to the house, and the blood appearing to proceed from the leg he bound up that limb. The accident occurred about eight o'clock, and at half-past nine Dr. Robinson arrived on the scene, and made a thorough examination of the injured man, discovering an almost imperceptible cut on the right arm abovethe wrist, one of the main arteries being severed. He took all necessary measures for stopping the flow of blood, but the poor fellow, who was 32 years of age and unmarried, died from exhaustion at twenty minutes to eleven. The inquest on the body was held at the Bull's Head, Halton-road, on Tues- day morning, before Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, Mr. Isaac Speakman was the foreman of the jury. —Evidence bearing out the abeve statement was given by Sarah Ashley, step-mother of the deceased, and Thomas Boden, the lodger. The latter stated that Dr. Robinson when he heard of the occurrence at once went to the house. —The Coroner, after summing up the evidence, said he thought the neighbours did what they could to save the life of the deceased. Mr. Hack, the minister from Halton-road Chapel, especially seemed to have been very good. The people, seeing the blood coming from the arm of the de- ceased on to his leg seemed to have fallen into the mis- take that it was coming from the leg, and they bandaged that limb with the idea that they were stopping the flow of blood, while at the same time the main artery in the arm was bleeding the man to death. It was a great pity that they did not strip him; but having found as they thought the cause of the mischief they searched no further. This was one of those cases which showed the great use that ambulance secieties would be if their objects were fully known, especially in a tewn. Had there been a person person present on Saturday night who had attended the elementary lectures of St. John's Ambulance Society, he would immediately have known what to do. He would have stripped the man, examined him, found the wound, and by tying a piece of string round the limb have saved his life. Ihe use of these societies could not be exaggerated, for no one knew—ministers of religion anl policemen especially— , how soon they might be called in to a case of life and death. Had any of these kind neighbours, who were cer- tainly doing their best for the poor man, attended the ele- ueentary lectures of this excellent society, he had no hesita- tion in saying that the life of the deceased would have been saved. He thought the only verdict the jury could return was that this man was striking his stepmother when his arm went through a pane of glass and inflicted a wound causing bleeding, from which he died.—The jury then recorded a verdict to the effect that death was caused accidentally.
ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT FROM A
RUNCORN PUBLICAN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, John Needham, a young married man. I living at Winsford, was brought up, under a warrant, charged with having, on the 13th October, and divers other days, at Runcorn, being the servant of William Chadwick, fraudu'ently embezzled the sum of £4O, received by him for and on account of his master.— From the evidence adduced it appeared that Mr. Chadwick is a licensed j victualler, and keeps the Greenway vaults, Greenway- road, Runcorn. He is the owner of the fiat, Agnes, to which the prisoner had acted as captain for a considerable period. According to arrangements he was entitled to two-thirds of elle profits made on each trip, the owner (Mr. Chadwick) twpropriating the other third. Each time the prisoner drew a freight he had to settle with his master, but he had not accounted for a penny since the Nth of last May, when he handed over a certain rum. From that time he had made nine trips, and Mr. Chadwick calculated that he had received £lO, to which he (Mr. Chadwick) was entitled. About three weeks ago the prisoner absconded, and he was only apprehended on Wednesday. It is supposed that the prisoner has spent the money in dissipation. On the application of Superintendent Williamson, the prisoner was remanded for eight days, bail being allowed, himself in £4O, and two sureties of £2O each. In the event of bail not being forthcoming, his Worship ordered that the prisoner should be detained in Chester Castle, as he being ill he would be better attended to there.

PRIMITITE METHODISM IN WIDNES. The members of the Hutchinson-street Primitive Methodist Chapel celebrated the ingathering of the harvest on Sun- day last, when Mr. W. H. Gyton, of Warrington, preached in the morning on" Our Father," and in the eveniug on the text "I ata the bread of life." There were pod con- gregations at each service, and the collections amounted to upwards of £5. The chapel was prettily decorated with cereals, flowers, and fruits, and in one corner of the edifice was a miniature corn held, in which were rambling about rabbits and fowls. This unique "decoration," which created ! great interest, was the gift of Mr. Josuha Midwood. The I following persons contributed cereals, fruits, flowers, and vegetables :—Mrs. Abbot, Mrs. Leigh, Messrs. James Baker, Whea:ruff, Jonathan Naylor, Thomas Baker, Newport, J. midwood, H. W. Deacon, Joseph Littlemore, John Owen, Abraham White, Wm. Longton, Charles Clifton, and King. On Monday a fruit banquet was held in the chapel. Fruits were displayed in tempting array, and at various times during the evening the ladies distributed them amongst the large audience which bad assembled. The Rev. .7. Morton, of Warrington, occupied the chair, aud delivered an address appropriate to the occasion. There also spoke Messrs. John Owens (Helsby), H. Thornton (Warrington),. Shuttleworth, T. Barker, and J. Cason. The choir of the United Methodist Free Church, Oakland-street, was present, and under the conductorship of Mr. John Betney, rendered several anthems in an unimpeachable style. A choir under the conductorship of Mr. Lamb also rendered a good ac- coun't of itself, and a pleasant evening's enjoyment was brought to a conclusion by the usual votes of thanks.
THE TROUBLES OF A WIDNES PUBLICAN.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr. J. O. Swift, solicitor, St. Helens, applied on behalf of Mr. John Barrow for the transfer of the license of the George Inn, Waterloo-road, Widnes, from Frederick Siincock to his client.—Mr. Swift said there were circumstances in connec- tion with the application which rendered it difficult for him. Mr. Barrow, whilst he kept the Waterloo Hotel, Waterloo- road, in Mil, was summoned for permitting drunkenness, ' but the ctse was dismissed on Mr. Barrow paying costs. Unfortunately, in February of this year he was again sum- moned. The Bench considered that personally he was not to blame, but as be was liable for the actions of his barmen, he was fined 40s. and costs —After this conviction, Messrs. Walker, the owners of the hotel, turned Mr. Bat row out, and since then he had kept a fish shop in Manchester. This business had, however, not been successful, and he was desirous of again entering the " public business" to gain a livelihood. —Mr. Swift handed to their worships, Mr. Holbrook Gas- leell, senr., and Mr. F. H. Gossage, several testimonials as to the applicant's character, and observed that Mr. William Millar was in the court ready to speak as to the manner in which Mr. Barrow conducted the house he previously held. —Mr. Gaskell said it looked as if the applicant was careless when he was convicted twice.—lnspector Wood said he was instructed by Supt. Barker not to oppose the applic ttion, as he thought that Mr. Barrow would conduct the house pro- perly if he had another chance.—Mr. Gaskell supposed Supt. Barker had good grounds for the course be had adopted, but in his own mind he hesitated to grant the ap- plication. In consequence of the representations that bad been made, however, the Bench would permit the transfer of the license.

LAUNCH OF A SCHOONER AT RUNCORN. At noon on Thursday, a three masted Fchooner, of fine proportions, was launched from the yard of Messrs. Brun- dritt and Co., shipbuilders, Runcorn. A large number of ladies and gentlemen resident in the neighbourhood assem• bled to witness the event, which, in spite of a somewhat foggy atmosphere, 'passed off with considerable eclat. Amongst those present we noticed the Rev. Canon Barclay, Miss Barclay, Miss Hazlehurst and Miss Eva Hazlehurst, Miss Malcolm, Mr. and Mrs. John Brundritt, Dr. and Mrs MacDougall, Mr. and Mrs. E. A. Cherlton, Mr. J. Foulkes, Rev. W. C. Safford, Rev. T. W. Arrnson, Rev. R. Edwards, Rev. D. Llewllvn, Rev. Mr. arrl Mrs. Vause,. Mr. W. Mellor, Mr. and Mrs. lirice, Mr. and Mrs. Ravenscroft, and Mr. Davies. As the vessel left the stays amid the cheers of the assemblage and the roar of cannon, she was cl r'stened "Sunbeam" by Mrs. Mclvoy, wife of one of the share- holders. The vessel, which has b.en Luilt to the order of Mr. James Foulkes and a number of other Runcorn gentle- men, is of the following dimensions :-103 feet long, 23 feet 9 inch beam, and 11 feet deep: she has a carrying capacity of 250 tons, her registered tonnage being 135 tons, her frame is of English oak, her bottom and bilges of rock elm, while the cabin is of cedar wood, and comfortably fitted up. She is yellow, metal fastened, provided with double action pumps, and has the full complement of nautical instruments. In the after cabin accommodation is provided for captain and mate, and in the fore cabin for six seamen. 'there are also two state rooms in the after part of the vessel. The carving has been executed by Mr. Clotworthy, of Liverpool ; and the vessel has been painted and decorated by Mr. 'Yar- wood, of Church-street, Runcorn. The schooner has been rigged by Mr. Jokn Bate, of Blantyre-street, and Mr. S. Ravenscroft has supplied a full suit of sails. We must not omit to mention that the vessel, which is classed 13 years A 1 at Lloyds under special survey, has been constructed from the designs of Mr. John L. Davies', manager and draughtsman to Messrs. Brundritt ; and that she will be commanded by Captain John Jenkina, late captain of the Snowflake, a vessel recently launched from the same yard. The Sunbeam is intended to engsg, in the Newfoundland fish trade.
A BEERHOUSE KEEPER HEAVILY FINED AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Patty Sessions, on Monday, Ann Payne, landlady of the Cornwall and Devonshire Arms was sum- moned to answer a charge of assaulting Mrs. Ann Green- wood, dressmaker, It...gent-street. There were also cross- summons charging Mrs. Greenwood and her daughter with assaulting Mrs. Payne.—Mr. Burton appeared for Mrs. Payne.—Mrs. Greenwood stated that about four o'clock on the 18th October she was sitting sewing in her own house, when there was a knock at the door, which was opened, and she saw Mrs. Payne, who was drunk, standing there. Mrs. Payne asked her" Who authorised you to say I keep a bad house?" Witness denied making auy such assertion. Mrs. Payne called her a " stinking liar," and struck her a blow on the eye, which sent her reeling against the table. Mrs. Payne struck her two or three times afterwards, knocking her to the floor on to the top of her child. When she was lifted up, Mrs. Payne was coming over the board which was , placed to prevent the child from going out of the house, and she rushed to push her out, when Mrs. Payne seized her by the "hair of the head," and I - threatened "to do six months for her." Mrs. Greenwcol's daughter then attempted to push Mrs. Payne out with a sweeping brush, but the latter wrested it from her hand, and struck her on the head. The door was then closed, the leg and arm of Mrs. Payne becoming fastened, but she released herself, and going into the middle of the road, doubled up her sleeves, and challenged Mrs. Greenwood to fight.—Two witnesses were called in cor- roboration of this statement.—Mrs. Payne said she had on different occisions heard statements affecting the character of her house, originating from Mrs. Greenwood, and on the day in question she went to the latter's house to complain. Mrs. Greenwood swore, and her daughter struck her several times on the head with a brush, Mrs. Greenwood also struck her on the face, scratching her hand with the pin of her brooch. Mrs. Payne denied striking Mrs. Green- Wood, and also the statement that she was drunk. She was never in Mrs. Greenwood's house. Mrs. Greenwood re- moved' the board from the doorway and threatened to knock her brains out with R.—About half a dozen witnesses were called, who supported Mrs. Payne's statement, and were unanimous in stating that Mrs. Payne never struck Mrs. Greenwood.—Mr. Btu ton having addressed the Bench, the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell (chairman) said there was no doubt Mrs. Payne had committed a gross assault on Mrs. Green- wood in her own house, and the magistrates considered they were justified in lining her 403. an costs. (Sensation.) The summons against Mrs. Greenwood was dismissed. Mrs. Payne had also to pay costs amounting to £1 lie. 6d.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

FALSE RUMOURS.-THE BISHOP OF LONDON.- THE LORD MAYOR AND THE LORD CHANCEL- LOR. - CLOSE OF THE FISHERIES. - FIRST NIGHTS. - MARY ANDERSON AS PAULINE.- A FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE. - CHARLES READE'S NEW NOVEL. - MR. SANTLEY AT THE CARME- LITES -MR. BURNE JONES. - PHIZ IN BOND- STREET. - THE FENIAN OUTRAGE ON THE UNDERGROUND.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The Society Journals have been very busy filling up the vacancy to be caused by the resignation of the Bishop of London. We were told what Dr. Jackson's retiring income would be, and which of the episcopal residences he would select. This anxiety to settle matters in advance has turned out to be quite unnecessary. The Bishop of London does not think of resigning, and did not think of it. His return to Fulham in good health, and his readiness to transact busi- ness in his diocese, contradicts the report put forward re- cently with so much circumstance. Let me also contradict two other rumours still to some extent believed. We are not going to have our Lord Mayors' show shorn of its ac- customed grandeur. It is not yet settled whether we shall have anything as ambitious as that triumphal chariot dragged along the Thames Embankment in the rain by horses from Astley's and surmounted by fyttrantes repre- senting the four quarters of the world cower- ing under umbrellas. But the men -at - arms will certainly figure in the procession, and certain novel features will be added for the amusement of the populace and the profit of the pick-pockets. The other rumour relate.; to a matter of a little more importance. Lord Selborne has no notion of giving up the Woolsack, and even if he did, Lord Coleridge would not accept it. He is not a rich man, he has a family of several children, one of whom will be a peer and must have a peer's incsme, and he would gain very little dignity by the change. The Lord Chief Justice is a bigger man in the world's eyes than when the Common Pleas and the Exchequer had their chiefs also. His income is very nearly as large as the Chancellor's, and does not de- pend on his party being in.

The Fisheries were closed on Wednesday after a success quite unexpected, and quite unprecedented. There was a curious contrast between the enormous throng collected on Tuesday night and the orderly and highly-respectable con- course who were present to witness the closing ceremony. It was held in the large hall of the Inland Fisheries, and the decoration of the dais fitted up with fishing gear, nets, tackle, oars, flags, and cordage was at once very ingenious and very picturesque. No One could have been more gracious than was the Prince of Wales. He has the royal faculty of recognising anl of showing recognition, and needed no master of the cere- monies to point out to him tke persons who should be noticed. The Baroness Coutts was, as she deserved to be, very prominent. No lady in London, and few gentlemen, have such an interest in the Exhibition. Of the speakers I think Sir William Harcourt was the best; he certainly made himself the most audible. In that great Hell neces- sarily a large number of the guests could only gratify their sense of sight, and it was curious to see the waves of applause roiling beck to the remoter parts of the building and caught up and repeated by persons who could not possibly have heard the sentiments they so loyally clapped. The Prince of Wales' speech was specially good. He was listened to with great attention, and with considerable interest, when he came to speak of the purposes to which the surplus money was to be devoted. The ap- plication of science to the catching as well as to the culture of fish has all along been admitted to need support in this country. We want such an institution as the Austrians have founded at Trieste, and it is likely we shall have it. The Exhibition has at least wakened up Londoners to one of the most important of British interests. We are now well into the season of First Nights. All the leading theatres have their novelties in action or in re- hearsal. During the last couple of years a fashion has arisen which has been pushed so far thet it has become a nuisance.. It is the fashion of floral tributes. When a great actress achieves a wonderful success the flinging of a bon- qeet is a kind of relief to excited teethe:, In Italy :on a first night the men egement has always great baskets of flowers ready,and if the enthusiasm reaches the proper pitch the baskets are brought forth ; but where there is little en- thusiasm there are no dowers. With us the flowers are sup- posed to come direct from the audience. Latterly they have been given where they have not been deserved. I was at a first night this week and saw a play nearly lost by the folly of friends who had brought flowers and insisted on throwing them. The pit and gallery thought this delicate attention was not quite deserved, the actress looked very foolish, and the fate of the piece was for a few moments jeopardised. Instead of enthusiasm, there was something very like derision. If the public had been mischievous the result might have been serious. Private friends may send as many bouquets as they like round to the stage door, but it is an absurdity for a pertisan to think that he cm n deliver a verdict, and it is an impertinence for a hireling to think he can do so. I fancy at that theatre the management will see to it in future. Miss Anderson has rather surprised the public and her critics by sticking to the old fashioned and exploded drama for her debuts. We cannot measure her capabilities when the tests of them are such plays as Ingomar and the Lady of Lyons. What Artetnus Ward called "the natural style of doing things" does not belong to these plays. Her acting in the present piece is very graceful, but artificial, and sometimes inconsistent. The truth is, the pretty Ameri- can poses. She is always conscious of the camera, as if she was sitting, standing, walking, or kneeling for her photo- grapher. She has not yet got the art to conceal her art, or at least she does not show that she has it. The very selection of such a pity as the Lady of Lyons argues a kind of weakness. But it is unfair to prejudge her. She has beauty and she has grace. She is pre-eminently a lady on the stage; what is wanted is a little nature, a little forget- ting of the actress, a little unconsciousness. In Pauline she is handicapped by the artificiality of the play. Will she have the courage to try Shakespeare ? It seems so strange that the most popular actress in go-ahead America should seek to bring us back to the artificial drama. One of the prettiest girls in London is going to be mar- ried. The daughter of Arthur Chappell, of Bond-street, has been for the last three seasons pre-eminently a belle, and has never been what is called a photographic beauty. Her portrait has been lately painted by Sandys, but other- wise I am not aware her photographs have only been seen by her friends. At a private view at the Grosvenor a couple of winters ago it was quite a question whether she or one of Professor Huxley's daughters was the prettiest girl in the room. She is engaged to Mr. Calley, of the let Life Guards; and St. George's, Hanover-square, will be pretty sure to be crowded next Wednesday at two o'clock. It is a long time since we have heard of Charles Reads, at all events as fiction writer, but he is going to come forth from his seclusion. He is just finishing a work for the sheets of which America seems as anxious as England. In the lull which has fallen on novel writing, the author of "It is never too late to mend," will find many readers to welcome an old favourite. Messrs. Harper have secured for Canada and the States the copyright across the Atlantic. At home Meisrs. Tillotson hold the serial right, and the work will appear in some first-class provincial weeklies, simultaneously with the publication in America. The Carmelite chapel at Kensington has latterly got to be one of the most fashionable of West-End Sunday rendezvous. It was always rather electic in its assistance, but now the vesper service is thronged, while the pro- cathedral is not indeed deserted, but certainly not overfilled. This influx of fashion is singular, but has its-reason. Some time ago, Mr. Santley, with the ardour of a convert, showed his devotion to the creed he had adopted by offering to sing at the vesper service of the Carmelite church. Of course the offer was accepted, and of course the rumours were abroad. The music was always an attraction, but new the attraction got to be paramount. Mr. Santley was not always able to attend, but the choir of the Carmelites contains a very admirable baritone amongst its members. People went and heard that baritone, or if they did not hear him they heard Santley ; whichever it was they heard, they always thought it was Santley, and they always said so. Thus the little church got to be very crowded, and the carriages in waiting show what sort of crowd it is. I wonder whether Mr. Santley's. marriage will affect his attendance in the choir. His bride will be of the same religion as her hus- band, and she is a foreigner, at least her ancestor. were Spanish grandees. I am happy to hear that a great deal too much has been made of Mr. Borne Jones's illness. fie iaus peen suffering

div.head: DETECTION OF AN INGENIOUS RAILWAY FRAUD. A RUNCORN CLOTHES DEALER HEAVILY FINED.
div.p: DETECTION OF AN INGENIOUS RAILWAY FRAUD. A RUNCORN CLOTHES DEALER HEAVILY FINED.

Roger Rooney, a well-known second-haud clothes dealer, of Regent-street, Runcorn, was summoned at Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, for having, on the 15th ult., ridden in the London and North-Western Railway, from Broadheath to Warrington, without previously paying his fare and with intent to defraud the company.—Mr. Preston, Jun., of Chester, appeared for the company, and said that the case was one of a most ingenious attempt at fraud. On the arrival of the Manchester Laudon-road train at Tim- perley the defendant was asked for his ticket, and he pro- duced one from Knott Mill to Stretford. The stationmaster requested him to pay 31., the additional fare to Timperlev, and he did so. In answer to questions, the defendant told the stationmaster that he was going to Broadheath, and the latter replied that he must book to Broadheath if he was going there. The defendant said, "Oh, I can pay when I get there," but the stationmaster insisted on his taking a ticket which he ultimately did. The conduct of defendant had thus aroused the suspicions of the stationmaster, and he gave instructions to the guard to " keep an eye on him." On arrival at Broadheath the defendant went to the guard's van for his bag. The guard asked him if he wanted to get out there, and the defendant then said he was going farther on. Inspector Massey then entered the train, having re- ceived a hint from the guard. When the train arrived at Widnes the defendant alighted and gave up the return half of a ticket to Warrington. Lie was then charged with rid- ing from Broadheath to Warrington without a ticket, and he admitted the fact and offered to pay the fare, but it was refused.—Robert Farrow, stationmaster at Titnperley ; Amos Cooper, guard; and Mr. Smith, stationmaster at Widnes, gave evidence corroborating the above statement. Cooper added that when the train arrived at Thelwall the defendant offered him some coppers and asked him to get a "drink." Smith also added that the defendant for a long time was in the habit of taking a return ticket for Manchester, but latterly he had taken one for Warrington, and since the summons was issued had again commenced to take one for Man- chester.—The defendant made a plausible explanation, equally ingenious with thefraud, hut the defendant ordered , him to pay 40s and costs, in all £3 17s.

ROBBERY FBOAI RUNCORN COLLEGIATE SCHOOL. Before Mr. Jno. Brundrit and Captain C. W. Hazleburst, a. Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Frederick Geo. Leach (13) and Arthur Williams (11), sons of respectable parents living in Irwell-street, surrendered to bail on a charge of having, on the both October aria other days, stolen two tame rabbits, belonging to Joseph King, aud three others, belonging to John Bright White, David Livingstone White and Fredk. Hardley.—From the evidence, it appeared that the prosecutors are all boarders at the Runcorn Callegiate school, where tl.my have a rabbit hutch. At various times during the past week rabbits had been missed from the place, and on Monday night Gerald George Powell, a boarder at the school, watched the cote. About half-past nine be Saw the prisoner Leach climb over the wooden fence, drop into the playground, and walk up to the rabbit cote. Powell followeil, and Leach, seeing him, fled, but he was pursued and captured in Irwell-lane. There was another boy looking over the fence, but it was too dark to distinguish his features. Subsequently P.C. Wal- lace took Leach into custody and locked him up. He then went to his parents' house and found one of the rabbits pro- duced. He then went to Williams' house, and there found four of the rabbits which had been identified that morning. When charged with the robbery neither of the prisoner's replied. Leach now pleaded guilty, but Williams made a somewhat incoherent statement, in which he explained how two of the rabbits got into his possession, but admitted that he had received other two from the prisoner Leach.—Leach said Williams was with him when he stole the rabbits.—Mr. Brundrit severely censured the boys for their conduct.—The Bench did not think it right that the parents should suffer for their misdeeds, and instead of fines being inflicted Leach was ordered to receive 12 and Williams six strokes with the birch rod at the hands of Sergeant Walley. PROPOSED NEW BAPTIST CIIIPEL FOR WIDNES. On Wednesday afternoon a bazaar was opened in Lacey- street Wesleyan Schoolroom, by the Rev. Eli E. Walter, president of the Liverpool Baptist Union. Its object was to raise funds to build a new Baplist Chapel. At present the members of the Baptist denomination in Widnes worship in a dilapidated.structure in. 'Nelson-street, a somewhat nn- savoury locality, which when the chapel was erected it was . thought would be what may be called the " West-end of Whines." The traffic of the town was, however, diverted into another channel, and the Baptists find their edifice sur- rounded by squalid tenements, and enveloped in the gases from numerous chimneys. As many of the congregation live on West Bank, and a still greater number at Appleton and Similes' Cross, the position of the chapel is also very inconvenient, and on the one day in the week when the people desire to evade the vile smelling fumes from the works, the Baptists, if they wish to worship in their own sanctuary, are compelled to worship in their very midst. The present chapel, too, is becoming too small for the congregation, which numbers about 200 persons, and under the energetic pastorate of the Rev. It. Yeatman, who two months ago took charge of the place, shows great promise of developing to a much larger extent, whilst the attendance at Sunday school is on the increase. Mr. Yeatman was trained at Mr. Spurgeon's College, Lon- don. From thence be went to B. oad Green, near Liverpool, to conduct a mission for Mrs Robt. Gladstone,and nis labours in that place were highly appreciated, and his departure for Widnes was much regretted. He has earnestly set to work to better the condition of the people amongst whom his lot is now cast, and he is pushing forward the project for a new chapel with vigour. It is contemplated to,ereet a buildin' at a cost of not less than £l,OOO, and towards this tale sum only £3O has been as yet received. To raise this amount to at least £lOO was the object of the bazaar, for which the ladies of the congregation have for some months been assi- duously labouring. A sewing meeting has been held periodically, and the lissom fingers of the ladies have trans- formed plain stuffs of all descriptions into desirable articles of wearing apparel, aim Help, too, has been vouchsafed outside the town. Valued presents have been received fro in Mrs. Robert Gladstone, Wootton ; Mies Ruff, Liverpool; Mrs. Greenhough, Manchester; and Miss Holme, Man- chester. The result was three stills heavily laden with a variety of articles of fine texture and brilliant hue; and a fourth stall was a tempting display of confectionery. Mrs. Barker and Mrs. Priestnall presided over stall No. 1, while No. 2 had for its attendants Mrs. Bailey, Mrs. J. Davies, and Mrs. Lloyd. The yonng ladies' stall was in charge of Miss Bailey, Miss Priestnall, Miss Davies, Miss Passey, the Misses Thompson, Miss 'Hai vey, Miss Seddon, 'Miss Welling, Miss Mackereth, and Miss Bennett. Mrs. C Aland and Mrs. Lomax had charge of the refreshment stall.—ln introducing the Rev. E. E. Watters to open the bazaar, the Rev. R. YEATMAN said they had a great deal of hard work before them in Widnes, and it was necessary that they should have a new chapel,, as the pre- sent one was very badly situated, and Mr. Walter had come that day to express his sympathy and render willing help.— The Rev. E. E. WALTER said the Baptists of Widnes had his truest sympathy in their undertaking, which he hoped would succeed. He hoped the general Christian public of Widnes would come to their support on that occasion. He was pleased that Mr. Yeatman was so happily situated amongst them, and that the work of the denomination had began to revive. Hitherto it had riot been particularly flourishing, and he did not know how it could flourish under the inauspicious conditions by which it was surrounded. No man could do very much under such circumstances, and ne hoped the time was not far distant when they would be worshipping in a new chapel. (Applause.)—The Rev. R. YEATMAN then spoke a few words in acknowledgeine it of ' Mr, 7.•e!tefe, .seeice!) en'.l t'ee tales were commenc:el.

div.head: – HARTLAND WESLEYAN CHAPEL,
div.p: - HARTLAND WESLEYAN CHAPEL,
WIDNES.

The annual sermons in aid of the Wesleyan Fereign Mis- sions were held to this place of worship, on Sunday last. In the morning Mr. J. Poulson, of Widnes, preached to a good congregation ; whi!e fn the eveninz the Rev. J. Hothersall occupied the pulpit. There was a good atten- dance. On Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was held, under the presidency of Mr. B. Brown. Tnere was a good audience, and the following (Zentlemen occapied s-ats on the platform :—Revs. J. Harper, J. H ithersall, S. Robinson, S. B. Stringer, and Mr. J. Houghton. Mr. W. Efartland was also present. The Caterrtelare. said he Mt somewhat honoured that evening in having the privilege to preside over the first missionary meetipg held ill that beautiful Chapel. (Hear, hear.) lie trusted there would be many sueh meetings in the chapel, meetings which had for their object the spread- ing of the glorious Gospel of our blessed SAviour. They had heard a great deal on former occasions of the theory of inissiens, and of the privilege of contributing to their sup- port; and he thought it would be as well if they had one or two facts of what missionaries had accomplished in various ports of the world. In the course of his reading during the last few weeks, he bad come across a narrative 4 the result of Christian work, which he considered to be encouraging. It was not in connection with the Wesleyan Foreign Missions. He referred to the Siudwich Islands, where Captain Cook was in ossacred in 1817. At that time the inhabi(ants of those isles were savages, but in 1835 an American Missionary Society seat out missionaries ampngst them Mr. McGowan, who preached earnestly, and when he to'd the people that ' there was endless life in Jesus Christ, and they understood the doctrines of Christianity, they rejoiced exceedingly. On one Sunday something like 1,700 of these savages were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and now these islands possessed all the machinery of civilisation; and were peopled by law-abiding and law-loving citizens. They hied missionary meetings like they in Widnes were holding that night, anal one church annually sent 1,200 dollars to support missions in other parts of the world. (Hear, hear.) This %vim whet Christian missions had accomplished, and Is need not .make an apoloey for advocating in any way he could the claims of Foreign Missionary Societies. (II or, hear.) Mr. JOHN' tforeGirroN read a few facts from the General Missionary Report, and urged those present to take greater interest in the glorious work. Mr. SAIMEL ROBINSON gave an earnest address, and was followed by Mr. S. B. STRINGER, who depicted England Decanted with savages Lie ancient times, the advent of the missionaries, and the conversion of England to Christianity, And he said it was our duty and our privilege to impart to the savages of other lands the blessings we now enjoyed. The Rev. J. HARPER remarked that the missionary enter- prise had his earnest sympathies, beciuse it provided a pinacemfor all the ills which afflicted humanity. He con- sidered the members of Hartlan I Chapel were not ambitious enough in subscribing to the Missionary Society, and he appealed for larger contributions in the future from those who were favoured by fortune. The Rev. J. HOTHERSALL, formerly a missionary in the West Indies, narrated his experiences in that country, describing in graphic languege his daily life among the people. The people in the West Indian islands were, be said, Methodists to the bock bone—(hear, beir,)—and some times their Methodism was pat to the test, for they had in the West Indiss, as in this cluntry, High Churchism. There were man who hated the name of Mchodisin, and who did all in their power to hinder the Methodist missionaries in their work. The rev. gentleman related instances, and con- ended by an appeal for the sympathy and aid of the audience for the foreign missions, A. collection wee then made. The amount realised was £3 is 41, which, added to the previous day's collection of £4 is Id, made a total of £7 14s sd, nearly double last year's amount.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

This Board held its fortnightly meeting at Dutton work- house on Tuesday, when Mr. John Aehton presided, there being also present :—The Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. J. Challoner, H. Neild, James Darbyshire, E. Wallington, C. Rigby, 11. Linalier (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy-clerk), and J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances).—The plan sub- mitted by Mr. Foulke, of Frodsham, for the building of seine hoases in Frodsham, were approved —Mr. CHALLONER gave notice of his intention to move, at next meeting, that a committee, consisting of the guardians and ex-officio guardians of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship be appointed to transact the business arising out of the new bye-laws for Frodsham, &c., and subinit their minutes at each Board meeting.—The following report was received from the medical officer (Dr. Bride): " Gentlemen, I have to report the deaths of Samuel Robinson, late of Town Well, Kingsley, and Thomas Parker, late of Deepinoor-lane, Kingsley, bath registered as having been due to typhoid fever. It is, how- ever, my duty to inform you that, in my opinion, neither death was due to specific typhoid feven, although probably there were present in the case what are known as typhoid , symptoms, which coma on in many other forms of s!ekness, I such as acute and chronic chest affections, &c. No fault could be found with either of the cottage premises or their surroundings. I may add that Samuel Robinson came from Liverpool for the purpose of being attended by his aunt at Kingsley. I have also to report an outbreak of scarlet fever in a cottage occupied by Margaret Clarke, at Sutton. One child, Elizabeth Clarke, is suffering from the disease, which still continues at Weston Point, where it has now made its appearance at the Rookery. The customary mea- sures have been adopted. It would be very advisable for the Sanitary Authority to authorise the Inspector of N uisances to obtain, for the purpose of analysis, a sample or samples of all waters of doubtful purity within the district for the purpose of reporting thereon."— A discussion arose as the advisability of securing legal as- sistarce for the Inspector in prosecutions instituted by the Board.—Mr. FARRINGTON Slid that in the c 1,9r3 of idilapi- dated cottage before the magistrates at Daresbury that day, he considered that the inatter bad been dealt with in an un- eatisfactory manner owing to the views of the magistrates' clerk not coinciding with his as to whether or not notice should be served previous to legal action being taken.—Mr. CHALLONER ultimately gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that they employ a solicitor—their deputy clerk—to prove ate in all c ases where their Inspector theuetat l'eo•al assistance would be required—Certificates of analysis of water from Budworth Heath farm, Goodscroft farm, Swinton's farm, Moore, and cottages at Weston Point were received. The three former were returned as being unfit for domestic use, and the Inspector was directed to cenimunicate with the owners of the property previous to legal action being taken ; an.l in the case of the cottages at W:st m Point, it was agreed that the houses should be sup- plied from the coup en's iniins, owing to the present sup- ply being at times insufficient.

SITOOKING FATALITY AT WIDNES ALKALI WORKS. At Widnss Accident Hospital, on Sunday morning, there died James Loftus, better known as Jemmy Cairns, who lived at 20, Wellington-street, from injuries he received on the previous evening. Loftus was a causticizer at the works of the Widnes Alkali Company, and on Saturday eveniog whilst following his employment he fell into a caustic liquor well. 'rue deceased was a tall, heavy man, weighing about 20 stone, and the well mouth being only 18 inches wide, would not permit him to slip bodily into the liquor. He was, however, immersed up to the waist in the c )rrosive liquid, with no one in the place to help him. At length two workmen arrived on the spot, rescued hifh from his painful position, and threw cold water upcn him. He was conveyed home on a stretcher, and thence to the Acci- dent Hospital, where he died.—On Tuesday, Mr. L. Rowbot- torn, the deputy coroner, held an inqaest on the body at the Mersey Hotel. Mr. Lewin was present on behalf of the rela- tives of the deceased, and Mr. Husband represented the Widnes Alkali Company, Limited. Mr. R. J. Wild was also present to represent the company. Matthew Carter, of 2.), Sankey-street, foreman of a chemical works, said the deceased NV,ie his brother-in-law, and was 32 years of age, On Sunday morning witness visited the scene of the acci- dent. The well, which was a large boiler, was 27 feet long and 7 feet in diameter; and it had three apertures. The one through which deceas'ad fell was 18 inches wide and 3.h fee in length. There was no covers over the apertures. 'here was a gangway round the boiler, but there was no gas light near the hole of the well. In answer to Mr. Husband, wit- ness said the deceased could not have fallen into the hole from the gangway. In his opinion the deceased got upon the boiler front a heap of lime lying near, to save himself from walking round the gangway, which would occupy five minutes. He had probably whilst crawling on the boiler fallen into the hole. Deceased had worked for the Alkali Company 12 ye Ira, and had been previously scalded at the same place.—Miss Downie, matron at the hospital, said the deceased was admitted on Saturday evening. He was severely cc sided about the legs and lower parts of the body, and died on Sancta}, morning consequent upon the shock to the nervous system. Deceased told her he had fallen into the liquor, which was strong. There was no semblance of drink upon the deceased.—Joshua Rigby Wild, manager of the the Widnes Alkali Works, produced- plans bf the works where deceased was engaged. The height cf the boiler from the floor was 8 feet 6. inches.— James Burns, of 11, Lacey-street, cassticizer, de- scribed the means taked to rescue the deceased•from his awful position. The deceased, when lifted front the well, walked about three yards away from the boiler, where he stripped himself, and cold fresh water was thrown upon him. The deceased was a very steady man, and he never saw him get upon the boiler except by the gangway. The jury then proceeded to the works to view the place where the fatality took place, and many of the jury expressni the opinion that it was very dangerous. On returning to the hotel, W. lieskothi of Viaduct-street, engine driver in. the employ of the company, depcsed that whilst he was shunt- ing some waggons on a siding he saw the deceased climbing upon the well from the lime heap.—The Coroner then summed up evidence, and remarked that there were three points to r the jury to consider: Whether the death was accidental, whether it was due to the culpable negligence of any other person, or whether deceased committed suicide.—The fore- man of the jttry said there was no doubt the place was den- gerous.—Tne Coroner said it was not for the jury to inquire whether the place was dangerous. It was simply their duty to inquire how. the man met his death—accidentally or otherwise. If they had a rider or a recommendation to add to the verdict, it would be forwarded to the proper quarter. After deliberating in private for some time, the jury returned a verdict of accidental death. They recom- mended that a light should be placed over the well.—Mr. Hustand, on behalf of the company, said the dece ssed was a faithful servant, and they were very sorry this accident had happened to hint. The firm would only be too happy to do anything they possibly could to prevent a similar occurrence in the future. The firm made their own gas, and it would be no trouble to fix a gas bracket wherever it was necessary. If it had been reported to them by the deceased that it was necessary to place a gas jet over the boiler, it would have been done at once .—The inquiry which had cccupled four hours and a helf then teranuated.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. The cause list comprised 115 origiteal plaints, five ad- journed plaists, and 26 original judgment summonses. BREACH OF THE BANICRI7PTCY ACT.—Thomas Jones of Frodsbam, sued Peter Knight, of King-street, Wigan, fruit and potato dealer, for £4 Is for goods supplied. The plain- tiff said that he had made many applicatioss for p tymest but to no purpose. The defendant did not appear, but his wife admitted that £2 was owing, and observed that her husband tiled his petition subsequent to the contracting of the present debt, and that • the plaintiff knew of this, and arranged with her husband that he should not be included in the defendant's statement of affairs, but should receive' the amount of his debt in full.—ln reply to the Judge, the

plaintiff denied having any knowledge of the defendant having filed his petition; but upon referring to the letters from the defendant to the plaintiff which were put in it transpired that the defendant had made an arrangement with his creditors similar to that mentioned by the defen- dant's wife, and the plaintiff was aware of thTe.—His honour said that both the plaintiff and defendant had put them- selves in very serious positions. He should make it his duty to inquire into the matter when next he was at the Wigan County Court, and if he could see his way to a pro- secution he should certainly rder one. It was an abomin- able arrangement to be made, and a gross breach of the Bankruptcy Act. He should give judgment for the defen- dant, but without Costs. ACTION AGAINST A RUNCORN GREENGROCER. James Woods, conductor of the volunteer band, claimed from Thomas Booth, greengrocer, Runcorn, the sum of £2, the value of a'deg killed through the defendant running over it with his horse and cart.—Mr. Burton appeared for the • plaintiff, who said that on the sth of October he was standing opposite the Royal Hotel, and his dog was in the street, close by, when the defendant drove past at the rate of nine miles an hour, and ran over the dog. He saw the defendant, and asked him for some compensation, but he declined to give any.—ln reply to Mr. Hitchen, who appeared for defendant, Woods said that the dog was about two yards away from him when the defendant drove past. He called out to the defendant, but he did not pull up.—George Hargreaves, in reply to Mr. Burton, said- be was with Woods, standing talking, on the night in question, and the dog was about a yard and a half away, when the defendant came driving past. Woods shouted to Booth to step, and the witness called to the dog but before the dog could get away, the horse and cart had gone over it.—Mr. Hitchen submitted that the plaintiff had not made out any case; and the Judge, whilst sympathising with the plaintiff, concurring, gave judgment for the defendant. CAUTION TO FRODSEAM FOWL KEEPERS.—Thos. Jenee, Frodsham, sought to recover from James Hancech, of Fred- sham, the sum of LS Bs., for damage done to the plaintiff's crops by the defendant's fowls.—Mr. Burton appeared for plaintiff, who said he had frequently seen fowls in his field, mid had always gone to the defendant and asked if they be- longed to him. On receiving an answer in the affirmative he then told him that he should charge 6d. a day for every day the fowls were allowed to trespass. The defendant promised to keep them up, but did not do so.—ln reply to Mr. Hitchen, who appeared for defendant, plaintiff said Mr. Harrop's fowls had been on his land, but Mr. Harrop had paid 15s: 6d. to the plaintiff as damages.—James Ainsworth, in the plaintiff's employ, said he had seen the defendant's fowls in the field many times.—Mr. Hitchen called defen- dant's wife, who said the hens were kept fastened up, and when she did turn them out her daughter was sent to look after them.—Mary Palin said she bad seen a horse and a donkey and also some children on the plaintiff's land, and seen them damaging the straw stack.—His Honour in giving judgment said the plaintiff had made out his case, and he must say the defendant's wife was not what he could call a a truthful witness. She had certainly over-reached herself in the witness box. The only weak point of the plaintiff's case ras as to the amount of actual damage be had sus- tained. He thought from the evidence the plaintiff was entitled to £2 dawages, for which sum lie ga,. jed6inent witk costs.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

ALLEGED MCRDER.-------1-11-01-1- man was murdered on Saturday night outside his own door in the vicinity of Killakee, at the foot of the Dublin mountains. He is variously described as a gamekeeper and as a labourer. It is said that a man of notoriously bad character entered his house on Saturday night, and a;ked him to come out. The old man did so, and his visitor strangled him. The Right Hon. W. H. Smith, M.P., who arrived in Dublin on Monday from Pakenham Hall, county West- -meatb, where he had been the guest of Lord Longford, on Tuesday, visited the City and County Conservative Club, and was shown over the premises by the chairmen and secretary. He spoke of the advisability of holding a Con- servative demonstration in Dublin at an early date. • INTIMIDATING AN IRISH FARMER.—Four farmers, named Clarke, Reilly, Madden, and Kelly, were charged, under the Crimes Act, at Woodford. on Monday, with attempting to intimidate a farmer named Delwin into giving up the land which he had purchased from the parish priest ta.the curate, ; and which was the scene of the recent affray. Clarke was sentenced to one month's imprisonment, Reilly to three weeks, and Kelly and Madden to one week. CRIME AND OUTRAGE IN TEE SOUTH OF IRELAND.— Owing to the large number of outrages ,which have recently taken place in Cork and Kerry counties, extra police are being drafted from headquarters into the disturbed districts, with sr-view to having a more perfect system of patrolling kept up during the winter. In districts where a revival Of outrage is anticipated, the police huts and protection posts vacated last summer are being re-tenented. Captain Plun- kett, divisional magistrate for Munster, will not, it is be- lived, permit any more meetings of the National League to be held in his district. Effarts to hold them will, however, continue. A singular development of the Irish land law agitation is reported from Limerick. The operative pork butchers have held a meeting to discuss their position. The chair- man, one Patrick O'Brien, asked who backed up the Land Leaguers in their demands, marched through the streets in thousands, and swelled the farmers' meetings, and he answered the question himself by saying that it was "the working men" who did all this, aud that it was only right that the farmers should now help them. The decision of the meeting was that the men should come out on strike unless they received one penny in respect of every pig killed in the local curing establishments, the impost to be levied On the farmers who sell the p7gs ORANGE FANATICISM AT DERRY.—An Orange outbreak, the seriousuess of which it would be difficult to exaggerate, disgraced Londonderry on Thursday. It had been arranged that Mr. Dawson„ M.P., Lord Mayor of Dublin, shoed addrese a meeting in Derry, ani the Corporation granted the use of the Town Hell tor that purpose. But before the time of meeting, a body of Orangemen, armed with revolvers and other weapons, took possession of the building, mounted upon the roof, and crowded to the windows. To prevent a serious collision, the Corporation hastily aesemblad, and rescinded their resolution allowing the use of the Town Hall to the Lord Mayor of Dublin' but when it became known that Mr. Dawson had entered Derry the Orangemen became g-eatly excited. Slates were thrown from the roof of the Town Hall upon the Catholics below, shots were fired, and the wildest disorder prevailed. Mr. DAWSOD issued an appeal to the people not to retaliate, and so helped to prevent blood- shed ; but when the Orangemen left the Toe n Hall they were stoned by the Catholics, and the excited mobs were charged by the police. What may be the extent of the injul y .lone it is impossible to say, but one man was so severely injured ty a revolver shot from the Town Hall that his depositions have been taken.

CHIMNEY FIRING Ar EARLESTOWN.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, John Roberts was summonel for wilfully setting fire to the chimney of his dwelling house on the 9th October.—The defendant pleaded guilty, and the Bench remarking that it was' a serious offence, im- posed a fine of 20e. and costs.—Henry Jolly was sum- moned for having the chimney of his dwelling-house on fire on the 17th ult„ and was fined 3e. 6d.--Claarles Gibbertlawaite was fined a like amount for a similar offence.
