This story is founded upon a scandal that-occurred in one of the noblest of our aristocratic families, which is well- known in the higher circles, and which appeared to the author to have remarkable dramatic capabilities for the ex- hibition of character and incident. It opens with the pre- parations for a dinner party and a grand reception after- wards at the mansion of the Earl of Harlaxton in Mayfair; an event looked forward to with unusual interest as being the first appearance in public of the widowed Countess since the death of her husband a year before, previous to which she had been recognised as one of the most distinguished of the female "leaders of society." While she is herself making a tour through the place to see thatal e sin accordance with her directions, she is sud- denly taken ill, the invitations are hurriedly countermanded, and two very different visitors are summoned, the doctor and the lawyer. From the doctor she forcers out the naked truth, which he tries for her sake to conceal till a more favourable opportunity, that she has heart disease; and that if she has any serious business to do, it would be ad- visable to get it done at once. She then acknowledges she has that to do which, if not done, she could not die in peace; and passionately entreats him (who thinks she may live many years with care) to at least secure her one day. Reluctantly he acknowledges he perhaps can do that with- out any serious increase of danger, and goes for the drugt Now the lawyer arrives, and her position is made clear. The earl is not her son. His supposed younger brother Stephen is The facts are known only to' herself and the lawyer. When she had revealed these to her late husband on his deathbed, and obtained his forgiveness, she had pledged herself to make the truth known to Stephen the day he came of age; but if she should be in any immediate danger of death, she was bound to act immediately. The presentillness has given the requisite warning. Thus hur- ried into action, her hope and aim is to promote the marriage of Stephen to a young and rich heiress (a relative, an orphan resident with her), and then to reveal the facts, in telling her own story in detail, and plead for eternal secrecy, including the abandonment of his rights. Supposing he could be influenced so to act, which the lawyer entirely disbelieves, she has another obstacle to sur- mount. It has long heen a settled idea in the two families that the Earl and the young heiress should marry, and the former is determinedly bent on winning the lady, and making the idea a substantial fact. On the other hand, Stephen and the young lady incline much more towards each other, though the former thinks he is in honour bound net to in- terfere with his brother's claims. While greatly admiring Miss Vandeleur's beauty and vivacious spirit, he has secretly grave doubts as to her steadiness of character; so that his love-making, if it can be called so, takes the shape of banter and satire—not always good humoured. And as they happen to belong to me, I propose to keep the difficulties of the thorny path before him. them." Whether or no the answer was different from what he expected, the soldier became in his way gracious. "Come up to the front. We shall soon have dinner. I auppose you can bolt lots of that ?" "I will try," said Stephen, with a smile. "I own to being hungry." "Don't imagine it will be up to the fine living you have been used to, judging from your fine clothes !" . "Are you content with it ?" asked Stephen, diplomatic- ally. . " Oh, it's well enough for the likes of us." "Then I am sure it shall be well enough for the likes of me," responded Stephen. "And if it weren't," retorted the soldier, "it would be all the same for both of us. To please us isn't their game." "So I suppose," said Stephen. "And I shall try like you to take things philosophically." The soldier looked hard at Stephen as if not quite sure whether this was meant as a compliment to him, or as a skit at his expense, but he finally decided it was all right. Just then the dinner came in. Stephen thought of his last dinner at his club in Piccadilly, only three days before, and prepared rather to enjoy the contrest. A large cen full of soup and meat was placed on the rough deal table, in the centre of the room; round which the soldiers sat with their small tin vessels c disci canteens. In these they received their soup, while the meat and unpeeled potatoes were placed on the canteen lids. Rough as everything was— spare as were the cendiments, conspicuotie by its absence the tablecloth, Stephen never ate a more enjoyable dinner. When he had done, and could find time to leek around, and study the faces—the expressions—the language, and the behaviour of his future comrades, the society he ha I voluntarily exchanged for the so-called "good society" to which he naturally belonged, the impression left was pain- fully depressing. It was not that he admired "good society" any better than before, but the contrast was terrible between that and this; when he remembered that be could have left the former when he liked, whereas to the latter he was bound as by links of iron. Vaiolv did he try to discover in the herd-heaaed, hard- faced, closed-cropped animal features about him, one single being with whom it seemed possible to hold some kind of friendly talk, some small letting free of mutual confidences "Well, I expected even that—did I not?" Andem say ing he relapsed into his own thoughts, and was happily left pretty well alone with them till tea time. Then the man who had threatened to bone his boots came again with his own cantsen of tea, and gave Stephen a drink. At the first taste he was about to put it down, but his good sense checked the movement, so he drank and thanked his entertainer. At the same time he received from the soldier a small piece of hard ration bread, with the explanation that he only got a pound to last him the whole day, and this was the end of it. The bread was worse than the tea to manage —but he was determined to give no chauca to any of the men to say he was putting himself above them-30 ate his hard dry bread with apparent content. At half-past nine all went to bed. Stephen found the feather bed or luxurious spring mattresses, and down quilts, of Harlaxton House, had now-to be exchanged for a little straw on a hard iron frame, with a coarse blanket and rug for covering. But there was intense relief in getting into, even a bed like this He had no longer to speak nor to be spoken to. He could resign himself to a review of the day—see how he had acquitted himself—how he ha-I borne the things that most troubled him—and so look forward ard prep are himself for the morrow, and for the many morrows, that he knew by th talk he bad overheard, must be gone through in hardship and humiliation before he could hope SO to emerge as to be free frontsthe things most painful to him— the subjection of his whole being—(so it seemed) to the

After so many, and BOMB of them unpleasant works of preparation, it was a relief to Stephen to be summoned to his first drill. Of curse he knew he would be pot with the new recruits, and !ze schooled himself not to know anything, but he taught everything; and it was with a laugh he thought to himself how he might win his teacher's heart by his docility and rapid progress. For as to the thing iteeif, Stephen felt certain he could ' learn faster than there would be men intelligent enough to teach him. But it was a settled point of policy with him to appeir as raw as his .comrades—without, however, any kind of actual deception. He fond the others nearly all like himself, in plain clothes, and the drill began under Drill Corporal Robinson. They marched straight forward, they turned to the right, they turned to the left, they stood at ease, they practised the goose step (engaged in which the wisest of men could hardly help feeling uncommonly foolish), and through all Stephen acquitted himself as a good average recruit. This went on for four days, when he was ordered to the Quartermaster's Stores for -his •lothing, boots, and kit. And then for the first urns did Stephen put on his uniform, and the same day displayed it on parade before the cominanling.officer and adjutant; who came, attended by tfie master tailor, to inspect the recruits in their martial garb. Now, whether Stephen forgot his caution, or did not chance to remember it, he looked so well, and so carried himself, without any sign of intention or display,"that the Colonel, in " passing " him, to use the technical phrase, spoke of him as a smart lad—one likely to get on. Sweet and precious were the words; they sank into Stephen's heart, and gave him new strength and fortitude for his career. That very day he was moved into the next, a superior squad, so that the praise and the puiding came together, as Stephen said, with a glee and light-heartedness he had not known for milk a day. This, however, was partly due to good luck. A great number of s )Idiers of the regiment had recently volunteered to join other regiments where reinforce- ments were needed for special duty, and likely recruits the efore were pushed an. He needed some break in the cloud, and it had come.

o He needed it—because another cloud was overhanging him. When he undressed at night be found that 'all the clothes he bad taken off to put on his uniform were gone; and in answer to his indignant questions—and then de- mands—he got nothing but ' jeers from some, insults from others, and angry shouts frona men who were reading or listening to a newspaper, to bid him hold his jaw, or it " would be worse for him !"

Something was worse for him. Remembering the threat about his boots; which after all had perhaps been only barrack fun, or at the worst try.ng it on, to see what the new re- cruit would stand, be had taken everything out of the pockets, and watching his opportunity to shake up his straw bed when no one seemed to notice him, deposited the more valuable of tke contents and the whole of his little store of money—a few shillings excepted—below the bed, where he thought .no one would look for it while seeing his clothes in, their usual place; and if they did go to them, finding his money and other sniall matters left there in confidence, would search no farther. It was shrewdly thought—but his was one man's experi- ence under entirely new circumstances, whereas his com- rades had the experience derived from long habitude as well as front individual sharp practice. The upshot was chat everything was cleaned out. Below the bed and about the bed all was in the same category—Stephen had lost every- thing.

law possibly of some ignorant and brutal drill sergeant, and the jealousies of the men around him which he felt sure would be fiercely aroused, at any sign he was advancing in the good opinion of his officers. Ah—but what would they be like? That Colonel he had seen on the deck of the Banner, and fortpately not got intoconverse with? If, now, a man with the look and voice of that Colonel were there, in the Camp, as the head of his (Stephen's) regiment—how would he get oa if he had to appeal to him? "I may wrong him," said Stephen to himself.; "but if I ever saw a man who I could fancy would feel a pleasure in the punishment he inflicted it is be. Fortunately, he at least is not my colonel—that much I do know." While thus ruminating, a strangely prolonged sound came to his ears from the open air. Ile thought at first it might be a cry of distress, and raised himself up a little to listen. Presently he heard it again, but more faintly, and then again and ag tiu at equal intervals of time, dying off in the distance by degrees. When it ceased he lay down again, wondering what it could have been. Presently he heard the faintest of the former sounds repeated, as though on the way back. And so it proved. Each cry gradually became more dis- tinct, and it drew nearer, and at last, through a clearer, stronger voice being employed, he knew the meaning of the whole. The sentinel at some point near Stephen's hat had called out the hour, and made known all was well. When his cry had quite ceased the next sentinel took it up, and so it went round the whole camp till it came back to the place from whence it started. Anything more striking or picturesque to the mental vision than this linked chain of voices shutt- ing in the whole camp in safety, Stephen thought he had never heard. What if any man failed to respond when his turn came? What, if under some extraordinary circumstances, he had fallen asleep? And then Stephen pictured to himself the behaviour of the guard for the night in their but—the hurried turnout, after a brief Pause to be sure there was a dead stop, the hurrying to the place, the wakening of the unfortunate, the marching him away as a prisoner, and then the court-martial, and the dreadtul punishment that would surely follow. Should he, Stephen, ever be in that danger? And then instead of going to sleep he tried to summon up for examination all possible inflaences that might lead a man to yield to slumber, and see if any were likely to be specially dangerous to him. Such was his last remembrance before sleep for which he had long to wait. And when he did wake it was to experience another and less agreeable sensation in the form of a violent and most inexplicable shock. A bullet passing through his brain could hardly have more affected him. And coming as the blow did between sleeping and waking, he,was for a little time scarcely able to speak, or even to guess what had happened. • The immediate sound in all directione, as though they waited till then, of bands, bugles, drums and fifes, followed by the rousing of the man, and a question Stephen put, and which was answered by the nearest soldier enlightened him. It was the cannon that was always fired at half-past five as signal, which had come upon him so apparently near, so sudden in its violence, and became so instantaneously still.

The clerk added that he had invited the different authori- ties to send representatives to a conference to be held at the Union offices, Whiston, on the 15th instant.—With reference ; to a complaint that Dr. Wood, medical officer for Woolton district, had delayed attending a poor person named George Robinson, a letter was read from Dr. Wood giving an ex- planation, which the guardians resolved was perfectly srtisfactory.—A special committee was-appointed to con- sider the rearraneentent ef Dr. Wood's district, particularly in relation to Widnes aed Ditton.—An application by the I clerk (Mr. S. AN EXTRAORDINERY CASE. - A.A4I74..y_EMALES' ATTIRE. - At the Newton Petty Sesdons, on Saturday last, Joseph Si!cock was brought up on a charge of being drunk and disorderly at Rixton, and assaulting P.C. Barry while in the execution of his duty.—Mr. Moore appeared for the prisoner, who pleaded guilty.—P.C. Berry said that about half-past four on the afternoon of the 19th ult. he was celled to the Bowling Green Inn, Hollins Green, to turn out the prisoner. He went there and found hiin dressed in women's clothing. He was in the back yard of the house, and witness requested him to leave the premises, and he did so. He afterwards heard that the prisoner was cinducting himself in a very diserderly manner, women and children being afraid to go along the road. Witness went,in the direction, and met the prisoner about quarter of a mile outside the village. He was still dressed as a woman, but wore a pair of trousers beneath the dress. Witness asked him why he was carry- ing on in the manner he was, whereupon he struck the constable a very severe Vow on the left eye. The witness " closed " with him, and a struggle ensued. During the struggle he (vriteess) was struck a great meny Itimes, being kicked on the back of the head and also on the Icheek bone. He was very violent, and witness had to pro- cure assistance before they could handcuff him. The prisoner behaved more like a madman than an ordinary man. When they got him into the village it took three or four men to carry him.—Superintendent Jackson said the prisoner had been convietel for many assaults on the police. He asked the Bencli to deal with him very severely, because he was a man who seemed to set the law at defiance. When he got drunk the police seemed to be the objects of his attack. He had been repeatedly fined and punished for assaults on the police. The big and pow. rful man went to some outside village where there was only one policeman and no assistance could be obtained, and then made his attack on the constable.— Colonel McCorquodale, J.P. : And in the garb of an old woman. It is a very bad case indeed.—Mr. Moore (on be- half of the prisoner) said it might be a bad case, but he hoped the Bench would look at it in a lenient light. The prisoner, for 18 months par, had tried to turn from his wickedness and earn a honest livelihood, and had a wife and four young children depending upon him. A week before the day on which the offence was committed it was Hollins Green "wakes," and the prisoner unfortunately went on the spree." The devil again got hold of him, and the devil persua..:Ted him to dress in women's clothes. He did not ask that justice should be thwarted of her rights, but that the case should he dealt with leniently for the sake of the prisoner's wife and family, who would suffer for the faulis of the husband and father.—The Chairman said the case was a very serious one indeed, and it was made much worse by the prisoner attiring himself in women's clothes. It was quite clear that he had tried to reform bimeelf, but he had*tallen back to his old pursuits, and-however Wishful the Bench might be to consider his wife and family by im- posing a smell penalty, they had a duty to discharge, and they were bound to protect the public abd the police in the execution of their duty. Thy could not pass a less sen- tence upon him than that Ile be imprisoned for three calen- dar months with hard labour.

Meetings of that kind were calculated to promote cordiality, and lo lead them to think well of those from whom they differed, and that was a point of very great im- portance. He founded his conviction that that was the object of the meeting from the wonderful change which had taken place in the great annual gathering of the Church called the Church Congress. He had been present many years ago at meetings of the Church Congress, when-per- sons who differed very materially met, and sometimes there were very painful scenes, but latterly the same persons had met, the same differences of opinioa had been clearly put forth, and yet t ley had been able to lis'en to one another with Christian courtesy and gentlemanly feeling. ( Ap- plause.) As proof of the accuracy of that statement, he would point to the last meting of the Congress at Read- ing. At the conclusion of that meeting, when they dis- cussed the means of promoting spiritual life, men like Canon Hoare and Mr. C. Woad met on the same platform, heard one anotter quietly with courteous and Christian feeling, and went away thinking in all probability that there was not such a gulf between them as they had previously supposed was the case. (Applause.) • An interesting paper on " Sone results of the Oxford movement" was read by the Bev. Canon DODD, vicar of Stretton, who commenced by referring to the very remark- aele and widespread change which bad taken place in the Church of England during the late fifty years. The force and permanency of that change might be pertly due to its gradual growth. It was not the plant that grew most rapidly that gave promise of longest life, The gradual nature of the change, however, might causu some difficulty in appreciating its magentude and imp°. tanc . any the older men among thsetn knew of the torpid condition in which the Church of England was before the Oxford move- ment began. In that case, as in most others, probably many causes contributed to the great result, but the chief cause of the change, that without which it was doubtful whether the Church of England would even yet have raised itself from its decaying position, was the quiet and deep stirring of heart which was felt by a few choice spirits on the banks of the Isis—in a word the Oxford movement. (Applause.) But it did not follow because they reverenced the leaders of the movement, and believed them to have been wise and godly men, that they were bound to accept without dis- crimination everything they proclaimed, or to sub- scribe to every paragraph in the "Tracts for time '1 lines." Still less were they bound to agree with every interpretation of 'their teaching and every addition to their practice that had been conspicuous during the last few years. There were probably some present who disapproved of the excessive ritual in some churches, who found a difficulty in receiving the whole body of High Church doctrine, and who felt a strong irritation against the attitude of some of the clergy towards the chief pastors of the Church. Now he was not a member of the English Church Union, nor had he any intention of becoming a member of that or any other association in the Church, for he saw in such things a pos- sible element of disruption. Although not prepared to deny that they might have their uses, still he surveyed them with something of regret, almost of dismay. In trying to form a just estimate of the result and value of the Oxford movement we had no right to dwell upon certain cases of extravagance, or to denounce the practices and opinions of the many on aceount of the eccentricities of the few. (Ap- plause.) Arnoag 20 000 parsons, of " all sorts and conditions of men," there were sure to be a c !stain number of irritating irreconcilables. (Hear, bear, anti laughter.) To judge fairly one must survey events as a whole, and he would put it to anyone as to whether, since the Oxford movement was started, the standard of worship had not been distinctly raised in the large majority of churches through- out the land, whether there was not a greater respect shown to the sanctity of a church; whether the services were not more frequent and labours more abundant; whether the primitive, Apostolic, Biblical, sacramental, and Catholic doctrines of the Mauch were not mote plainly and fre- quently taught; whether the offensive distinctions between rich and poor were not being gradually broken down, as they ought to be entirely, in the house of God; and whether there was not more eartnestness, more zeal, and more con- scientious work done for Christ? They might discover other causes which bad helped to accomplish these objects, but as honest men they were bound to confess that the Church of the present day owed more than she could well express to the doctors and fathers of 50 years ago. There were three gains to the Church as the result of the Oxford movement for which gratitude was due. They were, first, a wider appreciation of distinct Church doctrine; second, a truer appreciation of the value and dignity of worship ; and • third, a kinder appreciation of differences of opinion among men of separate schools'. When it, was remembered that the English Church, like the English nation, had a bad habit of washing her dirty linen in public, that her faults and quarrels were all patent to the world, that every foolish vicar and unruly curate had his words and actiobs paraded in the peess, that whatsoever was 'spoken in the ear in the closet was proclaimed upon the housetop," he thought they might well be content that there was practically so little nesunderstanding and se little disagreement in the Church of Eueland. (Applause.) The Rev. Canon KNOX-LITTLE, in a practical address, observed that the firsefatilt formai with the Church of Eng- land was that she was a State Church, that she belopged to the State, that she was governed by the State, and _Roman Cathelics had told him that she was created by the State, but that WAS all nonsense. He granted that the State Courts bed certainly tried to govern her, and if he might say so in a whisper, a pretty mess they had made of it. (Laughter) But the Cluch had got on un- commonly well notwithstaeding. Toe lioyal Commission had issued a report, which was a ;hest splendid document, and the final result of that Commission was this, that when the State courts parted company with the old lines of the Church that step was a piece of bad management. It was a grand thing for the State of England to be allied with a Church of God. If men by saying that the Church of Eng- land was a State Church meant that she was the slave of the State, then the Royal Commission said, as plainly as wore.a could- do, that such persons were mistaken. (gp-

plans.) Then the second fault found with the Church of England was that she was a privileged Church. Well, there wat no harm in that if the privileges were divine. She was a Church that every Englishman was privileged of attending if he wished to serve God. What some people seemed to iNdicate by calling her a privileged Church was this: that they would like uncommonly well to put their bands into the pocket of the Church. By all means let thzm have justice and equity, because being and old-fashioned fellow, he thought a breach of the eighth commandment was unsatisfactory. (Hear, hear.) It was alleged that the Church of England was, unhappily, a divided Church. Regarding this paint, he told the story about the Irishman and his wife who had a quarrel, when someone interfered, and said it was very serious to create such disturbances. "Och, not a bit of it," said the woman; "shure its rather dull if it always goes on the same." (Laughter.) There must be dissension and disagreements, but there ought not to be intolerance and hatred. (Hear, hear.) He maintained that the Church of England would not be the Church of the nation, that she would not fulfil her great mission, if the extreme fanatics of any party succeedei in driving their brethren out. What was desired was a broad platform where truth, in its many- sided magnticence, might be seen by many minds. Instead of such being a sign of the Church's death, it was the sign of the Church's life._ (Hear, hear.) They belonged to a historic Church, which did not appeal to empty trnagina- _ _ _ _ _ _

tions or dreams, or fancies, bat st:l;ich had behind her a splendid ancestry and a great record of the past. As he had implied before she was a church widely extended with her broad, low, and high church nick-name them as they-might, it mattered not, she had freedom. (Hear, hear.) The Eng- lish Church was thoroughly English and Catholic. ' She was not Latin; she bad her faults, and had been very res- pectable; highly respectable, and a great deal too stiff. (Laughter.) But as she got to work she had the starch taken out of her collars. (Hear, bear.) The Church re- cognised the solemnity of home life, and had been fighting courageously against all tampering with the marriage law. (Hear, hear.) She was a power of education, and worked for the people when nobody else would work for them. They might laugh at the parsons, but the latter had been the great paymasters of the poor. They should love the Church, and ought not to be hard upon her. They need not re-write her history but study it as it was. They were apt to re-write old things and endeavour to make them new, but he wished to persuade them to study not to re-write the his- tory of their mother Church. (Hear, hear.) Canon- HORNBY, in proposing a vote of thanks to Canon Dodd and Canon Knox-Little, expressed a hope that as they continued to progress so might an entire catholicity find its way into their ritutl, and make the Church what it was intended to b.:, viz., the reformer and improver of that great State of England. ILLEGALLY REMOVING CATTLE. HEAVY FINES AT NEWrON TOWN HALL. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, before George McCorquodale, R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and C. Pilkington, Esqs., the London and North-Western.Rail- way Co. and Henry Warburton, farmer and cattle dealer; ballam, Warrington, were summoned for rethavieg cattle contrary to orders made under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878.—Mr. T. Swift, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Messrs. J. 0. and W. Swift, of St. Helens), prosecuted oil behalf of the county police authorities.—The - London and North-Western Railway Comprny were repre- sented by Mr. Preston, jour., of Liverpool, and the defen- dant Warburton by Mr. Jenkins, 0f... Warrington.—Mr. Swift observed that it was the duty of all common carriers and cattle dealers to be acquainted with the cattle disease ordere, and maintained that copies had been well circulated throughout the country and inserted in, newspapers. Cattle could be moved in codn- ties upon the owners complying with certain tegulations and conditions, but by an order made on the-17th September last, under no circumstances whatever could cattle be removed out of a municipal borough or Ireland into a district controlled by county authorities. —The Chairman : That is, they cannot be landed in any part, but may pass through on the railway.—Mr. Swift re- plied in the affirmative. He maintained that the London and North-Western 44ailway Company were fully aware of the orders in question as they had published an abstract of them. As to Mr. Warburton, it was his duty as well as that .of every citizen and member of the comtnunity to know and observe the laws of the country, and it was doub'v Mr. Warburton's duty because the regulations related to a matter peculiarly his fandtion. But he tried to evade the law and escape the vigilance of the authorities. Cattle un- lawfully came over from Ireland, through Holyhead and on to Warrington, where, if they had been unloaded it would have been all right. But instead of that he brought them on to Newton Bridge station, with the full knowledge of the law to the contrary. He had no right to bring them out of a borough and unstruck them in the county as Mr. Warburton and the 'defendant railway com- pany had done. He thought it was a case in which the full penalty of £2O should be imposed, because there did not appear to be one redeeming feature about it—Both Mr. Jenkins and M. Preston addreseed the Bench on behalf of their clients, m detaining that they had removed the c Lttle from Warrington to Newton Bridge on the certific ite of an Irish magistrate to the effect that there was no cattle disease existing in the neighbourhood from which the cattle came. There had not b:.en the slightest attempt to break the law or offend against any order. The Chairman said the Bench had carefully considered the case, and they thought there was no intentkn on the part of th, railway company to evade the orders. It was quite an accident that the cattle were forwarded to Newton Bridge. They also thought that Mr. Warburton had had no intention of interfering with the "carrying out of the law. Still. it had been interfered with. and the Bench c .nsidered it their duty to inflict a fine of £5 upon the railway company, and a similar fine upon Warburton. He (the Chairman) wished to take that op- portunity of mentioning that the regulations had been so efficient that there was a great and important diminution of the disease, and it was hoped that the restrictions would be modified to a certain extent. • He thouget the regula- tions might be made more clear for the benefit of the fa-rmers.—Mr. Preston stated that farmers could not un- derstand the legal language in which such orders and regu- lations were usually couched.—The Chairmen said he would bring the matter before the Ex:cutive Committee, of which he was a member.—Mr. Swift asked th it the defendants should pay the advocate's fees for the prosecution, and the 'Tench made a further order for one guinea up'en the defen- dants.

HARVESC FESTIVAL AT FCCLESTON.—The usual harvest festival in connection with Christ Church Eccleston, was held on Sunday last, when the R-v. J.l'. Crockett, pastor of the church, preached in the morning, and the Rev. H. H. Higgins, in the afternoon. There were large congregations at both services, and the united collections amounted to £lB Cs. ed. The usual decorations had been made in the interior of the church, the materials of decor ation—cereals, fruit, flowers, ate.—having been arranged and disposed in a pleas- ing and effective manner. The wt rk of decorating the church had been done by a number of ladies and gentlemen of the congregation. • A " PRIZE FIGHT" AT ST. HELENS —Two young men named John Connolly and Thomas McC"rmick, one of whom lived on Greenbank and the other at Smithy Brow, were on Friday summoned before the St. Helens magistrates for having committed a breach of the peace. It seemed that on the Sunday previous P.C. Robson had noticed a large number of the lower element, belonging to the quarters of the town where these two men live, leaving the town in the direction of Lea Green. His stfspicions were aroused and upon inquiry he heard that there was to be a prize tight. He then went to Lea Green, and in a fiaed there he saw the two defendants fighting with each other.—Connolly was the only one who appeared at court, and he was bound over to keep the peace for three months; a warrant being issued for I McCormick's arrest. -

- -- FRAUDS BY RAILWAY TRAVELLEBS.-At the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, a young man named Edward Bury was charged with having ridden on the railway be- tween Edge-hill and St. Helens Junction on the previous evening without a ticket. The prisoner it seemed had taken a ticket at Lime-street for Edge-bill, but being suspected by a special examiner of tickets named Thomas Heath, he was matched, and was noticed to go tight through Edge- hill and on to St. Helens Junctioa. When accosted there he offered a second class ticket, which had bem issued in May last year. 'The witness Heath said there were so many frauds of this kind thtt the London and North- Western Rtilway Company had been under the necessity- of bringing special ticket examiners down to Lime-stret in ordee to try and stop them —A fine of 203. and costs was

mposed. A CoNviver. COUPLE ^ Ellen Thompson, a married woman living at Sutton, was charged at the St. Hrlens Police Court, on Monday, wih having asstulted her hitsband, William Thompson, on Saturday night. I, appeared that on Saturday afternoon the prosecutor after leaving work went to a beerhouse and was there enjoying himself when his wife came to seek him. They went home together and then commenced a quarrel, in the course of which prosecutor ran at his wife to strike her, whereupon she tiarew a larriP at. him, which she had in her hand, and cut him oti the upper lip. He then gave information to the police of what his wife had clJne.— The Chairman (Major Pilkington) said it was quite plain they had both been drunk and they both deserved to go to gaol for a month. They had both been drinking together and that sort of thing often ended in manslaughter and sometimes murder. 'lle bench would not have fined the prisoner but that the money would have t, be paid by the prosecutor, and they would therefore fine her 193. and costs.

•THE BITTER CRY OF ourcAsT LONDON." Sir,-..A small pamphlet with the above title has been issued by the Congregational Union. It is an appeal suffi- illeatly striking, one would think, to stir up all Christen- fl; and yet we may• be sure, that-while all the world Wonders, things will go on much as usual. The conscience of the people seems to be case-hardened. We go on sending out large sums of money for missionary purposes, quite ig- 112ting the fact that at our very doors we have a seething ass of poverty, misery, and squalor, such as no Asiatic, or African has any conception of. I read in an Indian paper „lately that with the introduction of 'Christianity and Earo- wean civilization, India had to deplore not only the loss of her morality, but also the loss of her chief virtue, temper- This is not the only bad feature of the missionary, alartein. In the recent revelations connected with the Scat- tali Ladies Association in Calcutta, such abominations '4„ Ve been brought to light as are entirely unfit for print. -It has long been a complaint with those behind the scenes, that the Scotch people should he heavily taxed in the name of Indian mission work for establishments that reach the 'rtar level of Miss Pigot's association." Thus we see large stems of money are being yearly drawn out of the British Pop'e's pockets and squandered in foreign lands. lam lure few will read the "bitter cry" without heing per- -raded that all the facts produce' apply equally to all our large towns. As the writer says, "Whilst we have been building our churches and chapels, and solacing ourselves with our religion, and dreaming that the millennium was Coming, the poor have been growing poorer, the wretched More miserable, and the immoral more corrupt; the gulf has been widening which s:parates The lowest classes of the etmlneunity from our churches and chapels, and from all decency and civilisation ;" and we are compelled to believe that this "terrible flood of 'sin and iniquity is gaining Up on us," The misery is chilly becoming intensified. The writer is careful to „say that the information given "does not 2Ver to selected cases," but "we have been compelled 10 tone down everything, or the ears and eyes °of our readers would have been insufferably outraged." Of course the writer deals with his subjecr.from a Christian or Church point of View, never for a moment grappling With the fact that for eighteen hundred years this Church has had the power in its own bands, and now when we cry out for an account of its stewardship, this is the report. Truly a splendid balance sheet. "In one street containing 246 *families, only 12 of these are ever represented at the houee of God." In another, "39 persons out of 4,235 farnitiee." • This is the Church of the people with a ven- geance. Well may Archdeacon Denison oppose Education. had not this been the policy adopted by the Church in the Past, aye, adopted up to the present time, such a power as is contained within the mighty multitude of workers would not have been content to gather the crumbs from beneath the feet of Dives. Can one go over the list of the salaries Paid to bishops, clergymen, and ministers at fashionable yhapels, without asking the question-" What have ye given in return ?" The honest answer would be-.--" To the poor we gave neglect; when they asked for bread we gave them stones. But to the rich we fawned; to the rich we knelt as to Baal." The Primate, Preaching at St. Michael's Church, Croydon, said "It made °be tremble to think of the mine of ill which lay buried for the present among the Suffering and toiling classes." Well May the receiver of £15,000 a year tremble. Lately Archi- bald Boyd, Dean of Exeter, died, leaving a fortune of nearly a hundred and forty thousand pounds. div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.

BURTON WOOD. A BATCH OF NEGLECTFUL PARENTS.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, the following parties, all resident in Buttonwood, were fined the amounts stated for neglecting to s ni their children to school :—James Anders is, Henry Singleton ss, Thomas Mullineaux 55' Adam Howarth 23 61, Samuel Lloyd 2s 61, Thomas Rigby 2s 61, George Griffiths 23 63, Charles Pennington is, Alexander Catterall 2s 63, James Dennett 2s 61, Thomas Costello ss, Thomas Fairclough is, and Thomas Knowles 2s 61 FIDDLERS' FERRY. THEFT AT FIDDLERS' FERRY STATION.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, two girls named Kate Brooks and Betsy Bouch, of Widnes, were charged with stealing the sum of 2s 7d from the booking office at Fiddlers' Ferry station, on the 17th October.—Mr. Preston, jun., appeared for the railway company, Mr. Moore represented Roach, and Mr. Knowles appeared for Brooks, both prisoners pleading not guilty.—The evidence showed that the two girls hawked fish in various places, and had been in the habit of return- ing from Fiddlers' Ferry to Widnes. The stationmaster had missed small sums of money from the booking office win- dow, and suspected the two girls. He secreted himself inside the office while the prisoners were on the platform, and some time after they had booked for Widnes Brooks ap- proached the window, and putting her hand through the apperture, took up copper money, amounting in all to the sum of 23 7d. The stationmaster then came out of the office, and save the girls into custody.-I'.S. Rogers deposed that he charged the girls with stealing the money. Brooks replied," It was not 2s 7d; it was only is 61." Bouch made no reply.—The Bench observed that there was a slight doubt in the case as regarded Bench, and the charge against her would be dismissed. They hoped, however, that it would be a warning to her. The case against Brooks was clearly proved, and she would be fined lOs and costs or in default of payment 14 days' imprisonment with hard labour. FR,ODSHAM. RAID ON CHESHIRE POACHERS.—At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Mr. B. Woodhouse in the chair, Thomas Clarke, George Fletcher, Williom Briscoe, Frederick Garner, Samuel Whitby, Samuel Stubbs, and Frederick Woodcock, were charged by Sergeant Johnson with being in possession of 378 yards of netting, 134 yards of beating line, 42 pegs, and eight beating sticks, at Fred- sham, on the Bth October, for the purpose of taking game.— They were each fiaed £2 and costs. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.—On Sunday, two sermons were preached in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, by the Rev. Henry M. Harvard, of Southport, on behalf of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions; and the annual meeting was held in the same chapel on Monday evening, when John Simpson, Esq., of Dunsdale, presided, and addresses were delivered by the chairman and the deputation, Rev. John S. Pawlyn, of Liverpool, and Rev. James McTurk, of Warringtog. The yearly report was read by the Rev. G. Lupton Allen. At the close of the meeting a vote of thanks was accorded to the deputation en the motion of Mr. Turner, seconded by the Rev. G. L. Allen; and a vote of thanks was given to the chairman on the Motion of the Rev. F. F. Edmunds, seconded by Mr. Hadfield. The total collections amounted to £2l 193 43/4d, being an increase of £7 13s 7-id ever the previous year. VOLUNTEER SUPPER.—Tae annual supper and distribu- tion of prizes in connection with the volunteer corps took place in the Town Hall on Saturday evening. The silver cup has this year been won by Sergeant Thomas Davies, of Five Crosses, but the conditions are that the cup must be won for two successive years, or on three occa- sions by the same member before it becomes his own property or passes from general competi- tion. In previous years the same cup has been won by Corporal R. Lloyd, Corporal Daniel Holland, Private C. E. Hitcheo, and Corporal R. Lloyd (s emd time). The maxi- mum number of points which could have been made at the shooting competition was seventy, but the prize meeting was held on the 29th September last, under very unfavour- able circumstances, the rain and mist at times completely obscuring the target. The following is a complete list of the competitors and prizes, also the number Of points made by each, viz :—Sergeant T. Davies, silver medal, cup and £2, 44 points; Sergeant T. Earlam, El 103, 41: Paivate J. Faulkner, Ll 10s, 41; Corporal J. G. Davies, Ll, 3d; Private J. Holland, table and 123 61, 31; Private S. A SHORT Roan TO HEALTH AND WEALTH.—lnstead Cf a bottle of champagne every day at dinner, drink a bottle of CAMMACK'S sparkling POMMETTE.—Advt. • CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.--70H Tues- day evening a Band of Hope for Huyton was commenced under the auspices of the above society; the Rev. Canon Penrhyn and Mr. E. B. Williams, who have energetically identified themselves with the temperance cause in Hayton Quarry and the neighbourhood, were present, and several ladies ant gentle-men assisted in organising. About 50 children joined, and it is expected that the number will be largely increased at the next meeting, when members will be properly enrolled. GOOD TEMPLARISM AT EAULESTOWN.—The weekly en- tertainment, under the auspices of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Saturday evening. There was a pretty (air attendance, and Bro. George Warbuiton presided. A • capital programme of song?, recitations, lie., was nicely gene through.—The usual weekly meeting of the members of the lodge was held on Monday evening, when Bro. Hy. Warburton, W.C.T., occupied the chair. Three new members were initiated. Several items of lodge business were dis- cussed, and arrangements were made for holding the Juve- nile Temple Council, at Earlestown, in about a fortnight. The nomination and election of officer for the ensuing quarter then took place; and the meeting closed about 9-30. LARCENIES AT ST., HELENS.—A young man named John Callaghan was, on Monday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having stolen a hat from a stall in the I Market-place.—On Saturday, it seemed, the prisoner had gone to a stall in the Market-place kept by a pang woman named Mary Jones, and there purchased a hat tot 6d. Whilst making a selection, he had managed to fix another hat into his old one, and when leaving the stall he took them both away. He had, however, been seen by a neigh- bouring stall-keeper, who acquainted Miss Jones with the fact, and she followed the prisoner, and got the stolen hat from him.—A fine of 10s. was imposed.—James Seddon. another young man, was also charged with having stolen lie., the property of an old woman named Catherine Need- ham.—On the 20th ult., it seemed, the complainant sent her nephew, a boy of 10 yeirs of age, with some money to pay a grocer's bill. The prisoner met him before he got to the grocers, and took 7s. oat of his pocket, and afterwards per- suaded the lad to give him the other 4s.—A fine of LL was imposed. STABBING A WOMAN AT ST. HELENS.—A middle-aged man, named Edward Feeney, was charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, with having unlawfully wounded Catherine McDermott. The prosecutrix in this case is a widow, and keeps a lodging-house at 26, Mounl-street— About six o'clock on the evening of Saturday, the 20th inst., the prisoner came and wanted to lodge with her, but owing to something she had heard abeut him, Mrs. McDermott refused to take him in. He then went away, but came back again soon after, and again asked prosecutrix, who was standing at the door of her house, to let him have lodgings for that night. She once more refused, whereupon Feeney took a lame clasp knife out of his pocket, opened it, and stabbed her in the breast, and also just over the right eye. The stab in the breast cut through her dress and into the flesh, and made her feel yeti unwell; and the stab over the eye bled profusely. As soon as he had inflicted those wounds the prisoner turned round and ran down thd street. Information was, howe'ver, given to the police and he was appeehended.—He' was clmmitted to the sessions. ST. PAAIL'S CHURCH, WIDNES. LAYING OFTHE MENltettlAts PRESENTATION to MR. T. S. TIMMIS. The ceremony of laying the memorial stone of St. Paul's Church took place on Tuesday afternoon, in the presence of a large assemblage of people. The erection of this church forms part of a scheme for the extension of church accom- modation in Widnes, which has been under consideration for many years. Previous to 1856 Widnes was included in the parish of Farnworth, hut the rapid increase of popula- tion consequent upon the establishment of chemical works in the neighbourhood rendered a more direct spiritual over- sight necessary; and in that year the parish church of St. Mary, in Waterloo-road, was greeted. The inadequacy of this unsightly structure to accommodate the church-going population of the rising town, was in a few years apparent. The 3,000 inhabitants in 1850 had increasel to nearly 20,000 in 1870, and the Rev. Mr. Whitelegge, the incum- bent, commenced an agitation for the ereetioa of another church, but no practical result foilmeed. In 1874 the sub- ject was again discussed, ant the manufacturers, with the generosity which always distinguished them when the good of the town is involved, promised £6,000 towards a scheme for the erection of two churches, the payment of the meney to be spread over a number of years. In public meeting assembled th parishioners decided that the first church should be ete c'ed at Halton View, in the parish of Farnworth, and the second at A subsequent period at Anderson's corner, Widnes-road, in the parish of Widnes. The church of St. Ambrose was thereupon com- menced, and at a cost of upward of £5,000, was completed in 1879, and will shortly be consecrated. While this editice was being raised the proposed church at Anders in'e corner was kept in vie v, the committee of the Extension scheme having reserved £3,000 to defray the cost of its building. Previously the owner of the Leigh estate had promised 1,000 yards of land as a site for a new church at Widnes, but it was not until 1881 that this promised was fulfilled, and in August of that year Mrs. Leigh generously made the 1,000 yards an acre. Tee Executive Committee (consisting of the Rev. J. Wright-Williams (vicar of Widnes), the Rev. George Bond (vicar of Farnworth), Messrs. T. S. Timmis, H. W. Deacon, J. Brock, Major Cross, H. Brun- ner, G. Pilkington, J. Matthews, T. Balme, L. Kilcross, G. Rogerson, J. T. Allen, and James Hurst) at once took steps to transfer the land to the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, and this accomplished the committee secured plans of an edifice estimated to cost £B,OOO from Mr. H. Shelmerdine, architect, of Liverpool. Towards this large sum only £3,503 had been obtained, and, after much earnest conference, the committee decided to only erect the nave and aisle. The parishioners were strongly opposed to this idea, and the committee bowing to their desires undertook to erect the whole of the church with the exception of the tower, and building operations were commenced at Mid - summer. Toe new church will be cruciform in shape, and will ba built in the early English style. It is estimated to accommodate 750 people. 'The walls will be of picked gray bricks, relieved by red brick- bands and terracotta string courses and dressings. At the south-east corner it is proposed to place a tower, rising to a height of 90 feet; while at the south-west corner an open porch of bold design whl be built, the spandrel over the in- ternal doorway having e terracotta panel, designed with the cross and emblems of the Evangelists. Thnwest end will have two-light windows, while a decorated rose win- dow in the gable will be flanked on either side by bold tourelles. The internal length of the nave will be 85 feet 3 inches, consisting of five bays; the chancel and transept will measure 36 feet in length and 24 feet in width; while the total internal length will be 121 feet 3 inches. The total width of the church between the aisle walls is estimated at 49 feet 2 inches. The chancel is to be 24 feet wide, and the nave between the piers 24 feet 6 inches. The width of the aisles is to be 10 feet 5 inches. The nave columns will be of red Ruabon stone, with alternate octagen piers and moulded capitals and bases, and will greatly en- hance the beauty of the interior. The arches will be built with moulded bricks, and the arcade of red pressed bricks with terracotta bands. Above this will rise a row of elevating lights with terracotta linings. Between these windows terracotta shafts spring from corbels in an orna- mental band at the end of the clerestory sills. The roof principals will have curbed ribs, and high .pitched rafters springing from shafts. The underside of the spars will be boarded, stained, and varnished. There will be excellent ventilation. The floor will be finished with wood block paving in geometrical pattern under the seating, while the aisles will be tiled and furnished with iron hot air gratings of ornamental design. The seating will be of pitchpine. varnished. As we have previously in- timated, Mr. El. Shelmerdine is the architect.; the work is being carried out by Messrs. Morrison and Sons, of Waver- tree; and the red tiles and terra colts are beingsupplied from the works of Mr. J. C. Edwards, of Rnabon. It is important to state that none of the seats in the church will be appro- priated. The erection is already pretty well advanced, and a good idea of the fine proportions of the edifice obtained, and we venture to affirm that when completed it will be one of the finest chucrches in the town. The ceremony NVAI announced to commence at three o'clock, and by that hour the interior of the walls erected was crowded, while hundreds of people gathered round the building, it being computed that 2,000 persons were present. The following c:ergy took pert in the proceedine. :—The Ven. Archdeacon of Warrington, Revs. J. Wright-Williams (vicar of Widnes), Geo. Bond (vicar of Fern worth), J. C. Brown (vicar of Ditton), J. W. Diggle (rural dean), W. Preston (vicar of Holy Trinity, Rancordy' S. A. Spooner and J. Holden (curates of Farnwortn), R. Edwards and D. Llewellyn (citrates, Runcorn.) Amongst those present were— Mr. and Mrs. T. S. Thninis and Miss 'Finvnis, Messrs. F. H. Gossage, J.P., John Brock, J P., G. Pilkington, J. P., H. W. Deacon, E. Carey, W. W. Gossage, Mr. and Mrs. J. B. Imison, Mrs. and Miss Bond, L. Kilcross, J. Matthews, Mr. and Mrs. James White, W. Treacy, senior, F. H. Pankhuret, • G. H. Denby, J. C. Crawford, Mr.aud Mrs. Fowler, Mr. and Mrs. J. Hough, Mr. and Mrs. Heyes, S. B. Stringer, Mr, Mrs., and Miss Kershaw, Mr. and Mrs. F. Neil, Mrs. C. Neil, Mrs. G. Treacy, Thorpe, F. Cave, T. Atherton, Mrs. Lea, A. Lord, &c. The proceedings commenced with the hymn, "The Church's one foundation is Jesus Christ her Lord," after which the Rev. J. W. Digele read the appointed lesson. Prayer was then offered by the Rev. J. Wright-Williams. Mr. John Matthews. a member of the executive committee, ...placed a bottle containing the local papers beneath the stone.—Mr. J. B. Imistag cone forward, and addressing Mr. Timmis, said it was n unusual on an occasion like the pre- sent to invite a stranger to perform the ceremony he ( Mr. Timmis) was about to perform, but the Organising Com- mittee were unanimous in their desire to ask him, and ne e saw around him people who, he was sure, would readily . allow that upon no one better than Mr. Timmis could the shay have more fittingly fallen. (Hear, hear.) He held in his hand an illuminated address signed by over 400 sub- scribers, and he might there say that the silver trowel, about to be banded to him, was the result of many small sub- scriptions from many admirers. The add-rees read as follows:— To T. Sutton TittIMIS. Mg.—Dear Sir,—We, the undersigned parishioners of St. Mary's, Widues, having loog been the silent recipients of your sympathy and substan ial help, desire to place on record how sincerely we think you for having at all times so generously come forward to assist us in the accom- plishment of the many and urgent works we have from time to time berm called upon to undertake. When all our schemes have been met by you with so much kindness. it would per- haps be difficult to single out examples. But wheresoever our difficulty has presented itself—whether in the shape of arrears of grount rent, or new boundary wall at the Vicarage, renova- ting our church. enlarging our sChoolz, the curates' fund, your kind-heartedness and generosity have very largely contributed to a successful issue. Still more sensible are we of your deep Interest in Widnes Church extension particularly in the erec- tion of St. Paul's, and your consent to lay this stone to-day fills us with sincere gratification. Whilst asking you to accept from as this expression of hearts, we pray God that health, happiness. and comfort may long be yours. and that the benacient and ever-widening result of your kindness, the only reward we venture to think that in this world you will care for, may be seen by you with increasing clearness as the years roll on.—We are, dear sir, most sincerely, JOHN B. IMISON. LEWIS KILCROSS, churchwardens; JAMES WHITE, JOHN MATTHEWS, lay representatives. Then follow 421 signatures. The address which was in tge form of an album had been sapplied by Mr. J. Hough, of Waterloo-road. It was handsomely bound in red morroceo, and bore the following inscription on the exterior :—s* Pre- sented to T. Sutton Timmis, Esq., on the occasion of laving the memorial stone of St. Paul's ChurcheOctobsr 30, 1883." The address itself, metheval in style, is pre-eminently a work of art, end proclaims our townsman, Mr. J. B. unison, who executed it, an artist of the pen of great capabilities. It is written in German text and Old English, chastely illuminated, and in the centre is a fac-simile of the memorial stone, while at the left hand corner is a faithful pen and ink sketch of SL Paul's Church. The trowel, a handeo.ne piece of silver workmanship from Messrs. Elkinuton, of Liverpool, was enclosed in an elegant case. Timers was also handed to Mr. Timmis a mallet and Nuare made of black ebnny by Mr. Dixon, a workman at Messrs. Gossage'e es- tablishment. Mr. Timmis, who seemed much affected, then laid the stone, which bore the following inscription in gold letters :—" To the glory of God. Church of St. Paul. This Stone was laid by Thomas Sutton Timmis, October 30, 18832' He then faced the audience, saying, "In the faith of Jesus Christ we place this memorial stone of the church of St. Paul, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen.. An appropriate hvmm was then sung, and Archdeacon Bardsley read prayers. Mr. T. SUTTON TIMMS, who was received with enthu- siastic applause, said he felt almost overwhelmed with the kindness they had shown him that day. What little he bad done for the extension of church work in Widnes did not deserve such a splendid recognition. He should treisure the gifts he had received to the last day of his life, and he hoped that his children would also traaeure thorn highly. Tee fact that the album and trowel were the results ot sub- scriptions limited to a small amount was highly gratifying, aeld he could not express to them how much he felt their kindness. Perhaps it would not be out of place to say a few words on that occasion about this church. He was afraid that many of them began to think that the church would aTways remain a project. The proposal had been before them now for a great many years, and they had -waited, hoped, and prayed for it, and it seemed as if it would never come. But he thought it was not altogether an unmixed evil that they had waited; for he believed that bad the church been built at an earlier day it would not lave been of anything like the same noble proportions they saw it that day assuming. He thought this was worth waiting for. (Hear, hear.) Something ought also to be I said ha recognition of the services of many gentlemen who had contributed so much to the erection of the building. In the first place, he hal:eyed that Mr. Whitelegge, their former most excellent vicar, was the first to suggest a church on that eite, arid t,90,4,VtiV0 Steps to promote the project. As

soon as the plans were drawn out, Mr. Whitelegge was promoted to a much easier position, and one which his labours in Widnee very well deserved, and, although they were sorry to lose him, they all rejoiced at his promotion. That caused. a delay; and the health of Mr. Welsh, the vicar who succeeded him, unfortunately broke down. He was followed by their present most worthy vicar. (Hear, hear.) He need not say anything in the praise of that gen- tleman, but he thought it was due to his energy, and the energy with which he had been able to inspire others, that that church had now become a fact. (Loud applause.) When the committee decided to commence riperations, it was their intention only to build part of the church, as. to use a homely phrase, they had to cut their coat according to their cloth. But the parishioners, when they beard of what was going on, ware not satisfied, and they appointed a deputation to wait np3n the committee, ant point out how very desirable it was that the church should be built in its entirety, except as regarded the tower. But the deputation did a great deal more than that. The deputation most nobly said that if the committee could see their way to build the church they would raise £l,OOO, and amongst working people next day guirantees were o'gainc.d for the whole of • that money. (Applause.) Now, he c tllee that very great energy and zeal. Tuese nettle gifts were from men who were not by any means rich men, and when that £l,OOO was promised the committee didnot hesitate any longer. They decided at once to build the whole cLurch. There were, however, very considerable obligations to be discharg-d, and the committee hoped that with a revival of trade, which was now dawning on the district, and the commencement of new industries in Widnes, that the money to build the church would be forthcoming. He did not doubt but that it would. Let him again thank them for their great kindness to him. He could assure them he should never forget it. (Loud applause.) Archdeacon BARDSLEY then delivered an address. Mr. H. WADS, deacon, proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Timinis and Archdeacon Birdsley for their kindness in giving their services that day. Archdeacon Berdsley, he stid, had taken great interest in the development of the church extensiod scheme. He had been of great, assistanc.±. to Mr. Williams and the various committees, and they owed him their gratitude. Of Mr. Timmis he need sty very little. He wasa gentleman wry well known to all of them, and his actions spoke for themselves. He was sure he might say in the name of those present that they gave him a hearty welcome that day, and that there was no one ' who was more deserving of the honour it was intended to convey in asking him to lay that memorial stone. (Hear, hear.) Ile had been assciated with Mr. Timmis on many committees, some for business affairs, and many on public matters, and he could affirm that Widnes gained by his ability and advice, and he sincerely hoped that he would I live long to see the results of his generosity and to be of use to them. They must remember that although the memorial stone of St. Paul's Church was laid, they cluld not rest from their efforts. There were a great many bricks and other things to be paid for, and they had not money to pay. He knew that those proceedings were not arranged principally with the view of getting money; the mein object was to lay the memorial atone and honour Mr. Timmis. Still there was no reason why those who were disposed might not sebscribe that day, and he sincerely hoped they would. Mr. Deacon then spoke of the energetic labours of the %letr in eulogistic terms, and the generous help he had received front numerous parishioners, and resumed his seat amid warm applause. . Mr. JAMES WHITE seconded the motion in an appropriate speech. He paid a compliment to the labours of the vicar, who, he said, ought to have the assistance of two curates, , for whom they could find plenty of work. He enumerated the many movements which had recently been undertaken in the parish, and he concluded by wishing Mr. Timmis long life to see the results of the work he had done that day. (Applause.) Three cheers were then heartily given for Mr. Timmis, who briefly expressed his acknowledgment. The afternoon's proceedings concluded with a collection in aid of the building fend, the amount realised being £93 Bs., which included a donation of £:5O from an anony- mous contributor. - _________

WIDNES CRICKET CLUB- The annual meeting was held last evening in the Simm's Cross Hotel, under the presidency of Mr. E. Carey. There were present the Rev. George Band, Messrs. H. Wade, Deacon, James White, W. H. Longton, Kyle, Cozier, Pritchard. Sadler, W. Oakden, Brown, W. Rey, Sayce, Watson, Young, and Colquitt. Mr. PRITCHARD, the treasurer, read his annual report, in which he stated that the eqaenses during the past season had been reducei to a marked degree, every item of ex- penditure being under the previous year. As a result of this 1 economy, the adverse balance from the year 1882 had been reduced by £l6. There were subscriptions outstanding from last season to tha amount of about £4O, but he thought there would be sufficient of this sum received to wipe off the deficiency. The total receipts amounted to 99 15s 81. and the expenses to £75 lie 81, leaving a balance of £24 4s. The deficit now stood at £22 2s 7d. Mr. Pritchard moved the adoption of the report. Mr. DEACON seconded the motion, and referred with pleasure to the satisfactory statement that had been sub- mitted, and made a few remarks upon the general state of the club. There was every reason to believe the deficit would be wiped off; the ground was in very fair condition, but the cricketing apparatus would have to be renewed next season.

The report was adopted. On the motion of Mr. James WHITE, seconded by Mr. Coeclurrr, Mr. F. A. Gossage was re-appointed president, and Major Cross, Rev. George Bond, Messrs. E. K. Maspratt, and E. Carey vice-presidents. Mr. PRITCHARD was unanimously re-elected treasurer, on the motion of Mr. KYLE, seconded by Mr. MOORE. Mr. Jemes WHITE moved the appointment of Messrs. H. W. Deac m and Colquitt as hon. secretaries, and spoke in flattering terms of Mr. Deacon's services to the club in the ptst. Mr. COZIER sacended the motion, which was unanimously carried. The cordial thanks of the meeting were accorded to Mr. W. EL Longton, the retiring hon. secretary, on the motion of the chairman. Thanks were also accorded to the pre- sident. vice-presidents, officers, an! committee; Mr. Frit- cteerd and Mr. Deacon responding. The last gentleman retnarlsol that the committee had decided that it would be better not to hold the annual dinner this year, as in the past the interest manifested in the event had been very slight. In place of this annual fixture, Mr James White, an energetic number of the committee, had promised to organise a concert, which would be held shortly, and the support of all the members was solicited. The election of the committee was then proeeeded with. The Average Committee reportel that they had been un— able to get out the 2nd eleven bowling averages, the score sheets being very impecfect, eod suggested that next season new score books should be obtained and arrangements made to ensure a regular and co,rect record being in de. The first eleven prize bat had been won by Mr. C. IL Watson, with an average of 19 5 runs per inning. The first eleven bowling • prize bat had been won by Mr. IL R. Colquitt with an average of 184 runs ier wicket. The second eleven batting prize had been won by Mr. W. Oakden with an average of 19.1 runs per wicket. The junior club had been a success, and would form in time a grand recruiting force for the first end second elevens. Of the first team matches six had been won, three lost, and seven were drawn, most of which were in favour of the Widnes Club.. Of the second eleven matches one WAS won, one lost, and four drawn. while the jeeiors won eight, lost five, and tied once. These results were, on the whole, an improvement compared with .the previous season.
THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC AT WIDNES.

It is gratifying to be able to announce that smalipex is being rapidly eradicated from the town At present there are only three cases under the care of a medic 11 attendant, and these patients are in a fair way to recover. The disease has not spread since last Saturday ; and when the patieets are isolated in the tents, which are expected to be ready for occupation to-day, there is every reason to believe the disease will entirely disappear. The tents have been ereeed under the superintendence of Mr. Higginson, the surveyor, who has been aided by the advice of Dr. O'Keeffe, the chairman of the Health Committee. The friends and rela- tives of patients need have no fear in permitting them to b,' treated in the tents, which, are very warm and comfortable structures. They have double-skin walls, and a boarded floor, raised 18 inches from the ground. '3 he large tent provides accommodation for 12 persons, and the smaller one, which it is intended to use as a convalescent hospital, can be used by 8 patients. The public will not be allowed within 126 feet of the host:Oats, to which water and gas have been laid, and sewers made, and all appliances necessary have been provided. The total number of people affected with the disease since the outbreak is 22, of whom two have died. All cause for alarm is now at an end.
ATTACKING THE BLUK RIBBON ARMY AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr: John Brock and Mr. F. H. Ceossae.e, John Tansev, a respectab:e- looking mac. was brought up in custody charged with having on Saturday night been drunk and disorderly, land also woh aseaulting P.S. Robinson and P.C. Collier, and Walter Elutes, "Captain" of the Blue Ribbon Army.— Inspector Wood said if the Bench were satisfied after hear- ing the evidence, he should ask them to inflict the highest sentence in their power.—P.S. Robinson said that about half-past eleven on Saturday night he and P.C. Cellier were pissing down Waterloo-road near the Railway Hotel, when the prisoner stepped from a dark place and struck witness on the head. He then struck Collier, but the constables overpowered him, but the aid of two other constables had to be obtained before he could be removed to the polce station, he was so violent.—P.C.'s Collier and Barker col-- roborated.—Walter Eltnes, " Captain" of the Blue Ribhee Army, said about half-past six on Saturday night, whi's', the Army was passing Hutchinson-street, near the Public Hall, the prisober rushed into the ranks to seize the fleg. In doing so be knocked witness's hat off.—lnspector Wood seid the prisoner was a very bad character, and had been to times convicted for various offences. In September, 1872. he was tried at the Quarter Sessions, and sentenc-d to 12 months' imprieenment for assaulting the police.—Mr. Broce said the charge of drunkenness had been withdrawn. Fir each assault on the constables he would be sent to gel er six weeks, and for the assault on 'Captain" Elmer; he would be fined 5s and costs, or seven days in default, neakine in ill I#l weeks' imprisonment.

DEATH Or Mil. RIMNIER, ST. HELENS. - On Saturday last, 'Mr. John Rimmer, chief clerk and assistant registrar in connection with St. Helens County Court, died after a very short illness. Mr. Rimmer was 59 years of age, and had occupied his poshion at the county court for about 13 years. and had been altogether 47 years in the service of Mr. Ansdell, the registrar. He was first taken ill on the Toes- law previous to his death whilst engaged at his usual avo- cation, and was attended by Dr. Twyford up to Saturday. when he died. The funeral took place on Tuesday, aid was at tended by 2d m2mbers of the Rose of Sharon Lodge of Oldfellows, of which the deceased had been permanent sec- retary for more than thirty years ; Councillors Belsher and Hanson ; Nit% W. ryrer, Mr. Massey, and other officials con- nected with the county court, and several other gentlemen. The body was interred in a vault in the churchyard con- neco-d with the Parish Church, the Rev. Canon Carr and the Rev. Mr. Thomas officiiting at the service. Tba "Dead march in Saul " was played on the organ by the organist of the church, Mr. Woodward. A considerable number of people witnessed the List rites in the churchyard.

The CLERK presented the following return, showing the cest of pauper lunatics for each of the last five years ended September, 1883 :-1879, gross cost of maintenance, £1,977 4s ld, amount of Government grant, £775, repayment from Unions, relatives, &c, £92 3s id, nett cost, £l,llO Is ; 1860, grass cost, £2,070 9s 31, Government grants, £833 Bs. repayment; £135 is 01, nett cost, £1,096 13s 9d; 1881, gross cost, £2,187 6s ; Government grants. £347 He, repay- ments, £229 103 11d, nett cost, £1,109 19s Id ; 1882, gross cost, £1,925 12s sd, Government grants, £7Bl Hs ; repay- ments. £l3O 104 11d, nett, £1,013 5s di ; 1883, gross cost, £2,031 9e 10d, Government grants, £BOB ete, repayments, £175 de lid, nett cost, £1,017 18elld In the year ended Sept., 1882, an extraordinary amount of £3BB was recovered after very lengthened correspondence and controversy by the Clerk in the case of Caldwell, lunatic, which reduces the actual nett cost for the year to £025 5s 61. The repay- ment was, however, in respect of previous years, so is not entered above. Amount received for all paupers from Government during the past year, £1,321 10s 8d; 1873, £268; increase, £1,056 108 81. POOR-LAW CONFERENCE. The Board agreed that the Chairman and Clerk should atten4 the Poor-law Conference in London in December, and, on the suggestion of Mr. Derbyshire, they were directed at the same time to visit Broedmoor Asylum to see the lunatic paupers the Board had there.—Mr. CALDWELL asked if much was gained by sending representatives to the Con- ference ?—Major CARTWRIGHT: Very little.—Mr. CALD- WELL: Then it is money thrown away —The CHAIRMAN: We mast make it a great deal of good.—The CLERK ohserved that when the Chairman and himself went to the Conference he sepposed they would not venture to say a word, but would gather susetreetions from the speeches of others.— Major CARTWRIGHT: And if it does very Bale good, it will do no harm. div.head: LYIIII LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LYIIII LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly ineeting of this Board was held at the Board-roo.n. on Thursday evening. There were present : Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Rogers, Gibbon, Forster, Woolley, Thomason, Appleton, Ridgway (clerk), and Mul- lard (assistant clerk). .

THE COST or THE SEWERAGE WORKS. Mr. THOMASON, referring to the minute of the special meeting, held on the 19th ult., respecting the Board's ap- plication for a further loan of £1,200, asked whether that amount would complete °the whole scheme.—TAe CHAIR- MAN : Well, we hope so.—Mr. THOMASON thought the Board was spending far too much money. They had employed engineers to prepare plans and an estimate of the cost of tho work, and now that estimate was being exceeded. There was something wren he thought, and he would like to know who was morally responsible for the plans. He would think it was not altogether straight unless seele explanation was given.— The CHAIRMAN said there had been a detailed account given of the whole in ttter. It was well known that esti- mates were often exceeded.—Mr. THOMASON said that with- out a fill explanation he would not he a party to borrow- ing £1,200 more.—The CHAIRMAN. said that a very detailed account was prepared by the clerk and laid before the Board ,at its last meeting. Mr. Thomason knew very well that the compensation claims had been very great, and had far ex- ceeded whit was at first contemplated.—Mr.THomAsoN said that the. special meeting being on a Friday he was unable to attend it. It wae just what he said some time since, that the rates woald be increased to such an extent that the ratepayers NvJuld not be able to bear the weight of them, and ; would be driven out of the town.—The ENGINEER said that it was impossible to get out a 'scheme and foresee everything. The additional work had been sanctioned from time to time at the Board's meetings. The alterations between the canal and the trill, which were made to aveid compensatien, the railway culverts, and several minor .nitters had considerably swollen the esti- mates.—Mr. ROGERS Said it Appeared to him from an exami- nation of the accounts that the descrepancy was caused by the compensations. The estimate.d coqt had been but very little exceeded in the work proper. The railway company claiming to have two culverts made had greatly increased , the cost.—The CHAIRMAN sail that Mr. Thomason could se the accounts, and he thought he would find they were I satisfactory.—The matter then drepped.'

div.head: PROGRESS OF. THE SEWERLGE WORII.
div.p: THE PROGRESS OF. THE SEWERLGE WORII.

Messrs. WiLso-rg and 114HLLINER Eoard's engineers) reported that the principal work ce at L:-.-min during the last month bad been the completion of the alterations under the canal and between the canal and the flour mill. The remaining short length up to the bridge, together with the automatic flushing chamber at the juncture of Eagle Brow had yet to be done. The railway culvert for the Lymrn branch was complete, and the culvert through •the railway in Statham-iane was also in progress. The ploughing of the 3utfall land had been delayed owing to the recent wet weather, but would be in hand in the course of a few days. In accordance with the Board's instructions they had seen Messrs. Hall and Ardern in reference to the sewer through their property. All they required was that the ex- isting sewers crossing the private road should be connecteJ, and junctions provided for present and future requirements. That was E more taan would have had to be done in the ordinary w.:7..--The CHAIRMAN-remarked that Mr. Ardern 4nd Mr. Hall bad written to the Board saying that they would not Irak any claim for compensation if the require- lints jus;', men, hued were carried out.
