SUPPOSED BURGLARY AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday night the George and Dragon Inn, Egerton- street, was entered by robbers, and several rooms ransacked. The thieves effected an entrance to the house by removing ftquare of glass in the back window, and succeeded in carying off considerable property. The police are in- vestigating the matter.—During the earlier part of the week a robbery was committed at the Egerten Arms. Bridge- street, a gold watch and other articles, worth altogether about £B, being taken.

_ DRUNKENNESS AT RAINEJRD. ames Whalley and Henry Bradshaw were each fined, at the St. Helen's County Petty Sessions, on Monday, for having been drunk, ttc., at itainford, the former ss, and the latter 76 6d. and costs. ALLEGED ILLEGAL HAWKING IN EA.RLESTOWN MARKET. —At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, James Carney, a hawker, was summoned for refusing to pay toll on Earlestown Market-ground on the 22nd September.—Mr. Worsley appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Newton CommisAoners, and stated that the defendant exposed goods for sale in the market at Earlestewn, on the date named, and refused to pay the toll demanded of him, on the ground that he was a licensed hawker and was exempted from toll. ife claimed to be exempted becaus ) having taken out a hawker's license be thought he was entitled to hawk in any place whatever, independent of what market regulations or tolls there might be.—Before the case was farther gone into, the Bench observed that in consequence of what their law clerk said they could not adjudicate upon the case, and it ;Tula be dismissed.

ENTERTAINMENT AT RAINHILL NATIONAL SCHOOL.—OR Wednesday evening Mr. Plummer. of Liverpool, gave two entertainments, entitled, "A night with Uncle Tom and Eva." The entertainment cJnaisted of disgolving views Ws- trating Mrs. Stowe's well-known "Uncle Tom's Cabin," accompanied with appropriate songs and instrumental selec- tions. There were very fair audiences, all seeming pleased with what they had seen.

A CHILD BURNT AT PRESCOT.—Yesterday, a little boy named Richard Wood, three years ef age, was fright- fully burnt. The child's mother had occasion to leave the house for a few minutes. and during her absence the child, in trying to reach something which Mrs. Wood had left preparing for dinner, came in contact with the fire and wee soon enveloped ia flatnes. In awful fright the poor child ran into the street, where happily a gentleman who was passing. acting with great presence of mind, enwrapped the little sufferer in his great coat, and so extinguished the flames. Dr. Green, who was immediately sent for, promptly appeared and rendered all necessary aid. Little hopes are given of the child's recovery.

SUNDAY FISHERS IN TROUBLE—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, John Heaton and Michael Gornall, both of Haydock, were charged with damaging shrubs an 4 grass on the grounds of Colonel George McCorqu, dale, at Newton —The defendants pleaded guilty.—Mr. Moore, of Warrington (who appeared to prosecute). said thedefen- dants were caught on Colonel McCorcpindale's grounds fish- ing in the Mere. For some time past people had been in the habit of coming to the neighbourhood on the Sunday and climbing over the wall of Colonel MeCorquodale's garden, and thereby damaging the shrubs a•Pxl trees. They wished to put a stop to the practice as it was a grat nnisance.—Superintendent Jackson said the two men had given wrong names, and asked them why they did so.—The defendant Heaton : Because I thowt th' police would'nt know us.—A tine of ss. and costs was imposed upon each.

A RUNAWAY HORSE AT NEWTON: SERIOUS ACCIDENT. —On Thursday afternoon, last week, a serious and alarming accident occurred at Newton, by which John Cain, em- ployed at the Vulcan Foundry, and living in Newton, was badly injured, so much so as to incapacitate him from fol- lowing his e:nploytnent. It appears that Cain, in company with Henry Hibbert, butcher, George Burrows, licensed victualler, and another person—a trainer of do.tts—was returning from the Haydock Park coursing meeting and hired a cab belonging to Ward Burks, of fitdme, Manchester, and driven by Anthony* Hines, a lad 15 or 16 years of ag,,, employed by Burks. Aftea getting a little distance from Haydock Park gates the horse became very rest:ve—it is stated through the driver whipping it. It showed signs of taking fright, and the lad Hines jumped off his seat, whi!e Cain and Hilbert, who rode outside, seized the reins. An attempt to pull up the horse was made, but the reins brnike, and as the animal dashed along the road at full speed Hibbert and Cain were thrown into the roadway. flibbert escaped with a cut on the back of hie head and a severe shaking, but Cain sustained serious injuries, and on Drt'' Patterson,. of Earlestown, subsequently examining him it was found that one of his arms was broken near to the shoulder. The animal continued on ita mad career towards Newton, the. greatest fears being .felt for the men inside the cab. When entering Newton, near the Oak Tree Inn, the horse ran tit& cab straight against one of the trees planted on the footpath, smashing and twisting the iron guard. A few yards further the horse ran full tilt against the tree and iron guard near the entrance to the police station, 'and these were also smashed; while before the animal could be brought to a standstill a third tree and guard had been smashed. The driver of a horse and cab coming in an opposite direction saw the d ingerous position of affair., and jumping from his box resolutely seized the .runaway animal and stopped it, The two inmates of the cab were glad to leave; and it is a' wonder how they escaped unhurt. P.S. Commins, who happened to be in his station at the time, took charge of the horse and cab, and on the owner coming to claim them he promised to pay all expenses and make good the damage which had been caused. The occurrence, as might be supposed, caused considerable alarm and excitement. We understand that Cain is pro- gressing as satisfactorily as can be expected, though it will be some time before he can return to his work. He is still being attenthd by Dr. Patterson.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—A serious breakdown occurred on the London and North-Western Railway mein line from Crewe to Liverpool on Wednesday night. The 4-40 pm. fast goods train from London to Carlisle was running past Winsford when an axle of one of the wagons broke, and five of the trucks were thrown off the line; doing consider. able damage to the permanent way. Both lines - were blocked, and the passenger traffic was completely stopped The trains from Liverpool, Warrington, and the North were worked via Chester. CHESTER FARMERS' CLUB.—At a meeting of this club on Saturday, Mr. John Roberts, of Saltnev, presiding, the secretary (Mr. Beecroft) stated that Lord Richard Grosvenor, to whom he had forwarded the resolutions ot the club con- demning the Lords' amendments to the Government Land Bill, had replied as follows:—" House of Commons, August 21, 1883.—Dar Sir, I had much pleasure in banding Mr. Dodson this evening the document which you kindly sent me giving the views of the Chester Farmers' Club on the amendments made by the Honse of Lords in the Agricul- tural Holdings Bill. I am, sir, yours faithfully, RICHARD Gnosymore."—Mr. Henry Tollemache, to whom the reso- lutions had also been forwarded, wrote, statine, that he had sent them on at once to Mr. Dodson. As regarded the first resolution, it had his he erty approval; but he could not but feel that the second resolution was expressed in somewhat stronger terms.—Mr. Scotson, of A;gburth, read an interest- ing paper on the subject of tillage, and in the course of a discussion which followed the opinion was expressed that in the course of time the use of the steam plough would become much more general than at present. The Speaker notified in last night's Gazette his intention ' to issue a writ for Limerick election six days hence. Messrs. Hollinshead; Tetley, and Co., a long-establishedl firm of cotton brokers in Liverpool, and chief creditors of i Mr. Ranger, have suspended payment. The liabilities are estimated at £lOO,OOO. A collision occurred yesterday in Shields harbour between the steamer Cilendowe, while proceeding up the harbour, and her Majesty's Customs cutter Active, the latter being much damaged. I The late Bishop of Natal's will has been proved by his son, Mr. F. E. Colenso. The lamented prelate has left little beyond the proceeds of the three English policies which form the bulk of his property in England. Suraors FIRE.—At six o'cleck yesterday morning the . outfitting establishment owned by Mr. Samuel Barret, Con- way-square, Newtonards, was completely destroyed by fire. ; The damTge is estimated at over £l,OOO. All the family. I • escaped. A SENSATIONAL CASE.—It is stated that the cause celeb-e I of Nunn v. Nunn, involving the ownership of the family I jewels, about which some extraordinary disclosures were recently made, will be taken on appeal from the Irish Master of the Rolls to the House of Lords. Among the cases listed for trial in Dublin during the pre- sent sittings is that of County Inspector French, head of the constabulary detective force, against Mr. O'Brien, M.P., editor of United Ire.?and for a libel published in that journal. At Durham yesterday, Peter Bray, militiaman, was chargel with murdering a pitman named Thomas Pyle or Cross-gate Moor, in the spring of last year. It was alleged that the prisoner asked other miners to help him to murder the deceased, because he had been a blackleg at a strike. They declined, but Bray kicked Pyle to death. A tingle woman named M'Carroll was sentenced to four months' hard labour at Sheffield, yesterday, for neglecting her inrant child. It was her custom to leave the child alone in the house whilst she was drinking in the neighbourhood. It was found the other day on a wretched mattress in a cm- dition so weak that it could not take food. It was stated that the child was a living skeleton, ANOTHER GREAT FAILURE.—A petition in liquidation was filed at the London Bankruptcy Court yesterday by George Stanley Derbyshire, trading as merchant and com- mission agent under the firm of John Carver Derbyshire, and Co., John Dalton-street, Manchester, and Carver, London, and also as merchant under the firm of Carver, Derbyshire, and Co., Gibraltar, the liabilities being estimated at £120,000. TIIE STOPPAGE OF CREW CATTLE MRKKET.—The di- rectors of the Crewe cattle market and abattoirs are applying to the Executive Committee of the county authority under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act to remove their restrictions on the importation of Irish cattle into Cheshire. The extensive market and abbattoirs at Crewe hive been entirely closed now for over two months. Should the county authority decline to relax the regulations, an appeal will be made to the Privy Council. MINERS' CONFERENCE AT ROTHERHAM—Delegates repre- senting 141,000 Yorkshire miners met in conference at Rotherham yesterday, and passed resolutions endorsing the action of the Manchester conference. It was decided that all the Yorkshire miners shall give notices for 15 per cent. advance, such notices to terminate on the first making up day in December, nothing less than the unconditional 15 per cent. advance to be accepted. and any offers from individual employers to be submitted to Mr. Pickard, miners' agent at Barnsley. It was stated at the conference that Mr. Bradley, of Featherstone Manor Colliery, and other employers, are prepared to concede the full advance claimed. THE RAILWAY EXPLOSION.—CoIoneI Majendie and Cap- tain Caudhill, Governmeat Inspectors of Explosives, and Dr. Dupree, the eminent analytical chemist, met at Pad- dington yesterday, and took formal evidence respecting the explosion in Praed-street tunnel. The officials in charge of the injured train, one of the passengers, and some officials from Edgware-road station were examined, but for obvious reasons it has been thought necessary to keep the enquiry strictly private. It is, however, understood that no fresh facts of importance were elicited yesterday, and that no sub- stantial clue as to the authors of the outrage or their modes operandi has yet been found. ALLEGED LIBELS.—The Central News Co., Limited, v. Dalziel. Mr. A.M. Sullivan applied yesterday morning, be- fore the Lord Mayor (sitting in his private roam), for a summons against Mr. Dalziel, proprietor, and Mr. W. J. Sinkins, publisher of Judy, for an alleged libel contained in the issue of Judy for 31st October. The libel complained of was contained in the cartoon and certain letterpress sup- plementary to the cartoon, and contained in an article headed " Political Palava," calculated to injure the reputa- tion of the Central News by impeaching the bona fides of their telegrams.—The application was granted.--The Central News Company. Limited. v. Pro- prietors of the Sportsman : A secoud application was made for the issue of a summons against Mr. Charles H. Ashley and Mr. Sidney Smith, proprietors of the Sportsman, for having, in their issue of the 29th September, published an article reflecting on the bona-fides of plaintiffs' telegrams; This application was also granted, and both summonses wilt be heard on Wednesday next. A REMARKABLE FEMALE MISER—An extraordinary dis- covery was made yesterday morning respecting the career of a feminine miser living in a small cottage, at a rental of 3s a week, at Shirley, near Birmingham. The woman in question, who was 83 years ef age, was unmazried, and had for twenty yeus resided at this small dwelling, which con- tained only a few shillings werth of furniture. She lived on the cheapest food procurable. and in order to save exnenses would rarely have a fire or light in her hone. Notwith- standing this she possessed a firm of about 100 acres at Quint3n, several houses at West Bromwich, and, it is stated, other property. Not having gone to receive her rents at West Bromwich last Monday, the cottage was broken into, and the woman was found in a dying condition by the hearth. Mr. Hardwicke, of Solihull, was called in, but the woman remained speechless till yesterday morning, when she died. Stitched up in an .old dress body was found a bank book on Lloyd's lank, showing a credit of £l.lOO. Besides this was a savings bank book, with deposits exceed- ing £lO3. The aged miser is described as being a woman OI very eccentric habits. On both posts to the garden gate was written the Lord's Prayer, to drive off, as she said, persons who wanted to rob her.
